entry.title: [A Life in Board Games] Episode 1: Once You Enter, There Is No Easy Way Back
entry.content:
Since falling into the hobby during the summer after my final year of high school, I have played and collected quite a few board games over the past two years. I have met people online and gone out to play with them several times, encountered all sorts of personalities, and even drawn a few of my roommates into the hobby. I had always wanted to write something about board games, but I could never decide what to say. Then one day someone asked why I liked board games, and I found myself unable to answer. If love at first sight really exists, perhaps that is the reason.


Wooden meeples from Carcassonne

This series will look at classic board games I have played, one per installment, from the perspective of someone somewhere between a beginner and a veteran. Along the way, I will revisit parts of my own life in board gaming and mix in a few scattered reflections. Whether it draws more people into the hobby is not really my concern, and this is not meant to be an advertising post recommending board games either. (Board gamers are still a niche group, unlike Dota players.)

A conventional introduction to something new usually begins with its origins, development, and important people and events. I do not think that is necessarily the best approach, since you rarely begin to understand something by learning where it originated. Still, here is a quotation.

Modern board games originated in Germany and have been popular in Europe and North America for decades. People make friends through games. Overseas, board games cover subjects such as war, trade, culture, art, urban development, and history, and most use printed components accompanied by finely crafted models. They are face-to-face games that place great emphasis on communication. Board games are therefore an excellent way to connect during family leisure, gatherings with friends, and even breaks from business. They arrived in China at the beginning of this century and became popular among white-collar workers.

(The solemn-looking paragraph above was copied from Baidu Baike.)

If you walk into a board-game café today, you will notice a few very strange things—at least in most of them. Shelves are packed with all kinds of games, yet the customers usually play nothing but Legends of the Three Kingdoms. Many titles are opened only a handful of times all year. The owner may not even be able to explain their rules properly, or may teach them unprofessionally while omitting important rules. Imagine that you are a beginner entering a café like this. By the time you leave, will you have learned only Legends of the Three Kingdoms—or, in the worst case, come to believe that it represents all board games? If you are unlucky and the staff leave out even more rules, one player may become absurdly overpowered while everyone else has nothing to do, making the whole game dull. Worse still, you might be eliminated before you understand what is happening and have to sit around waiting. That would certainly reduce your interest in board games, especially when a newcomer has little enthusiasm to begin with. So I think people who want to enter the hobby today should not begin with Legends of the Three Kingdoms. I will explain why in detail when I write about that game.

Some readers may now wonder: everyone around me knows only Legends of the Three Kingdoms, and that is what most people in cafés are playing. If it is unsuitable for beginners, why are the cafés full of its fans? Are they all experienced board gamers who disdain simple games? To answer that, we have to look at the development of China's board-game industry. I first encountered board games—or rather, Legends of the Three Kingdoms, since I did not know what board games were then—during the summer after high school. Yoka was extremely shrewd. It spotted an untouched market in China and adapted the classic game Bang! with Chinese elements, opening up the domestic market. Its characters drew on both history and Romance of the Three Kingdoms, its abilities matched them remarkably well, and its card-drafting mechanics created variety. All of these factors helped make it a commercial success. (As an aside, if we set aside what it borrowed from Bang!, the standard edition of Legends of the Three Kingdoms is undeniably a model of successful design.) But it is not suitable for someone just beginning to play board games. This helped produce the spectacle we later saw: board-game cafés sprang up all over Shanghai like mushrooms after rain, then quickly failed and closed one after another. Those that remain today must be doing something right. Legends of the Three Kingdoms was not the only cause, but it was one of them. Here we have to mention its most important mechanism: Variable Player Powers. This mechanism certainly makes players feel that they are inhabiting distinct roles and identities, but it also increases complexity tremendously. A first-time player cannot possibly understand every character's abilities or know each character's role in the game. Beginners are also unfamiliar with basic rules, such as how judgment cards work, so play can head in a direction entirely different from what the designers intended. Yoka had actually considered this problem: the first-edition rulebook instructed everyone to use blank characters for their first game so that they could learn the rules. But once people are offered a choice, will they really choose the boring option? Because of this design, many newcomers spend hours in a café without discovering the fun, then leave in a hurry with a worse impression of board games than before. The café loses customers as a result. And we know that board games cannot be played alone; their appeal emerges through interaction with friends. The minority who enjoy their first few sessions of Legends of the Three Kingdoms then cannot find anyone to play with. What can they do? Yoka was clever: it developed an online client so everyone could play over the internet. At that point the game arguably changed its nature, but the move was very successful and cultivated a huge population of Legends of the Three Kingdoms players—note that I did not say board-game players. Returning to the question at the beginning of this paragraph, the game's dominant position in China's board-game market and the advantages of its online edition mean that many players know it but know nothing about board games more broadly. That is how the scene described above came to be.

Having analyzed the state of the board-game industry, its problems, and their causes, let me explain how I entered the hobby. Like many people, I discovered board games through Legends of the Three Kingdoms. What made my experience different was that I met some friends on a forum and went out to play with them several times. At first I simply felt a little silly knowing only one game, so I casually searched for board games online. Before I knew it, I was hooked. The first game that truly showed me the charm of board games was probably Chinatown. It ranked only 207th on BGG, but its rules are extremely simple and it gives players enormous freedom. Most of the game revolves around negotiation; deals may involve two people or several, randomness plays a substantial role, and even a beginner has a reasonable chance of winning. In short, it can become wonderfully lively.

(The game board)

The game follows a group of Chinese immigrants opening businesses in Chinatown in pursuit of the American Dream. The player with the most assets at the end wins. There are only six rounds, and a zodiac wheel in the lower-right corner of the board marks the current round.

(Property cards)

(Shop tiles)

At the beginning of each round, players randomly draw property cards and keep some of them, representing the lots they own, then place markers of their color on the corresponding spaces on the board. They also draw a fixed number of shop tiles. Players may build shops from their hand on property they own, or trade property, shops, cash, and anything else they possess with other players. There are no restrictions on the form of a deal: it may involve several parties, and players can even buy on credit. In short, anything you own can be traded. When nobody wishes to make another deal, the round ends and everyone earns income from the shops they have opened. A number in the lower-right corner of each shop tile shows the minimum connected group required to complete that type of business. Incomplete shops also earn money, just less of it.

(The game at the end)

What attracts me most about Chinatown is its clear, simple rules, its minimal memory requirements, and the fact that nobody suffers the embarrassment of being eliminated early as in Legends of the Three Kingdoms. In fact, most board games do not eliminate players early. You can plan a deal with one player while disrupting someone else's negotiations. Eloquence and a talent for persuasion certainly provide an advantage, but as the saying goes, appeal to emotion, explain with reason, and entice with profit. With a good view of the whole game, precise calculation, and effective use of public information, you can still win. Everything is public except the cash in each player's hand—and with a good memory, even that is effectively public. On the other hand, if fortune favors you and you draw both adjacent properties and matching shop tiles, everything I just said is irrelevant. You are going to win.

Board-game reflection: if you do not have unbeatable luck, think one step further than everyone else.

PS: I am not good at this game. I have never won when playing away from home.

PPS: Do you know how a three-way trade differs from completing two separate two-way trades?

Next episode: Small World—Fight to Sustain the War, or Settle Down and Prosper?

entry.title: [titanxxh Plays Chinese Paladin 5] 1. A Botched Preorder and One-Hour First Impressions
entry.content:
Baiyou, do you even know what a preorder is?

The game is already on sale and mine still has not arrived. What a rip-off. Some people who ordered through 3DM already have theirs, while those of us who used the official preorder are still suffering.

Back to the point.

I initially turned on every visual effect, but the game stuttered a little. Sure enough, my computer was not up to it. With no better option, I disabled anti-aliasing, which helped a lot. After a short and rather baffling opening animation, the game began. The protagonist is still dressed like a wild man, but this time he is already a junior bandit—or rather, the “crown prince” destined to inherit the bandit enterprise someday...

After a brief scene, the familiar hero-rescues-beauty setup appeared. The opponents were five monkeys. Seriously, could they be any weaker? I checked their attributes, threw out one skill, and the monkey vanished. Just as I was celebrating, another blasted monkey appeared. I assumed it worked like Chinese Paladin 4, where too many enemies had been pulled to display at once and replacements appeared when one died. So I tried a normal attack. The hero was impressive: twin blades flashed and the monkey dropped. Huh? What was happening? Yet another one appeared. Was this very first battle supposed to be unwinnable? Chinese Paladin 4 had the unbeatable Kui Zhao, and now Chinese Paladin 5 expected me to lose to an endless stream of monkeys...

Another cutscene followed, and the hero went up the mountain to gather herbs. I could live with a camera that could not rotate, but it moved along with the protagonist and made me dizzy. Who thought that was a good idea? Never mind; perhaps I would get used to it. At the first boss, the male lead told the female lead to stay back. As in earlier installments, the woman who looks gentle and fragile is often the stronger one. She rejected him with one short, forceful “No,” and they fought side by side. The enormous boss was helpless against a hero with a full energy gauge, which made me question Chinese Paladin 5's difficulty.

I will not recount the plot in detail after that. It was much like a television drama: the wealthy young lady was summoned home, an argument broke out along the way, and the groundwork was laid for later developments. I did not continue playing afterward because of that cursed database assignment...

This has turned into a chronological plot summary full of spoilers. Time to get back to the game.

entry.title: [titanxxh Plays Chinese Paladin 5] Part 2: The Funny Bits
entry.content:
All right, you stole the show. Xiaoman, are you laughing so hard that your stomach hurts?

 

Nice name, sir: Pu Songling.

 

You two leave me speechless. Even lovesick people do not usually go this far.

 

Even the game has crooked merchants. Unpaid wages are everywhere—what a miserable life.

Does this leave your mind in a tangle? It reminded me of that diagram explaining all the relationships in Chinese Paladin.

Man, you are taking this far too seriously.

Even Brother Xiaoyao has become obsessed with wine.

I strongly suspect Xiaoman is afraid of ghosts because of the stories her grandfather told her when she was little.

This scene is adorable. Young Master Long speaks in the Yaksha language, Xiaoman cannot understand him, and when he asks her a question, she gives him a taste of his own medicine. Ha!

Sister Huo, did you really have to be so ruthless? Three “kill without mercy” orders...

My eyes! It is all boys' love!

Yurou gets her own moment too.

Haiwan, will you marry me when we grow up?

No! I want to learn the art of gu, like Madam Haitang.

Then will you like me when we grow up?

No! I want to be like Madam Haitang and fall in love with a great hero.

Hmph! Grandma said Madam Haitang's great hero married two wives. I am going to marry two as well!

...Then I will put a love gu on you.

...

 

This conversation between the two children is just too sweet.

This boss is hilarious. It asks questions: answer correctly and it loses health; answer incorrectly and the whole party is wiped out. And that final question...

 

Why does our young Yunfan look like a puppet emperor here?

And why does his father look like a formidable regent?

Yipin always has the best lines, but this hiccup is something else...

One bug to finish. The game crashed only once in 38 hours, which I can accept. Better than Gujian.

entry.title: [titanxxh Plays Chinese Paladin 5] Part 3: Memorable Moments, Trivia, and Rumors
entry.content:
Friendly warning: this post contains major spoilers.

Yi Pin's identity is revealed for the first time

The heroine's lament

Is there some special significance to putting this painting here...

With one quiet aside, the game captures Ouyang Hui's sharp tongue and soft heart perfectly. (Come to think of it, almost every line that begins in a whisper is a gem.)

Ancient Qionghua—was it really that long ago...

The second time. Brother Xiaoyao's deeds really have become the stuff of legend.

A beautiful boss: Lanyi, guardian of the Wind Spirit Pearl

Ouyang Hui looks beautiful even when angry (though that 3D model...). Her words carry tremendous authority—hardly what you would expect from a young woman.

Ling'er's tears—paper truly is a marvelous thing.

Qingshi may be blind, yet he seems better able than most to see through worldly affairs and the human heart. No wonder he ranks second among the Seven Sages of Mount Shu.

Those who defy heaven will ultimately face its judgment—well said. The protagonists set up a heaven-defying formation, and the final result... sigh.

Still talking about Qingshi: do blind people see only black and white in their minds?

Look familiar? Years ago, that foolish young man also sailed to Fairy Spirit Island on a lotus.

Bringing the dead back to life? Could it really work? It was only a dream.

Xiaoyao and Anu; Yi Pin and Haitang. Thirty years have passed, everything else has changed, yet their feelings remain.

The imposing Demon Lord—especially that gesture as he raises his hand, as if the very idea of saying no were forbidden.

Look at their positions—isn't that the Big Dipper?

Beside Tianshu Palace, an enormous character for “Dao”

The Serpent Staff—does it bring back memories of that hill at sunset? Now the present-day descendant of Nüwa is about to shoulder the same responsibility.

The most intimate contact in the entire story (bromance doesn't count...): the two embrace without a word.

The three divine artifacts. How could a heroine this clever not understand the price of this heaven-defying formation...

P.S. This formation reminds me of The Scar of Sky...

What is the Kunlun Sect supposed to be... so useless...

entry.title: [A Life in Board Games] Episode 2: Small World—War or Prosperity?
entry.content:
Today is September 22. First, happy 35th birthday to my dear Ronnie. I hope your first birthday since retiring is not too difficult. (Perhaps it is we fans who should try not to feel too sad. Sigh.)

Last time I looked back at an open-ended negotiation game—please ignore that improvised definition—called Chinatown. I recently played two more games with my roommates and came away with a few new thoughts to share with friends.

1. Everything needs moderation, games included. If you do not take a game seriously enough, neither you nor anyone else will find much enjoyment in it. But there is no need to become furious because somebody misplayed a few cards, or to rage whenever you fail to finish first. Friendly reminders and jokes are fine, but know where to draw the line.

2. Think ahead. In Chinatown, for example, haggling over every last advantage in every deal is not necessarily wise. Later rounds have not yet arrived, and the cards drawn then may change everything. Yielding a little profit now to earn goodwill can lay the foundation for future trades.

3. Learn to adapt. To continue with Chinatown, when a round ends you should neither regret every deal that fell through nor simply hope to draw the exact card you need. Instead, review the round. Which player threatens you? Where does everyone stand? In general, it is good to offer some benefit to players behind you, and even a slightly unfavorable trade may be acceptable. Against anyone ahead of you, however, contest every inch. In my second game, I eventually accepted a small loss to complete a deadlocked trade with the player in last place. He posed no threat to me; finishing the trade quickly earned only a little, but it also prevented my direct rivals from profiting through him.

PS: This game gets noisy. Do not play it anywhere that requires silence.


Small World

Back to the main subject. Today I want to introduce a cheerful combat game: Small World. Just as the title suggests, its map is so small that wars break out constantly. Interestingly, victory is determined neither by military strength nor by the amount of territory you control. Instead, players collect income every round, accumulate wealth, and the richest wins. During China's Southern Song dynasty, the Han Chinese held only the south and faced an unfavorable military situation, yet ordinary people prospered, the economy flourished, and many great inventions emerged. The Mongols, by contrast, rode across Asia, at one point controlling an enormous territory through tremendous military power. That is another route to success. Small World lets you experience both approaches. Will the coin-hoarding Dwarves prevail, or will the Orcs sustain themselves through conquest? Let us enter this crowded world!


The map of Small World

The map contains several kinds of terrain—seas, lakes, farmland, hills, mountains, and swamps—and regions may also have features such as mines, caverns, and magic sources. These provide many direct or indirect bonuses when income is collected at the end of a turn.


Races in Small World

The base game contains fourteen races, each with its own power. Some improve combat: Giants need one fewer token when conquering regions adjacent to mountains. Some increase income: Wizards gain an extra coin each turn for every region with a magic-source symbol, while Orcs gain an extra coin for every active region they conquer. Others increase your forces: Sorcerers can turn another player's lone token into one of their own, and so on.


Special powers in Small World

The base game has twenty special powers, too many to explain one by one here.

The basic rules are simple. Players take turns, and each turn has several phases.

1. Beginning of the Turn


Choosing a race in Small World

Several random combinations of races and powers are displayed beside the board. On the first turn, you must select one. If you dislike the combinations at the front and choose one farther down, place a coin on each combination you skip, making them more attractive to later players so that none becomes worthless. Then take the appropriate number of race tokens: the number in the lower-right corner of the race tile plus that in the lower-left corner of the power tile. If a race is completely wiped out and later wants to conquer again, it must re-enter from the edge of the board. At the start of a later turn, a player may put their race into decline, skipping conquest for that turn. On the following turn, they can choose a new race and enter the map again. A race usually goes into decline only after it has expanded as far as it can. More about decline below.

2. Conquest

Now conquest begins. On the first turn, you may conquer only from the edge of the map—a coastline counts—unless you have the Flying power. On later turns, you may conquer only regions adjacent to territory you already occupy. You can conquer any number of regions in a turn as long as you have enough tokens. The number required equals the total thickness of all tokens and markers in the target region, plus two, though combat bonuses may reduce the cost. When a region is conquered, its defending race does not lose every token: only one dies, while the others return to their player's hand and may be redeployed after the active player's turn. Suppose Giants occupy a mountain and want to attack an adjacent mountain defended by x tokens. They need x + 1 for the mountain's defensive bonus + 2 as the normal cost - 1 from the Giant ability, for a total of x + 2. If you lack enough tokens for a conquest, you may select a region and roll the Reinforcement Die once. It has three blank faces and one each showing 1, 2, and 3. Add the result to your remaining force for one final conquest, then proceed to redeployment. You may also stop conquering voluntarily and redeploy.

PS: Later players can enter the map by trampling over the bodies of those who came before. Brutal, is it not? Players who move early should choose races with strong defenses or occupy favorable terrain.

3. Redeployment

During this phase, players may redistribute tokens freely among the regions they occupy. Reinforce places that need heavy defense and leave fewer troops in your own backyard. Most opponents will not launch a long-distance campaign, after all, and every strategist knows the danger of overextending a front.

4. Collecting Income

Everything before this leads to this moment. Think of it as taxing your land. Every region provides one coin in base income, plus any bonuses from race traits or special powers. Then the next player takes a turn.

About Decline

A race in decline leaves only one token in each of its regions, but those regions continue to generate income for its player. Whether bonuses still apply depends on the race's ability; most do not remain active. A player may have only one race in decline. When that player puts a second race into decline, the first is removed.

About Active Regions

Only regions occupied by the race a player currently controls are active. Regions occupied by neutral inhabitants or races in decline are inactive.

One point to remember during play: certain powers override the basic rules, so always follow the special power. This is similar to the priority of character abilities in Legends of the Three Kingdoms.

Now for the game's strengths—or, rather, what attracts me to it.

1. It uses a mechanism somewhat like Legends of the Three Kingdoms, but without the awkwardness of players leaving early. Randomness matters, though definitely less than in that game.

2. Your ability to communicate with others can profoundly affect the contest. Unite with allies and isolate opponents. Does that not sound a little like Zhuge Liang's strategy of allying in the east and resisting in the north, or the allied forces of Sun Quan and Liu Bei defeating Cao Cao at Red Cliffs?

3. You really do not have to win through constant fighting.

4. Quietly accumulating wealth is better than expanding ostentatiously. As the saying goes, the tallest tree in the forest is the first to be felled by the wind.

 

If you like the sound of this game, try it at a board-game café first. The genuine edition is far too expensive, and the expansions are even harder on the wallet.

Next episode: Carcassonne—The Distinctive Charm of a French Town

entry.title: [titanxxh Plays Chinese Paladin 5] 4. Combat Review
entry.content:
This article has nothing to do with the story. It is only about how the combat feels.

Ordinary enemies are not strong—at least they are weaker than those in Chinese Paladin 4—but some maps contain one unusually powerful minor enemy, such as that snake in Thunderbolt Wasteland...

The boss fights are much more interesting to discuss. If you do not grind, but clear nearly every monster on each map and keep your equipment up to date, bosses in the early and middle portions are fairly easy. They may take a long time, but I can swallow potions and the boss cannot heal, so its defeat is only a matter of time.

The monkeys at the beginning cannot be defeated. The bosses that follow—including the Magic Ape King, Shangguan Ya, and Blood Hand—are not difficult; they merely have a lot of health.

Ice Qilin is probably the first challenging one. It enters an enraged state, so watch your health when frozen. It is still relatively manageable.

By this point I had worked out a low-level boss strategy: consume medicine to build energy, then unleash ultimate attacks. As long as you can survive the incoming damage, you will eventually get a chance to turn defense into offense.

The next few bosses are not especially difficult either. Against a single target, win the war of attrition; against several, eliminate the softest target first.

Ouyang Hui is a hurdle because the protagonist must duel her alone. She is holding back, however, and if you pay attention to her fire spells you can still win. Those lightning orbs are annoying.

I recommend losing the sparring match against Young Master Long, since you can synthesize Eight Fiends yourself anyway.

Feng Gui was the first boss I found genuinely infuriating. It healed itself nine times and nearly exhausted my entire medicine supply, although it was not particularly dangerous.

If you are underleveled against the Bone Snake, bring Xiaoman. The Five-Poison Pearl provides excellent protection against poison; let the men handle the damage output.

The Three Monsters of Mount Huang are delightful, but their damage is no joke. The brush spray is single-target and can easily kill someone outright.

When you challenge Qiongwu again, the balance has shifted dramatically: its dragon attributes have fallen a lot while the heroes have gained levels, making the fight very easy.

The successive battles against the Four Great Families are easy too. They made me seriously question those families' supposed ability...

Yipin from twenty years ago is unbeatable, and twenty years later he remains unbeatable. Did Yao Xian simply refuse to let players see Li Xiaoyao defeated?

The Seven Sages of Mount Shu challenge is where the game's real difficulty begins. After failing twice against Lingyin, I realized how important buffs were. Otherwise the five Lingyins can chain their turns together; with bad luck, all of them use ultimate attacks and death is unavoidable. One talisman is crucial here: Spell Continuation. Extending a buff by two turns is invaluable, letting you deal more damage while weathering the assault. As usual, target the Lingyin with the easiest element first. I was underleveled, so I had Yurou use her sleep skill to lock down the real Lingyin and keep her from acting. Once you rebuild energy, control her again and prevent the enemy from chaining turns as much as possible.

The second fight against Yipin is unwinnable. The Jingtuo Spirit-Recovery Pill that Caogu gave you earlier is meant for this moment. You can also use an Invisibility Gu to dodge chained actions while applying buffs.

Taiwu! The difficulty rises sharply here, and I was still below the recommended level. If, like me, you enjoy pushing the limit, use plenty of immunity items to protect your fragile characters. The male protagonist can survive, but the other two may not. Equip spell-resistance talismans as well. Staying alive is everything! It took me four or five attempts. The changing elemental attributes are very well designed and genuinely challenging.

Demon Lord Jiang Shili and Li Xiao: kill the giant bird first. If you take too long and barely damage the father before the story trigger, the enemy's two ultimate attacks will certainly wipe you out. Fire immunity is still necessary; otherwise the fight is very dangerous.

Mo Yi, Zhi Su, and Jiu Ye: the two smaller enemies have area-of-effect spells, so immunity should ideally negate one of them; otherwise this battle is difficult too. If Mo Yi copies one of your units, the copy's spell damage is terrible no matter whom it copies and can be ignored. If it copies the protagonist, however, a critical hit against Xiaoman is dangerous. Keep every buff active.

The final boss is also the most outrageous one: the World-Annihilating Qiongbing.

When I fought it, Yunfan was probably level 54, Long You 42, and Xiaoman 53. The boss opened with an ultimate attack; Yunfan was left with only 53 health and the other two were knocked out.

For the first time I wondered whether my level was simply too low. I had not even doubted it during the Taiwu fight. Going out to grind would mean repeating the previous two battles, so I decided to keep trying. A few miraculous tools deserve mention: Heavenly Fragrance Life-Restoring Dew, Invisibility Gu, every throwable item, group mana recovery, Spell Continuation, Focus Spirit, Wind-Commanding Art, Rock-Fortification Spell, group spell barriers, and the ultimate attacks of Xiaoman and Yunfan. Be patient, hope for a little luck, do not surrender, and test the limit.

Even with every buff applied, one ultimate attack can leave Xiaoman hovering between zero and thirty health. It comes down to luck: the fewer times characters die, the more ultimate attacks you can launch and the faster the fight proceeds. Also, once inside the creature's body, throw items. They deal 1,200 more damage there than outside, which is excellent value, and the character inside can use ultimate attacks without danger. Make the most of that opportunity to deal damage.

Then sit back and enjoy the ending.

Overall, late-game combat becomes disconnected from the expected character levels. If you are obsessive like me, try pushing the limit: you will experience the appeal of turn-based combat. Which move each person should use, whether to take medicine, and the shape of the action bar are all critical decisions. If someone dies, revive them immediately; their position on the action bar is not pushed back, which is worth remembering. Early bosses merely have too much health and offer little novelty, but the later battles are very well designed and challenging.

entry.title: [A Life in Board Games] Part 3: Carcassonne, the Unique Charm of a French Town
entry.content:
If you search Google for Carcassonne, you may find a picture like this one—please ignore the people in it:


The fortified city of Carcassonne

Compare it with the game's cover:


The cover of Carcassonne

Pretty similar, isn't it? Such a town really exists. The game's premise is that you are building a city. By assigning the workers at their disposal, players take on jobs: building roads and castles, farming, or becoming monks can all earn points. Whoever has the most points when the game ends wins. First, let us admire a city sensibly created by its players!


A completed game of Carcassonne

Imagine how satisfying it would be to complete this city yourself. Let us step into the world of Carcassonne!

The game begins with a starting tile. On each turn, a player draws one tile and places it adjacent to the existing map: field against field, road against road, and city against city. If there is nowhere legal to place it, discard it and draw another. The player may then place one of their meeples. A meeple in a city is a knight, one lying in a field is a farmer, one standing on a road is a robber, and one in a monastery is a monk. These correspond to the game's four ways of scoring.

Knights score according to the size of their cities, with every shield symbol adding one to the city's size. Robbers score according to the length of their roads. Monks are simplest: count the tiles in the 3×3 area centered on the monastery. Fields are the most complicated; they score according to how many completed cities border that field, at three points apiece.

Those are the end-of-game scoring rules. During play, whenever a city is completed, the player with the most knights in it immediately retrieves their meeples and scores twice the city's size, making large cities very powerful. Completed roads are likewise scored immediately and return their meeples. When all spaces around a monastery have been filled, its owner immediately scores nine points and retrieves the monk. A field cannot be scored until the end, however, so a farmer placed there never returns!

The most important thing about cities, roads, and fields is that only the player with the most meeples scores; tied players all score, but anyone with fewer gets nothing. Because of this unusual rule, meeple placement is tightly restricted: you may place one only in a feature not currently occupied by any player, yourself included. Connecting occupied features later is allowed, but you often cannot draw the tile you need.

That is the entire rules explanation. Anyone with an iOS device can download Carcassonne to learn the rules. Its AI is strong! Feel free to add me on Game Center; my ID is titanxxh.

A few things new Carcassonne players should remember:

1. Meeples are limited. Do not put one on every tile you draw. Meeples are like cash, and Carcassonne has no bank willing to lend you more. I recommend beginning with a two-player game, where this lesson is easiest to appreciate.

2. Monastery > city > field > road. It is an iron law that is rarely broken. Players can discover why for themselves.

3. Cooperation in a multiplayer game is useful but not mandatory. Mastering the art of “piggybacking” lets you share other players' points or take them for yourself. But while you and another player are fighting over one giant city and piling meeples into it, everyone else will be quietly delighted.

4. Claim fields early. Once the game is halfway over, it is time to lie down in one. Do not underestimate the explosive scoring potential of fields.


A match I played against someone online

5. Sometimes you are simply destined not to win, and there is no point obsessing over it. As master board-game designer Reiner Knizia said, “When playing a game, the goal is to win, but it is the goal that is important, not the winning.”

Finally, I want to quote the ideas from someone else's analysis of Carcassonne, adapted from this article.

When the enemy is strong, answer with softness.

What counts as strength in Carcassonne? A great city. It scores heavily and can keep producing points; even unfinished, it is worth plenty. How should we respond when an opponent builds one? Share it—the strategy commonly called “piggybacking.” Start a city tile next to their great city and connect it later, letting them do the work while you share the points. You can even sabotage it afterward and prevent completion. That surely counts as overcoming hardness with softness. ^_^

When the enemy is soft, answer with change.

What if the opponent wants to piggyback on you? Change! Deny them the opportunity and fight through rapid adaptation. Develop a small city here, score it, and leave; build another small city there; later, make a short road... Before the opponent can latch on, your city is finished. It is like guerrilla warfare: keep changing, keep your meeples in hand, develop wherever you wish, and give the opponent no opening.

When the enemy changes, answer with focus.

What if the opponent also pursues small cities and short-term investments? Focus! Commit to the fields. Let them build as many small cities as they please: if I control the surrounding field, each four-point city they complete immediately brings my farmer three points. With the field in hand, every extra city is good news. ^_^

When the enemy focuses, answer with strength.

The importance of fields in Carcassonne needs no explanation. If the opponent fights for them, return to developing a great city. It does not even need to be completed, as long as it scores. Try to keep the opponent's field from becoming useful; then their farmer has been wasted, while your great city can continue producing points.

Next time: Modern Art—the wisdom of auctions

entry.title: Civilization V — My First World Map with True Starting Locations
entry.content:
Civilization does a great job with its map replays and statistics.

This was my first time playing the world map. I used a true-starting-locations mod and, to test my new computer's performance, enabled a whole lot of AI players. I set the difficulty to level 5.

At the beginning, our Empress Wu Zetian founded her first city right where she stood. For technology, after essentials such as Animal Husbandry, Mining, and Paper, I beelined for Chu-Ko-Nus. For policies, I went straight into the military branch.

Poor Beijing was surrounded by powerful neighbors. I had to hold out for more than eighty turns before settling Shanghai far away. Then I built three Chu-Ko-Nus, added the starting Axeman, and began my campaign of conquest. The capitals of Siam, India, Persia, and Egypt fell one after another. One city-state, Almaty, even dared to steal my territory, so I wiped it out later while completing a city-state quest along the way. Once I had artillery, sieges became much easier—that range of three is no joke. I took Hamburg and split Germany in two, cleared the African continent, and crushed Germany, which had spent the early game attacking everyone and earning denunciations. Then I turned to isolated Britain. At that point, shameless Japan actually declared war on me... When I went over to look, its cities were all tucked away at sea. But once bombers arrived, Japan was quickly swept off the stage of history. Last came the distant Americas. The United States had been developing in comfort; after buying off a city-state, we attacked Montezuma, who was blocking the way. In the end, I simply waited for the inevitable science victory.

I fought too aggressively early on and was constantly denounced. Later, I wisely made peace with anyone I was not planning to attack yet, securing my rear. Because the AI has such poor tactical intelligence and positioning, you can eliminate its field forces first and take cities at leisure afterward. (Ranged units are simply overpowered, especially those that can attack twice.) Keep an eye on the national economy. Build structures that grant experience and money, and skip wonders that do not help. Burn useless cities so they do not add unhappiness. You can pay city-states to join the war: let them charge in and die while you collect the kills. Overall, it was fairly easy. Stealing the AI's workers is also very effective.

entry.title: Xiaoyaoyou Demo Tournament Recap
entry.content:
I should have written a recap long ago, but I have been unbelievably busy lately and buried in assignments. Only now have I found time to sit down and type.

This event was organized by the Shanghai Chinese Paladin Fan Club. To be honest, I had hardly said a word in the group after joining it. Then I happened to notice an opportunity to try the game. Since I am also a board-game enthusiast, there was no reason not to go.

When I woke up on the 29th, it was already past eleven. I got ready casually and headed out. My luck was excellent: a bus arrived when I was only halfway to the stop. Was this an omen that I would become champion? I reached the venue promptly at 13:30. There were far more people than I expected, and knowing absolutely nobody made me feel rather nervous. Eventually someone asked whether I was there for the tournament, and before I knew what was happening I had been led into another room. The planned random draw had apparently become a first-come, first-formed team arrangement. I discovered that my two teammates were girls; I later learned that they also attended Jiao Tong, though only the high school.

The match began quickly. One opponent had clearly played before, which immediately increased the pressure. Neither side knew the game very well, however, so the match dragged on for a long time. If I remember correctly, ours was the last table to finish that round.

Looking back, the first match was probably the closest. The opposing team's leader was unfortunately knocked out by one of his own teammates. After we also lost one player, my three-health Brother Xiao stood firm thanks to immunity against all sorts of water and fire attacks. Meanwhile, the pets captured by the other side kept sharing the same element, forcing them into difficult choices. In the end, Brother Xiao and his four pets defeated their Brother Lou, giving us a narrow victory.

In the second match, we faced three older men. (Voice-over: I am not an older man...) They all looked very wise, but their play told another story. They selected no high-spirit heavy hitter and repeatedly activated Nangong Huang's ability, emptying the monster deck in no time. We won without suspense. PS: I was Brother Xiao again. Was that a coincidence?

When five teams were reduced to four, I had to admire the extraordinary luck of my two teammates. We advanced directly without enduring a long duel.

Our luck remained excellent in the semifinal. We captured both crucial monsters—the Evil Sword Immortal with 11 spirit and the Lava Beast King with 10—even though the spirit totals were tied both times. Those results immediately decided the direction of the match, and the other team eventually conceded. PPS: I was still Brother Xiao. Could this be fate?

In the final, our opponents unleashed a burst: two Heavenly Thunder cards and Wen Hui's ability immediately eliminated our poor Qiqi. With only Brother Lou and Yueru left, the situation looked grim. But Brother Lou kept winning his duels, while Yueru's participation wore down the enemy's health further, bringing the game back to two against two. In the end, the other team lost because it had no character with high spirit. PPPS: At last I was not Brother Xiao, but I was still formidable as Brother Lou! They rolled a five; I rolled a six. How about that!

To summarize, a team needs a heavy hitter such as Xuan Xiao or Chong Lou, a support character such as Qiqi or Xingxuan, someone disruptive such as Yueru, and somebody with plenty of health. Otherwise, late in the game nobody will dare interfere, and you will be at a disadvantage.

All in all, ours is a team with tremendous potential, and Xiaoyaoyou is a game with tremendous potential. My only regret is that my beloved Ling'er is absent—and there is no Jingtian either. All I can do is hope the official edition arrives soon!

Finally, I want to thank my two teammates, Li Yiru and Beibi, as well as the organizers and Softstar Beijing. Your prizes were amazing! (Prize photos below.)

entry.title: [A Life in Board Games] Part 4: Modern Art, the Wisdom of Auctions
entry.content:
Front of the Modern Art box

The background of the Modern Art box is a rather abstract painting—the paintings inside are even more abstract—paired with a simple title and the name of the celebrated designer Reiner Knizia. Modern Art is one entry in his auction trilogy; the other two are Medici and Ra.


Components of Modern Art

The objective is to make money by selling paintings and speculating on their popularity. At the end of each round, players sell paintings they bought to the bank at their market prices. After four rounds, the player with the most cash wins.

Everyone begins with some starting money and a hand of cards. Players take turns, and on each turn the active player must play one painting from hand for auction. The auction method is printed on the painting. There are four basic types:

Open auction: exactly what it sounds like. Everyone bids freely, and the highest bidder wins, as in a conventional auction house.

Once around: beginning with the player to your left, everyone gets one chance to bid or pass. Finally, you decide whether to bid yourself.

Fixed price: name a price, then ask each player in turn whether they will buy it. If nobody has bought it by the time the choice returns to you, you must buy it yourself.

Sealed bid: everyone secretly holds some money in a fist and reveals simultaneously. The highest bid wins.

There is also a fifth method, the double auction. A player may offer two paintings of the same color together when one bears the double-auction symbol. The other painting determines the actual auction method, so it cannot also be a double auction. Every bid is for both paintings combined.

The double auction also has an extended form. A player may play only the double-auction painting, then ask each following player whether they wish to add an eligible painting. The buyer pays half the price to each seller. If nobody joins, the original player receives their own painting for free.

Play then passes to the player to the seller's left. In the extended double auction, however, it passes to the player after the one who joined the sale. Declining to participate can therefore cost someone a precious opportunity to sell a painting.

When a fifth painting of one color is played, it is not auctioned and the round ends. The color with the most paintings—necessarily five—ranks first, and the color with the second-highest count ranks second. Ties are broken by the left-to-right priority printed on the market board; third place is determined the same way. Place 30, 20, and 10 markers on the board according to those rankings. Paintings of those three colors are bought by the bank at the accumulated value of their color. Values carry over between rounds: if a painter ranked first in round one, failed to rank in round two, and ranked first again now, every one of that artist's paintings sells to the bank for 60.


Front of the Chinese edition

Having heard the rules, many players may not feel attracted. The mechanism means the game is not inherently lighthearted, and the paintings are absurdly abstract, aren't they? None of that stops Modern Art from being a classic auction game.

Although everyone competes individually and the person with the most money wins, a conspicuous idea of teams emerges during play. If two or more players are promoting the same artist, they naturally form an alliance, while everyone else automatically forms an alliance to suppress them. Unlike the fixed rebel and lord camps in games such as Bang!-style Three Kingdoms games, however, alliances here are fluid. You may need to change course within the same round.

I also believe there is an invisible alliance. As in other games, whoever seems to be leading becomes the target. Trailing players often refuse to help the person they believe is ahead and choose another partner instead. Notice that I wrote “believe.” Money, like one's hand, is hidden, so newcomers to Modern Art frequently misidentify the leader. They spend the entire game suppressing someone, only to discover at the end that this person was nowhere near the true winner, leaving everyone frustrated.

This brings us to the game's only two sources of money: selling paintings to the bank and selling them to other players. Many newcomers see somebody return a large stack of paintings to the bank at the end of a round and receive a pile of cash, then assume that person is in first place. That is not necessarily true. They sell many paintings because they bought many paintings, and may have little cash remaining; the bank payment could represent virtually all their wealth. The truly frightening player is often the one who bought only one or two highly ranked paintings while earning heavily from sales during the auction phase.

How can you tell whether someone earned a lot from selling? That is another common beginner's question. Simply observe every bid and fixed price. Outside the extended double auction, there can only be one seller and one buyer, which makes the comparison straightforward. If a painting will be worth n at the end of the round, a buyer who pays more than n/2 loses relative to the seller on that transaction. With other players in the game, however, the buyer still profits in absolute terms, and some profit is better than none.

Precisely because other players exist, they will not merely watch you profit; someone will drive the price higher. Auctions therefore seldom stop at half the expected value. How high will they go? The value 2n/3 is a natural threshold. If nobody accepts that price, the seller buys the painting and makes one-third of its value relative to every other player. If someone does accept it, the buyer makes one-third, while the seller earns one-third more than the buyer and two-thirds more than everyone else. Bidding often stops there because any higher bid widens the gap between buyer and seller. You should exceed it only if you believe the seller poses absolutely no threat. This discussion concerns open auctions, but the other formats differ only in detail; the underlying principle is the same.

After all that, every calculation still depends on knowing n—the painting's final value. If your appraisal is wrong, everything that follows collapses. Besides considering the paintings in your own hand and those already auctioned, you must know who shares your interests. Otherwise you cannot predict the rankings and therefore cannot value a painting. Have I come all the way back to the beginning? Yes. Modern Art is a seamless whole, and that is where its charm lies.

Next time: Ghost Stories—can you defend the ancient seal about to break?

entry.title: DSDV Study Notes
entry.content:
Our networking assignment happened to be a simulation of the DSDV routing algorithm, so with nothing else to do on Singles' Day, I decided to write a summary.

DSDV (Destination-Sequenced Distance Vector)

When a link goes down, ordinary DV is prone to loops that make the cost grow without bound. DSDV solves this problem by cleverly introducing a SequenceNumber.

As in DV, each node maintains a routing table containing destination, next_hop, and cost, plus a seq value. This value increases only when routing information changes—for example, when a node disconnects or a cost changes—so neighboring nodes can update to the newest value during the next broadcast. If a broken link is detected, the sequence number for that neighbor must be increased by 1, forcing neighbors to update its cost to infinity. 

Parse command-line arguments
Bind the socket to a local port
Create a new listening thread
Inside the main loop:
1. Read data from the file. After the first read, some data may need to be updated. If there is an update, increment the node's own seq by 2. If a route is updated to a broken link, increment that neighbor's seq by 1. Also process routing-table entries that use this neighbor as their next hop.
2. Send the node's own routing table to its neighbors.
3. Sleep for 10 seconds.
4. Output the node's routing-table information.

Inside the listening thread:
Receive a record.
Use the message length to determine whether it is a valid record (because other classmates may be sending data too...).
If the received record does not exist in the local routing table, add it. (Initially, each person's routing table contains only the node itself and its neighbors, with no knowledge of the rest of the network.)
If the destination in the record is this node, check whether its seq is greater than the one maintained locally. If so, it means that node has lost its route to us while our own routing table has not yet been updated (its file update arrived before ours). We must force our own seq above theirs, or the routing information will become incorrect.
If the record's seq is greater than the corresponding record in the local routing table, replace the local record.
If the record's seq equals that of the corresponding local entry, and the route through the sender is shorter than the current route, replace it.

entry.title: A Study of Creature Strength in TITAN
entry.content:
I bought a secondhand copy of Titan some time ago but never had a chance to play it. During a rare break, I opened it for a three-player game while visiting Hangzhou with classmates—or, more precisely, a four-player game in which one person fell asleep. Afterward, everyone independently began discussing how strong or weak the various creatures were by design.

So over the weekend I wrote a program to simulate them. The basic idea was to make two unit types fight 1,000 battles. When a melee unit fought a ranged unit, I assumed that the ranged unit would get one attack before the melee unit closed the distance, since even the slowest unit can move two spaces and ranged attacks reach only across two spaces. The simulation results can be viewed here.

I found that the three weakest units—the Centaur, Ogre, and Gargoyle—were not equally strong even though each had a Value of 12. The experimental result was C > O > G. Now consider the Serpent and Archangel. Both have a Value of 36, yet the difference is clear: 455 wins, 418 draws, and 127 losses. According to Titan's hit table, when both sides have the same Skill Factor, a die hits on 4 or higher, giving a probability of one half, which is fair. For every point by which one side's Skill Factor is lower, the number required to hit rises by one, and vice versa. Compare that with the result. When the Archangel rolls nine dice against the Serpent, its expected number of hits is 9 × (5/6) = 7.5. In the other direction, the Serpent's expected hits against the Archangel are 18 × (1/6) = 3. The Archangel needs only 2.4 rounds on average to kill the Serpent, whereas the Serpent needs three rounds to kill the Archangel. The hierarchy is obvious. In fact, suppose a unit's Value is 12x and three units have statistics (3x, 4), (4x, 3), and (6x, 2). Pairwise fights should produce the same ordering as the Centaur, Ogre, and Gargoyle.

The designers clearly took this into account. The Gargoyle is the only flying unit among the lowest tier, and it also received the best recruitment path and the largest number of terrain advantages, allowing that army to develop quickly. In the other example, the Archangel can fly as well as being stronger, but it is correspondingly difficult to obtain and cannot be replaced once killed. The Serpent is the top unit on the Gargoyle recruitment path. Before the other two paths reach their peaks, the Serpent is the strongest creature in the game—stronger than the Hydra, Dragon, or Giant. A player should therefore use a Serpent force to hunt opponents before they finish developing, disrupting their progress, or block an enemy Titan legion so that it cannot grow.

PS: What matters is not the thrill of rolling eighteen dice at once, but the final sliver of hope they offer when all seems lost.

PPS: For a game published in 1980, Titan's survival to the present day is remarkable. Beyond its nature as a wargame and its roll-to-move mechanism, I am attracted by those familiar creatures. They make me feel as if I have returned to a legendary world of swords and sorcery.

entry.title: Board Game Session, December 8, 2011: Tigris & Euphrates and Agricola
entry.content:
Once I had finished the compiler assignment and the little object-oriented programming exercise, I eagerly ran upstairs to set up Tigris & Euphrates. Unfortunately, wzh and pp were both busy, so it took ages before the battle began.


The final position in Tigris & Euphrates

After I explained the rules, wzh took the Pot dynasty. After much hesitation, pp chose the Bull, while I chose the Archer. Eager for battle, pp immediately attacked wzh while I developed quietly to one side. Wzh was soon defeated and began relocating, while pp built the first monument. I had no blue farm tiles and could not score blue points, so both of us began targeting pp. In the middle game, I won two external conflicts and my blue and green scores soared, though black lagged behind. Pp then talked wzh into attacking me. Before long, pp had built a second monument and was earning steady red and green points every turn. Both of my leaders stood beside two temples, and I held plenty of temple tiles. Wzh cut a route with a catastrophe tile and attacked, but achieved little; instead, the conflict gave me enough red points. At one stage I wanted to contest the large region on the left bank of a river with pp, but wzh's harassment ruined that plan. I had to discard four blue tiles from my hand in exchange for temples. Later I used a catastrophe to break wzh's long, straight formation, then removed his black leader through an internal conflict. At the very end, I successfully built two black points and ended the game on my own turn; the final position is shown above. We removed our screens and revealed the answer. Pp and I were tied in both our lowest and second-lowest colors, but my third-lowest color was one point higher, so I won, as shown below. Wzh's score was too low, so I did not photograph it. It was everyone's first game, and our decisions felt rather hasty. Next time we play, I suspect somebody will spend the whole game trapped in analysis paralysis. (Evil grin.)


pp’s score: 9 + 9 + 9 + 10


My score: 9 + 9 + 10 + lots more


The position at the end of Agricola

Afterward we played a three-player game of Agricola. Midway through the first attempt I felt that I had made such a large mistake that we decided to restart. In the new game I chose a path from farming into improvements. Early on, I played an overpowered occupation that let me play a minor and a major improvement in succession. In the middle game, the wet nurse helped me expand my family quickly, and the seasonal worker carried me through one round. Late in the game, the Well–Village Well–Well sequence generated both points and food. I plowed six fields in two rounds, had another card that provided extra vegetables, and finally put two animals in stables to avoid penalties. More than ten points from my stack of improvements, plus a perfect agriculture score, brought me to 45 points and my first Agricola victory! In one round, pp took the starting-player space I needed and sent me into analysis paralysis for the first time. Across roughly four previous games I had barely thought at all, which shows how badly I had been playing. Otherwise, my Village Well would have come out smoothly. Pp later built fences chaotically, leaving no room to plow fields, and went to bed early. Agricola is fourth on BGG for good reason: it is fun yet strategic, players interfere with one another while developing, the opening combinations are diverse, and the game tests both long-term planning and the ability to adapt after choosing a direction. Sigh—there is far too much left to study. I will understand more next time. For now I have to return to that miserable OO assignment.


My pile of improvements—so many points


My farm: no wild boars and four unused spaces

entry.title: New Year's Eve 2011 Board-Game Night: Catan and Dixit
entry.content:
On the 31st, I finally finished my last exam, a compiler-principles paper composed entirely of multiple-choice questions, and could at last relax. Brother D happened to bring a classmate to visit Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Together with wzh, Jingzi, and Brother Dong, the six of us played from 9 p.m. until 8 the next morning. It was great fun, but on the way home my body finally gave out...

Since everyone was new, I did not want the rules to intimidate them, so I taught only the simplest game, Catan, and deliberately emphasized that it was a game of luck. The explanation went quickly. Brother D played white, wzh blue, Brother Dong orange, and Brother D's classmate red in the first game.

The dice were extremely uneven throughout. Eights and sixes arrived in clusters, while Brother Dong's eleven appeared only once. Early on, wzh had a sheep port, but settlements on the two and three hexes constrained his growth. Brother D's two central settlements should have been boxed in completely had his classmate and Brother Dong not gone easy on him. Brother Dong suffered poor rolls, while Brother D's classmate had tremendous potential.

The decisive turning point came when Brother D broke out and forced his way to a lumber port, although I personally think the 6-9-11 intersection would have been a better first choice. Meanwhile, his classmate tried to rush victory through both Largest Army and Longest Road but failed. Brother D then began collecting resources and upgrading cities at a ridiculous pace. At one point he could have built three roads in succession and stolen Longest Road; everybody saw it except him... It did not prevent his eventual victory. The final position is shown below.


Game one, the teaching game: Brother D wins

With more people for the second game, we added the five-to-six-player expansion. The board looked enormous, yet became frighteningly crowded once twelve starting settlements were placed. I was the last player in turn order and had almost nowhere left to choose. With my two consecutive placements, I had to take the brick port and the 6-11 brick intersection. That let me trade away a scarce resource, control much of the limited brick supply, and avoid constraining my development too severely.


The start of game two, a six-player game with the expansion

(Blue: me; orange: Jingzi; red: Brother Dong; white: Brother D; green: wzh; brown: Brother D's classmate.) Please be gentle with my color blindness.

What I did not expect was for the earlier players to roll sevens repeatedly and rob me, as shown below. Before I had even taken a turn, all three of my resources were gone. It was unbelievably depressing...


They stole every one of my resources before I began

Later, wzh tried to trade with me for brick so he could build a settlement. I saw through the plan and quickly built that settlement myself, wasting his two roads. Brother D's classmate and I monopolized brick, raised the price, and developed rapidly.


I secured the crucial settlement

The leader kept changing afterward. Jingzi, Brother D's classmate, and wzh each became the target of suppression in turn, while I developed gradually. Somehow everyone decided I was about to win and started blocking me, refusing to trade resources. I was also unlucky enough to roll a seven twice while holding ten resources. I fell behind Jingzi, whose Longest Road was unassailable and whose early cities generated abundant resources. Nobody could roll a seven against him, so he held first place firmly and ultimately won.


Jingzi reveals a victory-point card and declares victory

Afterward we played two three-versus-three games and one deeply tangled game of the dual-general national-war mode.

Finally, we brought out Dixit. To my surprise, everyone loved it; I had always assumed women would enjoy it more. Looking back, its simple rules and relaxed atmosphere probably made it especially welcome—we were quite tired by the second half of the night. Brother D won the first game, after which he could not escape last place... I won the second, and Brother D's classmate won the third. Using gaps in certain people's knowledge, or knowledge shared with one particular person, seemed to create the strongest clues and suppress other players effectively. Overall, it is a cheerful game and not something to take too seriously.

Finally, I must call out wzh. I strongly disapprove of the board-gaming philosophy that says, “If I cannot finish first, I will make sure nobody else wins either.”
