entry.title: Bullet Physics Engine Study Notes 1
entry.content:
I have spent two days tinkering, digging through every kind of blog and wiki I could find. That is what learning from scratch feels like: painful and enjoyable at the same time.

I am using Bullet 2.77 because Google Code provides precompiled demos for this version, so I could download and inspect them first. Compilation is simple: open the project in Visual Studio and build it. You may encounter a small error, however. Navigate to the failing location and comment out the entire PostBuild target.

At first I agonized over whether to use the open-source OgreBullet project. In the end I abandoned it, which still seems like the right choice. OgreBullet is a ready-made wrapper and is therefore not ideal for someone like me who wants to learn Bullet from the ground up.

The project's goal is a dodgeball game. My initial idea was to write a demo in which one object can be controlled to dodge other objects. I chose the simplest object: a box, one of Bullet's basic shapes.

I planned to reach that goal in stages.

First, integrate Bullet with Ogre: use the physics engine's calculations to display objects at the correct positions, and create and launch a series of boxes.

Second, detect collisions between boxes and delete any box that collides with a designated object.

Third, control that designated object with the mouse or keyboard so it can dodge.

Finally, control the object through Kinect.

The first three stages do not require Kinect and can be completed beforehand. Afterward comes polishing and tuning the game, which can wait.

Let us begin with stage one. We first need to create objects in both Ogre's world and Bullet's physics world. Before doing that, we initialize the Bullet world. Please do not ask what all of this means; I only half understand it myself. 

btDiscreteDynamicsWorld* m_dynamicsWorld;
btDefaultCollisionConfiguration* m_collisionConfiguration;
btCollisionDispatcher* m_dispatcher;
btBroadphaseInterface* m_overlappingPairCache;
btSequentialImpulseConstraintSolver* m_solver;
btAlignedObjectArray m_collisionShapes;

void initPhysics()
{ m_collisionConfiguration = new btDefaultCollisionConfiguration();
m_dispatcher = new btCollisionDispatcher(m_collisionConfiguration);
m_overlappingPairCache = new btDbvtBroadphase();
btSequentialImpulseConstraintSolver* sol = new btSequentialImpulseConstraintSolver;
m_solver = sol;
m_dynamicsWorld = new btDiscreteDynamicsWorld(m_dispatcher, m_overlappingPairCache, m_solver, m_collisionConfiguration);
m_dynamicsWorld->setGravity(btVector3(0, -10, 0));
}

Next, we begin creating objects. NodeInfo is a class I defined myself to store an Ogre SceneNode and some other information. 

// In the physics world
btCollisionShape* boxShape = new btBoxShape(btVector3(size.x,size.y,size.z));// Create the shape
float mass = 1.f;// Mass: zero means a static or kinematic object; see the User Manual for the distinction
btTransform startTransform;
startTransform.setIdentity();
startTransform.setOrigin(btVector3(0,5,0));// Set the position
bool isDynamic = (mass != 0.f);
btVector3 localInertia(0,0,0);
if (isDynamic) boxShape->calculateLocalInertia(mass,localInertia);// I do not know what this does
btDefaultMotionState* myMotionState = new btDefaultMotionState(startTransform);// Create a MotionState for later use
btRigidBody::btRigidBodyConstructionInfo cInfo(mass,myMotionState,boxShape,localInertia);
btRigidBody* boxBody = new btRigidBody(cInfo);// Create it
NodeInfo *nodeInfo = new NodeInfo(node, "KinematicBodyBox", "man");
boxBody->setUserPointer((void*)nodeInfo);// Use Bullet's reserved pointer to store the corresponding Ogre node so its position can be updated
m_dynamicsWorld->addRigidBody(boxBody);

Bullet advances the simulation with the following statement. Its parameter is the amount of time to simulate. 

m_dynamicsWorld->stepSimulation(etime);

We can then update each node's position and other properties: 
btCollisionObjectArray bodies = m_dynamicsWorld->getCollisionObjectArray();
btRigidBody *TObject;
for (int i=0;i(TObject->getUserPointer());
    if (TObject->isStaticOrKinematicObject())
    {
        continue;
    }

// Set position
btVector3 Point = TObject->getCenterOfMassPosition();
nodeInfo->node->setPosition(Ogre::Vector3(Point.getX(), Point.getY(), Point.getZ()));

// Convert the Bullet quaternion to an Ogre quaternion
btQuaternion btq = TObject->getOrientation();
Ogre::Quaternion quart = Ogre::Quaternion(btq.w(),btq.x(),btq.y(),btq.z());

// Use the quaternion with setOrientation
nodeInfo->node->setOrientation(quart);
}

You can set an object's initial height to 100 and print its height after every stepSimulation call. You will see it fall endlessly into the abyss... Or you can create a plane to stop it. 

// In the physics world
btCollisionShape* groundShape = new btStaticPlaneShape(btVector3(0,1,0),0);
btDefaultMotionState* groundMotionState = new btDefaultMotionState(btTransform(btQuaternion(0,0,0,1),btVector3(0,0,0)));
btRigidBody::btRigidBodyConstructionInfo groundRigidBodyCI(0,groundMotionState,groundShape,btVector3(0,0,0));
btRigidBody* groundRigidBody = new btRigidBody(groundRigidBodyCI);
m_dynamicsWorld->addRigidBody(groundRigidBody, COL_GROUND, groundCollidesWith);

Finally, through Ogre's FrameListener, you can launch a box whenever a particular key is pressed.

Enjoy yourself in Bullet!

entry.title: Bullet Physics Engine Study Notes 2 (MotionState)
entry.content:
Last time, I updated object positions by iterating over every object. That approach does a lot of unnecessary work, however, because some objects do not move at all.

To solve this problem, we need to use MotionState. As you can see, the previous article also used a MotionState, but it was Bullet's default implementation. This time, we will create our own to replace it. 

#include "linearmath/btMotionState.h"
#include

class MyMotionState : public btMotionState {
public:
MyMotionState(const btTransform &initialpos, Ogre::SceneNode *node) {// Set the initial position and node during initialization
mVisibleobj = node;
mPos1 = initialpos;
}

virtual ~MyMotionState() {
}

void setNode(Ogre::SceneNode *node) {
mVisibleobj = node;
}

virtual void getWorldTransform(btTransform &worldTrans) const {
worldTrans = mPos1;
}

virtual void setWorldTransform(const btTransform &worldTrans) {
if(NULL == mVisibleobj)
return; // silently return before we set a node
btQuaternion rot = worldTrans.getRotation();// Update the object's position information in Ogre
mVisibleobj->setOrientation(rot.w(), rot.x(), rot.y(), rot.z());
btVector3 pos = worldTrans.getOrigin();
mVisibleobj->setPosition(pos.x(), pos.y(), pos.z());
}

protected:
Ogre::SceneNode *mVisibleobj;
btTransform mPos1;
};

Now, whenever Bullet calls setWorldTransform, it updates the corresponding node's position, while objects that do not move are left untouched.

entry.title: First Board Game Session of 2012
entry.content:
The seven of us had planned to play ball, but the weather refused to cooperate, so we changed plans and began searching for a board-game café.

Ordinary board-game cafés usually stay open late and therefore open late as well. We tried three places without getting an answer and were despairing over where to go next when a bleary-eyed owner finally opened the door. Thank goodness. The café was called FF Board Games.

With seven people, it was hard to find a game that fit one table. After much indecision, we chose 7 Wonders. (PS: The owner kept asking whether we were sure we wanted to play it. What was that supposed to mean?) In the experimental game, Brother D and Egg Emperor invested heavily in military power, which proved unable to win. In the teaching game, Weinan and I tied for first with 57 points. Weinan earned at least 25 points from purple guild cards, while I scored heavily in science. My military performance was terrible, though fortunately I lost only a little there. In the second game everyone seemed familiar with the rules and began thinking about how to deny cards to the player on their left. Hjj was squeezed so hard by Brother D and me that he could not build the second stage of his wonder, greatly weakening the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. I benefited from completing the third stage of the Pyramids early. Neither neighbor developed military strength, so two military cards quietly earned me more than ten points. I finished with 52 and won by one. Weinan failed to block me at the end, though I also made a mistake at the beginning of Age III: I should have taken the six-point building instead of constructing the three-shield military card, since there would have been another opportunity later.

After lunch, we played several lighthearted games. I had not read the Small World Underground rules, much to my frustration. A woman who appeared to work at the café joined us, but the first game depended on knowledge of the United States and was painfully dull. I served as judge and did not even know its name. Then she introduced a horse-racing betting game. Egg Emperor's number-one horse led from the front and won him 100 yuan. Little Shou placed three successful bets on first, second, and third and finished second overall. My “last gamble” lost one space before the finish line and did not place. Otherwise I would have made a comeback. If the turn had returned to me just once more, I could have used the card I had drawn to pull my horse across the line. At least I did not finish last. The game seemed to end too quickly, before anyone had time to place enough bets. Were we playing it incorrectly?

I will skip the remaining three eight-player games of Legends of the Three Kingdoms.

entry.title: Bullet Physics Engine Notes 3: Collision Detection
entry.content:
Our objects can now move, and Bullet's calculations let us observe them moving and colliding as they would in the real world. The natural next question is: how can we tell which objects have collided with one another?

A Google search turns up several correct answers about collision detection in Bullet, but Bullet's own wiki provides the most comprehensive explanation.

For example, we can capture collisions with a callback function. The wiki shows one callback prototype: 

typedef bool (*ContactProcessedCallback)(
    btManifoldPoint& cp, // The contact point; ignore it if you do not need it
    void* body0, void* body1); // The two colliding objects

All we need to do is implement a function matching that prototype—myContactProcessedCallback—and assign it to Bullet's global variable gContactProcessedCallback. 

            gContactProcessedCallback = myContactProcessedCallback;

One final point: a collision between two objects may enter your callback several times during a single stepSimulation. Do not delete a body the first time the callback is invoked. The correct approach is to place pointers scheduled for deletion in a set, then delete them after stepSimulation finishes.

entry.title: Bullet Physics Engine Study Notes 4 (Collision Filtering)
entry.content:
Sometimes we want two objects to pass through one another instead of colliding, such as a ball in the Unstoppable state of a brick-breaking game. Bullet's wiki describes several approaches: some prevent a contact from being added, while others suppress it when the collision occurs. My personal favorite is the first approach on the wiki, a filter implemented with bitwise operations.

#define BIT(x) (1<<(x))// A macro
enum collisiontypes {
    COL_NOTHING = 0, //



const int groundCollidesWith = COL_AIRBOX;

const int airboxCollidesWith = COL_GROUND | COL_KINEMATICBOX;

const int kinematicboxCollidesWith = COL_AIRBOX;


Once those values are defined, add two parameters to addRigidBody to implement collision filtering:


m_dynamicsWorld->addRigidBody(boxBody, COL_AIRBOX, airboxCollidesWith);



One point deserves emphasis: in the latest version of Bullet, objects A and B collide only if A’s collision mask includes B and B’s mask includes A.

entry.title: A Simple Quantitative Analysis of Small World — Powers
entry.content:
I went back to Xiamen, played Small World several times with my two younger cousins, and then played many more games against the AI on the iPad (with Cursed! and Grand Dames). I came away with a new understanding of how races and powers combine. Here I will use a relatively intuitive quantitative approach to analyze the differences among races and powers.

All of the analysis below is based on the two-player board.


The two-player Small World map

Let us begin with powers. Broadly speaking, they fall into three groups: coin-generating powers, offensive support powers, and everything else...

Coin-generating powers: Alchemist, Forest, Hill, Swamp, and Wealthy all come with four race tokens. Merchant comes with two.

Because Alchemist gives a steady two extra coins each turn, we will use it as our baseline.

On the two-player map, there are four Forest, four Hill, and four Swamp regions. Clearly, these powers outperform Alchemist only when a player occupies at least three matching regions. Yet those regions are not adjacent on the board. In the process of reaching the third one, you will also have to occupy other regions, spreading your forces thin and weakening your defense. Once you suffer losses, you may no longer have enough troops to capture that third bonus region.

Wealthy gives a one-time payment of seven coins. At first glance that is 3.5 times Alchemist's benefit, which would make immediately going into decline after choosing it extremely efficient. In most cases, however, your first turn of conquest can take only three or four regions. If you go into decline with just three or four while another player does so with five to seven, you will earn two fewer coins on subsequent turns. That usually rules out an immediate decline. For every turn you remain active, Wealthy's initial advantage effectively shrinks by two. Balancing the two depends on reading the current situation. Near the end, you can rush to select Wealthy, or pair it with a race capable of an explosive opening, take the seven coins, and go into decline in one burst; that works reasonably well.

Last comes Merchant, unquestionably the most overpowered power in the game, which is why the designer gave it the fewest race tokens. Yet as soon as Merchant occupies three regions, it earns six coins, already reaching an average income. That shows just how strong it is. Its weak defense means it can only develop quietly on one side of the board rather than getting dragged into a prolonged fight; otherwise, the more it fights, the poorer it becomes.

Overall, coin-generating powers are all fairly overpowered. Normally, earning another coin requires conquering another region, which costs two or three race tokens and, more importantly, stretches the front line and makes defense difficult. If you can block your opponent's attack route, however, you can concentrate your defense. The disadvantage of coin powers is their smaller forces, which means they inevitably control fewer regions after going into decline.

Offensive support powers: Commando, Berserk, Seafaring, Flying, Underworld, Dragon Master, and Mounted.

Again, Commando reduces the number of tokens needed for every conquest by one, so we can use it as the baseline. Because each conquest costs less, you can take more regions. Suppose you have ten tokens and conquering a region normally costs 2.5 tokens on average. Now it costs only 1.5: instead of four regions, you can conquer more than six, gaining roughly two extra regions. That is basically the same benefit as Alchemist. If you want to attack regions occupied by another player, however, it is rarely possible to spend only 1.5 tokens per conquest.

Berserk lets you roll the die before deciding where to attack, which is ideal when you have several possible targets. Just remember that its expected value is still one, no different from Commando.

The next five offensive support powers all provide five race tokens, one more than Berserk and Commando.

Seafaring guarantees three inviolable regions, though it usually takes three turns to occupy all of them. Sometimes your opponent will block the way to one sea, leaving you with only two. The advantage is that sea regions remain occupied after you go into decline, which is extremely powerful. I therefore consider Seafaring slightly stronger than all the powers above.

Flying lets you attack anywhere on the map and can help you evade another player's pursuit (somewhat like Gypsies), but it provides no numerical bonus. Even when conquering empty regions, you can still take only five, so I consider Flying relatively weak.

Underworld and Mounted both reduce the number of tokens needed to conquer their corresponding terrain. There are only four cavern regions, however, compared with eight farmland or hill regions. Although caverns also provide an escape route from the battlefield, Underworld is still inferior to Mounted overall.

Dragon Master is a special power. It can strike at the heart of an opponent's territory and ensure that the region cannot be retaken. That is crucial for defense, because it leaves more troops available to guard other places (much like Seafaring). It is effectively one free region per turn, and since it also provides five tokens, its actual return should be close to average.

Other powers: Bivouacking, Heroic, Diplomat, Spirit, Stout, Pillaging, and Fortified.

These powers either provide no direct return or combine several types of benefit, making them difficult to compare with the average baseline, so I group them together as “other.” Players usually select them in response to the strategic needs of a particular game, giving them broader strategic significance.

Bivouacking provides five points of defense. It does nothing on the first turn, but once your front line stretches out, it can create an almost impregnable barrier. As mentioned before, defense is important not merely because it prevents an opponent from taking one region and avoids casualties, but because it blocks the opponent's intended route of attack and reduces their coin-gathering efficiency.

Heroic, like Bivouacking, is a defensive power. Its coverage is smaller, but its protection is absolute—it fears neither Ratmen, Skeletons, nor Dragon Master. Its heroes are literally invincible.

Diplomat's defensive value does not show particularly well in a two-player game, unless your race desperately wants to avoid being attacked—for example, when your opponent has Skeletons, Sorcerers, Orcs, or Pillaging.

Spirit is the quintessential strategic power. Its implications extend beyond the battlefield and require the player to understand the entire arc of the game. Choosing Spirit means abandoning the “one-stop” strategy—going into decline only once. Your goal is to use the advantage of having one additional race in decline to make up for the lost action caused by taking an extra decline turn.

Stout, like Spirit, affects the player's decline strategy. Selecting Stout to accelerate your own decline and grab a new race is a common approach.

Pillaging duplicates the Orcs' racial ability. It shines when paired with an aggressive race—Giants, Tritons, and Amazons are all good choices—but if your opponent hits you first, it may become useless.

Fortified is the second-most overpowered power in the game. Accordingly, it provides the second-fewest tokens—only three. As a combination of a coin-generating power and Bivouacking, Fortified demands absolute defense: the player must stay active long enough to construct fortress after fortress. Trolls and Elves are therefore excellent choices, as are numerous races such as Ratmen or Skeletons. If you manage to place a third fortress, you have succeeded. I once played with a woman trying Small World for the first time; she won with an Elves/Fortified “zero-attack” strategy, which left a deep impression on me.

That completes this brief analysis of all twenty powers in the base game. A four-token power should yield a benefit of two per turn, while a five-token power should yield slightly more than one (see Dragon Master).

**************************** Divider ****************************

P.S. Liking something may be a momentary impulse or love at first sight. Love, however, means persistence and thoughtful analysis. That is true of board games, and of people too.

entry.title: High School Reunion Board Game Session, February 8, 2012
entry.content:
We managed a small gathering before the winter break ended. This time, the participants finally turned out to be all men...


Final position in Ticket to Ride: Europe

Middle Finger (green), Softshell Turtle (blue), Army Flag (black), Cong (red), and I (yellow) arrived first, so we played a five-player game of Ticket to Ride: Europe. In addition to the base-game rules, the European edition adds stations and tunnels. Stations make long destination tickets relatively easy to complete, while tunnels introduce more uncertainty. At the beginning, everyone peacefully drew cards until Army Flag and Cong began fighting over the lower-left corner of the map. Nobody could hold back after that. Routes appeared everywhere as we rushed to keep others from taking the tracks we needed. Everyone soon completed their long ticket. Middle Finger and Softshell Turtle each drew two more short tickets, and I drew one. The wicked Army Flag tried to build all his trains quickly, ending the game before we could finish our new tickets, but his scheme failed. Middle Finger suffered terrible luck and failed every tunnel check, yet still tied Army Flag for second with 97 points. Softshell Turtle's flawless planning earned him sole possession of first with 117, including the longest-route bonus. My desperate attempt at a six-car tunnel failed, leaving me second from last with 82 points. What a shame—had it succeeded, I too would have scored 97.

Overall, Ticket to Ride feels rather luck-dependent. The key is how well your destination tickets fit together, and it is almost impossible to win without drawing additional tickets.


Our incorrectly played game of Power Grid…

The players were Softshell Turtle (green), Middle Finger (red), Army Flag (black), Brother Liu (blue), Cong (purple), and me (yellow).

Speaking of Power Grid, I am truly embarrassed: we played the rules incorrectly. First, as sixth player in the opening round, I somehow reversed the order of power-plant auctions and immediately surrendered the advantage of moving first. Then, when replenishing plants, we should have moved the lowest-numbered plant into the current market instead of revealing a new one directly into it. We made every kind of foolish mistake, and the session became pure comedy. I was forced to buy the largest plant, number 44, early in the game. That kept me high in turn order through the middle game and restricted where I could build. Before Step Two began, I deliberately built one fewer city in an attempt to break through. In one round I miscounted by a single Elektro and missed an opportunity to end the game early. During the final scramble for cities, my plants could power only fourteen, so I was limited to third place. Middle Finger made the crucial purchase of Seattle, which opened room for expansion, and finished second by powering fifteen cities. Softshell Turtle deserves special mention. Despite being boxed in by all of us, he persevered, successfully transformed his plant portfolio, and demonstrated excellent awareness in city construction. He eventually connected the east and west coasts of the United States, turning a natural chasm into a thoroughfare, and won by powering sixteen cities. Liu Mengyu was playing for the first time, chose a poor starting position, and tragically finished last.

Power Grid is undeniably a good game. For one thing, even while playing the rules incorrectly we could recognize its quality. It also helps players who fall behind, and the map is extremely well designed: every region has advantages and drawbacks that require patient consideration. I look forward to playing again!

After wandering around for a while, we watched a four-player Small World game at the other table. Wang Zhifei made a mistake in the penultimate round and threw away an excellent position, allowing Emperor Zhu to come back in the final round.

After dinner, we played four games of Shadow Hunters. I won three, twice by riding on someone else's coattails. Ha!

Thanks to A-Bao, Emperor Zhu, Wang Zhifei, Zhang Xiao, Cong, Liu Mengyu, Softshell Turtle, Middle Finger, and Army Flag for making it. I wonder how many people will be able to attend the next gathering.

entry.title: My First Solo Game of Ora et Labora
entry.content:
After studying the rules, I started a solo game. When it was over, I had only one reaction: this game is DBL.
The core rules are not complicated. Broadly speaking, it is worker placement: construct buildings, keep expanding the priory and building settlements, then add up building points, settlement points, and goods points for your final score.
But... the game has eight different goods, and sixteen if you count both sides! That is absurdly punishing. The complexity completely conceals the game's balance, because everything is so complicated that you cannot tell what is overpowered and what is trash. All I can say is, designer, you are ruthless. Is your next game going to challenge us with fifty kinds of tokens?

During the game, the first three settlement phases went fairly well and I got all the buildings constructed. By the fourth settlement phase, there were two buildings I could no longer afford to put up. It was obvious that I did not have enough rounds. Another reason was that I had not reviewed the buildings beforehand; if I had started converting goods into money earlier, I probably could have built one more. By the final settlement phase, I calculated and recalculated, squeezed every last resource, and ultimately used everything, leaving only cash and points...

My conclusion is that building placement matters enormously, and mine was awful. The trees on newly purchased district tiles are annoying: cutting them down yields little, but leaving them means you cannot construct buildings... I also barely used the Neutral Player from the rules—no more than five times, I think. It was usually when a certain resource had reached ten and I had no available worker, so I paid the neutral player to collect it for me...


End of the game

Right half

entry.title: Dorm-Room Ticket to Ride, March 19, 2012
entry.content:
While two roommates were away attending their second-major classes, I played a three-player game of Ticket to Ride: Europe with Brother D (black) and zxc (red).

After several rounds of drawing cards, I was the first to place a three-car route in the center of the map. Brother D saw that the situation was changing and immediately followed, while zxc continued hoarding cards. Then, at the beginning of one turn, zxc suddenly built four horizontal routes in succession starting from Brest, disrupting my plans and forcing me to detour. Since I was taking a detour anyway, I decided that I had to secure the longest route. I could also tell that zxc was concentrating on destination tickets, so by the middle game I had decided to complete the eight-car tunnel and try to end the game. Finally, with twelve trains remaining and seven cards of one color plus three locomotives in hand, I took the gamble and successfully built the eight-car tunnel. With the end now imminent, zxc and Brother D rushed to finish their final tickets. After the final scoring, I lost to zxc by one point. For all my calculations, I had failed to account for the fact that all of zxc's tickets were relatively large. Drawing another ticket at the end might also have given me a chance to win. My 44-car longest route, wasting only the final train, was no small achievement. Then again, if the game had continued, I might still have lost.


Final position

entry.title: Ticket to Ride and the Second Xiaoyaoyou Demo Event
entry.content:
March 8

Players: Brother D (blue), Brother Bo (black), zxc (red), and me (yellow)

This was our first four-player game of TTR, and we got the rules wrong: the long-route ticket was apparently optional. As a result, Brother D, Brother Bo, and I became hopelessly tangled in Western Europe while zxc had Eastern Europe all to himself. By the time we noticed, it was too late. Zhang Xiaocheng had completed a loop through Eastern Europe. At the end, he had finished his long route plus six short Eastern European routes and claimed the longest-route card, putting him far ahead. Brother Bo came second with 111 points, I came third with 107, and Brother D was third with 102.


At the end

Look closely at the red route in Eastern Europe: apart from six train cars, the other 39 form a Hamiltonian cycle.

Western Europe has the most stations, along with a jumble of train cars in three colors.

March 10

Xiaoyaoyou demo event

Players: Zhang Chi and me

On the eve of the retail release, Softstar Beijing once again partnered with fan clubs around the country to hold a second demo event. This version added new event cards, making a card game that already involved substantial randomness even harder to control.

Because we used the beginner-friendly 2v2 format, all cards with range effects were removed, as were characters focused on support and disruption. Characters with high spirit power, low range, and strong single-target attacks therefore gained a huge advantage, making Chonglou and Xuanxiao even more outrageous. Many event cards punish large hands, so Murong Ziying suffered badly.

The first round was best of three. In game one, when it was two against one, our card luck was terrible, and we somehow lost by 21 spirit power to 22. Game two was even more tragic: every time we emptied Chonglou's hand, we would draw an event that made players with more cards discard and players with fewer cards draw. We still scraped out a win. Our luck finally improved in game three. Acting first, my Chonglou used Duel in combination with the Lava Beast King's entrance effect and Xuejian's follow-up attack to eliminate Liu Mengli on the very first turn, laying the foundation for victory.

Every match after that was decided by a single game. We faced a team of two women, and I have to admit that women really do get incredible luck: right at the start, we drew an event card and were left with only one health... Things grew even worse afterward. The monsters that revealed high spirit power disappeared early, and they took the Five Venom Beast as well, leaving us with no hope of winning...

Those two women then defeated the other two champions from the previous event and beat last year's third-place team in the final to win the championship. We only lost to the eventual winners, so it was not too bad.


At the final table

You can see that the two women are ahead in spirit power and health, while the draw pile is nearly empty. The outcome is settled.


Demon Sword miniature

The Demon Sword miniature included in the retail edition. The woman whose half-profile is visible was one of the champions!

entry.title: Session Report: Celebrating the End of wzh's GRE
entry.content:
I have had rather a lot going on lately—interviews, written tests, assignments, projects, and every kind of trap—so it took me a long time to find time for a session report.

wzh endured a long period without board games for the sake of one GRE attempt. Apparently the score was an awkward one, neither high nor low. The good news is that the GRE may stop requiring every score in the future, letting applicants send only their best result.

We began with a four-player game of Agricola. I had nearly forgotten the rules, so naturally I finished last without suspense. The brain-burning finale was still very entertaining. At that point, cjr had led from beginning to end and was heading toward our highest-ever four-player score, while I still had as many as seven empty spaces on my farm. In the last round I plowed and sowed, then used an occupation card to build two rooms in succession and add stables. In the middle of it all, people mocked my intelligence because I forgot I could spend the vegetable I had just received to exchange for more resources... Miraculously, I finished with only one empty space. I could have sworn I had calculated a way to fill everything.

I lost the game at the beginning: I forgot to play Traveling Salesman and even forgot that sowing requires plowed fields. cjr also won at the beginning, using Lover to have the first child. zxc began with excellent momentum but had children too late and ran out of strength near the end. wzh lost first place amid endless analysis paralysis... When will he break that habit?

Next came the Ora et Labora game that wzh had long anticipated. To avoid looking as though I were bullying newcomers, I chose the French rules, with which I was not very familiar either. Somehow every game with wzh turns into a mutual-blocking battle. Although I ultimately won by a substantial margin, my total score was only about 213, which was deeply frustrating.

For more pictures, visit my album through this portal.


First place… Four settlements in the middle enclosed an eight-point building

entry.title: After Adversity Comes Good Fortune?
entry.content: The previous few weeks had brought one setback after another, along with enough assignments to make me cough blood. But everything seemed to stop on the sixth. The final frustration came when, after finishing my second interview full of confidence, Microsoft's HR representative merely told me to wait for news. Then yesterday, during class, I suddenly received a call from Microsoft HR. I felt a little surge of excitement. When she told me I could join as an intern, the gloom of the past few weeks seemed to vanish, and I felt much lighter. I spent the whole day enjoying myself, and just now played three games of Dominant Species with wzh. Is this what people mean when they say good fortune follows adversity? Perhaps.

entry.title: A Few Thoughts — May 1, 2012
entry.content:
I have noticed that my mind becomes incredibly active in the shower. Is this the legendary “think for 27 minutes, wash for three” routine?

1. I have been reading about word segmentation lately and suddenly thought of a question. If CAPTCHAs can help identify letters, why can we not use CAPTCHAs to help build a word-segmentation database? There is strength in numbers.

2. Once a system has been designed, suppose that only one out of every hundred errors is caused by a system bug while all the others result from uncontrollable factors. Is that bug still worth fixing?
If your answer is yes, consider this example:
In a certain language, when one person asks another to repeat what they just said, only one time in a hundred is caused by ambiguity. The other 99 occur because the speaker mumbled, spoke too quickly, or the listener was distracted. Does that language need to be corrected?
If not, why not?
3. People should try to avoid falling into a mental pattern of storing, searching, and retrieving. This pattern is devastating to human creativity.

entry.title: A Game of Thrones: The Board Game Unboxing—I Cannot Wait to Play
entry.content:
As someone obsessed with game boards and a new fan of A Song of Ice and Fire, I had wanted an Ice and Fire game for a long time. Unfortunately, I heard that the second edition's board was rather poor and held off. Then I learned that the publisher was sending out a revised board. I happened to be in a very good mood last week, so I bought a copy without hesitation, along with two T-shirts—Greyjoy and Lannister.

A quick introduction, based on one rough reading of the rules: this is a negotiation-heavy game in which diplomacy is crucial, especially for Lannister and Baratheon, both caught between enemies from the beginning. Alliances rest on verbal promises, while breaking one requires no justification at all. Backstabbing is entirely legal, though a player who values honor can still win. The game lasts ten rounds. At the end, whoever controls the most castles and strongholds wins; any player who controls seven during the game wins immediately.

The game is best with six players, so getting it to the table will probably be quite difficult. If I can find four, I may have to settle for that. Ideally they should all be Ice and Fire fans, or the experience could be frustrating. Here is an excellent session report: portal.

entry.title: A Game of Thrones Session Report: July 4, 2012
entry.content:
As the old saying goes, what has long been united must divide, and what has long been divided must unite. After years of peace, hidden troubles had begun to stir within the realm. The old king's death meant that Westeros would once again be drenched in blood. This time, six kings rose at once to take part in the game of thrones.

They were:

From Dragonstone, the yellow crowned-stag House Baratheon, beginning with the Iron Throne—the symbol of power and order. Regent of the realm and former lord of the Storm Kingdom: Xiaocheng Baratheon.

From Pyke, the black and ferocious kraken of House Greyjoy, beginning with the Valyrian Steel Blade—the symbol of war and strength. Lord of the captains of Ironman's Bay: titanxxh Greyjoy.

From Lannisport, the red and cunning lion of House Lannister, beginning with the Messenger Raven—the symbol of intelligence and intrigue. Warden of the West and lord of the Rock: Zihan Lannister.

From Winterfell, the white direwolf of the frozen north, Warden of the North and lord of the Northern Kingdom: Brother D Stark.

From Highgarden, the green golden rose of House Tyrell, Warden of the South and lord of the Reach: Ji'er Tyrell.

From Sunspear, the orange sun pierced by a spear, lord of Dorne: Xiaoshou Martell.

The rulers of Houses Lannister, Tyrell, and Stark were all newly crowned kings who had not been tested in the previous war.

At the council before hostilities began, the six kings swore together before the old gods and the new: whoever first controlled seven strongholds or castles would receive the immediate submission of the others, who would lower their banners and return their blades to storage. If ten years passed first, they would likewise cease burdening the people with war and acclaim as Protector of the Realm whoever commanded the broadest lands and richest cities.

I will recount the war from my own perspective, that of House Greyjoy. The black kraken began with unmatched military power and followed its family words, “We Do Not Sow.” In the very first year, I sent this letter:

Honorable Lord Lannister,

Our two houses possess the richest lands on the continent, and we are also its closest neighbors. I hope you will not believe the provocations of others. I promise not to attack you first. In exchange, I propose that you surrender Riverrun. If necessary, I am willing to return it when you stand on the verge of victory. Furthermore, if Tyrell or Baratheon dares invade your territory, I will support your battle without condition. May the red and black houses remain friends for generations and resist every foreign foe together.

Respectfully, titanxxh Greyjoy, ruler of Pyke and Ironman's Bay and King in the North—yes, all the same person.

The expected bargaining soon began, but it remained within an acceptable range. Red and black finally agreed that once Lannister controlled five castles, red could begin an attack on Riverrun. My private thought: heh, if you ever reach five, everyone else will be attacking you and you will probably have no attention to spare for Riverrun.

Meanwhile, at the southern end of the continent, Tyrell and Martell went to war as though bound by an ancient feud. Their conflict had little effect on me, but it benefited red and yellow and helped strengthen the red-black friendship by persuading Lannister that the south held more exciting opportunities.

Xiaocheng abandoned his usual opening of marching directly on King's Landing. He chose to muster at his home area, apparently hoping to exploit the white newcomer's mistake and seize the Narrow Sea. Unfortunately for him, I had already warned white about that strategic position. Stark decisively mustered at home and moved troops into the Narrow Sea, thwarting Xiaocheng's scheme.

I used our agreement to advance into Riverrun and Seagard. I deliberately did not march into Flint's Finger because an opening that appeared too dominant would provoke universal hostility.

In years two and three, the Westeros cards pleased me by producing supply and mustering, giving me four supply and the greatest recruitment capacity. What did not please me were two unexpectedly timed Clash of Kings events—one chosen by red. I failed to retain the Valyrian Steel Blade, which instead went to my direct enemy Stark. I remained last on the Raven track, and the tragedy of having no starred orders kept me from advancing quickly into Bay of Ice. My private thought: this was my best opportunity to pacify the north in a single move, but I failed to seize it and gave Stark room to breathe.

Green overextended aggressively. The Raven position he had just obtained was pushed to last by Doran Martell. Orange and green continued grinding one another down and lost their early advantage. House Baratheon profited and soon became everyone's target, drawing red into an effort to contain him. At this point my strategy had partly succeeded and partly failed. Riverrun remained alert for a Lannister betrayal, while Ironman's Bay increased its shipbuilding to secure the seas.

My awkward position on the influence tracks and lack of starred orders convinced me to consolidate political power and temporarily avoid war, hoping to win the Blade and Raven when the next Clash of Kings appeared. I also built two siege engines at home, intending to seize a better turn order and then take Winterfell directly. Heaven did not cooperate: the second Clash of Kings did not arrive until the third-to-last round, but that comes later. In the meantime I repeatedly probed white's Bay of Ice, hoping to draw out Eddard Stark. I failed, though at least I removed Roose Bolton and Robb Stark.

Green and orange eventually made peace after witnessing yellow's strength. Unfortunately, both had already committed their best commanders and could do little, so red became the principal force preventing a Baratheon victory. I kept my promise never to invade red territory, even when doing so would have been easier. My private thought: I also wanted to avoid distracting red from checking yellow and allowing yellow to grow unchecked. Nor did I want to become conspicuously powerful too soon. Red's lands were easy for others to surround, while white's were much easier to defend.

The radius of time's wheel is proportional to the scale of the war, and each revolution became slower than the last.

In the eighth year, Clash of Kings finally appeared, but circumstances had changed. The expected great war in the central lands had not erupted. Every house possessed increasing stores of power, while I had entered the awkward position of being unable to gain any. Forced by necessity, I spent every power token to accept rankings of second, third, and third on the three influence tracks.

Even without the Blade, starred orders helped me surge into Bay of Ice and capture Winterfell through three linked attacks. With Balon in hand, I could guarantee holding it until the commanders returned. But calculations cannot defeat fate. Clash of Kings appeared again in round nine, while every player simultaneously realized that black's momentum was becoming unstoppable. The treacherous red lion broke our alliance: Gregor Clegane brutally killed three of my knights and retook Riverrun. Lannister also incited Tyrell to use the Queen of Thorns to remove my starred support order in Bay of Ice.

The balance shifted in an instant and left me dangerously exposed. At that critical moment, I voluntarily returned Winterfell to white so he would not need to spend Eddard Stark. I counterattacked Riverrun, killed red's two siege engines, and stabilized my rear while temporarily easing my conflict with white. Pointing out that yellow held the Iron Throne, Valyrian Steel Blade, and Messenger Raven, I tried to redirect everyone's attention and coax green, orange, and yellow into fighting among themselves.

The final year arrived at last. A starred Lannister support order in Blackwater became the key to the entire contest. Castles around the Blackwater changed hands repeatedly. At the decisive moment, the red lion displayed a little honor and, following a principle of aiding the weak, held green, orange, and yellow to four castles each. I concentrated my forces, relied on King Balon and the Iron Captain to capture and hold Winterfell, and likewise reached four castles. Because I controlled three strongholds, I won!!!

The ten-year struggle among six kings ended. Every house had endured political contests, diplomatic maneuvering, and military confrontation. In the end, House Greyjoy proved that taking by force surpassed laboring in the fields. With iron and blood, it defended the honor of the ironborn, ascended the Iron Throne, and became the second king and Protector of the Realm.

entry.title: My First Two Weeks Interning at Microsoft
entry.content:
First experiences in life are always exciting. I should have published this last week, but my boss was away on a business trip and we moved offices on Friday. I spent almost the entire week installing software, becoming familiar with the environment, and meeting colleagues. In fact, I still have not met everyone; our group is simply too large. In other words, the week passed without my doing much of consequence.

My boss returned as the second week began, and we moved into a new environment. An office that had looked empty was filled within two days. I have to admire the speed at which Microsoft hires people.

To get to the point, let me first describe the Microsoft workplace. All the offices are in Building 01, which has five floors. Each floor is divided into a long wing and a short wing, and each wing has two office areas with a lounge between them. The pantry provides all kinds of food and drinks, though that is probably standard at any large company. I will mention a few details that particularly pleased me. Every handwashing area has recycled paper for drying your hands, and somehow even the restrooms smell pleasant. Disposable toilet-seat covers are provided. Many walls can be written on; I even saw notes on some of them telling cleaners not to erase the writing. What impressed me most was how conscientious the staff were. Cleaners seemed to patrol continuously and wiped up dirt almost as soon as they saw it. If you needed something, they responded quickly. As for dining, Microsoft has so many people that the cafeteria becomes rather crowded at peak times. Employees are considerate and push their chairs back into place after eating. The food is only average. Large meat dishes are a little expensive, while everything else is cheap, though the portions are smaller than at school. The soup is decent. But there is only one counter serving dinner!

I am in the HPC group within STB, and the group has a great many people. Zhang Heng is here with me, but his work is entirely unrelated to mine. Brother Xiong is in testing, so his work has almost nothing to do with mine either. A new full-time employee started this Monday, just as our director returned from a business trip, so the group took the newcomer out for a meal. Another intern and I were lucky enough to be invited. The restaurant had no table large enough for everyone, so we split up. I sat at the same table as the director and our PM and listened to much of their conversation. My only reaction was amazement at how much our PM knew. They discussed the character of Japanese people, their strengths and weaknesses, and some of our group's work. Listening from the side made me realize how little life experience I have. Another event this week is that the interviewer who hired me will leave for the US headquarters next week. This Friday was his final day in this office. A mood of farewell spread through the workplace, and it was clear that the employees have close relationships.

Finally, a little about my assignment, though I cannot describe it in detail. I seem to have been fortunate: immediately after joining, I became part of a new project intended to build a cloud marketplace. We have already held several meetings. Experiencing Microsoft's operating process from the beginning of a project is valuable. In the first meeting, the task my boss assigned sounded fairly simple. After this Friday's meeting, it no longer seemed simple at all. The PM listed five personas in the project, introduced each persona's story, gave the project goal a clearer character, and then discussed two questions with the director. Even so, this was not yet a formal, detailed planning meeting; many questions remain exploratory.

For now, I am reading development documents, learning the APIs, setting up the environment and running examples, experimenting on my own, and waiting for the UX mockups. I suspect we will have another meeting to refine everything.

entry.title: Recent Happenings
entry.content:
The biggest story lately has unquestionably been Liu Xiang's fall—so much so that you can barely find reports about China losing a diving gold or the women's volleyball team being eliminated. I watched Lao Liang's video on Sina, and his argument was both reasonable and compassionate. Liu Xiang is unquestionably the victim in this incident: he lost the race, ruptured his Achilles tendon, and, after four years of criticism, will continue to face it. Yet the mainstream media's response has been completely different from four years ago, with almost universal praise. Lao Liang cites this as evidence that the whole event was a performance. Looking back, the media had actually reported before the race that Liu Xiang's injury might affect him. By leaking that possibility, they effectively prepared the audience. As Lao Liang said, various forces pushed Liu Xiang onto the track, creating a situation in which he had to run whether he wanted to or not. Even the best possible outcome of that gamble would merely have eased the pressure of public opinion on the Chinese delegation. In reality, Liu Xiang paid a terrible price. Everyone knows what a ruptured Achilles means for an athlete; it is now almost impossible for him to return to his peak (that is not pessimism, simply reality). Liu Xiang is still fortunate compared with athletes forced into retirement by injury, because at least he once enjoyed glory. The episode also exposed some chronic flaws in media coverage: disregarding individual interests, overemphasizing moral narratives, and so on. More follow-up reports will surely appear, and we can only wait for the full details. Finally, I wish Liu Xiang a speedy recovery.

Now, work. The boss went abroad and should have returned this week, but he has not appeared for the past two days. With today's typhoon as well (the company emailed us saying we did not have to come in... which is why I have time to write this), I have gone nearly twenty days without seeing him. I cannot do his portion of the work, while another part unexpectedly requires building a UI... With no alternative, I looked into the ASP.NET MVC architecture. It feels extremely powerful, and I have gained a better understanding of some C# features (though there are still parts I cannot grasp... Microsoft's stuff can be such a pain). I spent all day yesterday wrestling with VS2010 and finally reinstalled it successfully. If only installing Windows software were as simple as copying it over and running it. I feel that my productivity is rather low right now...

As for entertainment lately, I have been following two TV series. One is Xuan-Yuan Sword, which leaves me at a loss for words (I am still persevering—do you know how much willpower that takes?), and the other is iPartment 3. Overall, iPartment 3 is quite good. Apart from having a few too many product placements, its content connects more closely with games. My favorite story is “If There Were No Ifs”; its slightly fatalistic arrangement feels original. I played a great many board games in July because, during the first month of summer vacation, most classmates had major summer assignments and stayed on campus. We probably played Small World most often. After getting Small World Underground, the game felt reborn. In second place was Mage Knight, jointly purchased by wzh and cjr. It combines deck-building, a map, varied player powers, and other mechanisms in a refreshing way, though its balance is debatable and its ranking of 13 feels inflated. I hope to try the PvP rules next time. I also played A Game of Thrones with friends from Gamer's Home. I drew House Martell and narrowly won in the end. This month, I also bought a used copy of Quarriors to try. If I do not like it, I will sell it third-hand and trade up to The Castles of Burgundy, haha.

Finally, I hope mighty Brazil wins the championship. It would be even better if they scored three goals in the final too. Three goals in every match must be some kind of record, right?

entry.title: Thoughts on My Beloved Brazil Team
entry.content:
The men's Olympic football tournament has ended, and once again Brazil failed to win the championship. Fans of other countries might consider second place a good result, but Brazilian supporters are demanding: anything short of the title is failure.

Here are some of the reasons Brazil lost the final.

Conceding at the start: by itself, this would not have created such danger, but Mexico's style made it hazardous. Mexicans get their feet to the ball as quickly as Brazilians. After falling behind, Mano was inevitably going to push the team forward, given his level of judgment. That greatly increased the danger whenever possession was lost in midfield, because both fullbacks tend to go forward without getting back. Marcelo is the senior figure, so nobody criticizes him; poor Rafael, the junior, takes the blame. Yet the two center-backs suffered most of all, because Thiago Silva and Juan had to move wide to cover, while both defensive midfielders were liabilities. Brazil became trapped between the need to attack and the fear of conceding. Once the players' mentality went wrong, the result was there for everyone to see: they failed to equalize in the first half. I would attribute 60% of the eventual defeat to the impatience produced by conceding early and attacking without success.

The referee: from the opening minutes, the referee allowed a great deal of contact, encouraging Mexico's aggressive challenges and influencing the direction of the match. The free kick that led to the second goal was also ridiculous, but officiating cannot excuse the goal, since the decision did not put the ball directly into the net. Refereeing accounted for roughly 10%.

The goalkeeper: Gabriel's poor form did not begin in this match. In several earlier games, he took risks coming for corners and failed to reach the ball. Without good fortune, he would have conceded long ago. Just look at how steady the opposing keeper was. Fifteen percent.

Finishing: after Hulk came on, the attack began to function properly. Perhaps the occasion affected them. The young players were behind in an Olympic final and understandably nervous, and they failed to convert several excellent chances. Ten percent.

Neymar's performance: Neymar remained dangerous when dribbling, but his physical disadvantage was too large. If he attempted ten take-ons in a match, perhaps only three succeeded, which is not very efficient. Given his youth, however, it would be difficult to demand that he change his style within a few matches. In my view, Neymar should not have kept looking for opportunities out wide. Once Brazil had to take desperate risks, the left flank should have been left to Marcelo. Neymar could occasionally drive through the middle to draw defenders, then release Marcelo and let Marcelo's individual ability determine whether to cut inside or reach the byline. Instead, the attack became too rigid. Five percent.

Losing a final is nothing shameful. Older generations of Brazilians also lost finals. The World Cup in two years is what truly matters, but without qualifiers it remains unclear how far this group of young Brazil players can develop. The good news is that Oscar and Lucas have both moved to Europe. I hope exposure to the European style makes them more mature.

Mano can more or less be dismissed now. His only contribution was completing the national team's generational transition, replacing the Dunga-era side that neglected young players with the current team led by those born in the 1990s. He was always going to bear responsibility for the pain caused by such a dramatic change. Comparing the two coaches, Dunga's flaw was stubborn self-confidence. His selections denied opportunities to Brazil's 1985–1989 generation, creating a gap in the talent pipeline and storing up trouble for the future. Unfortunately, after winning title after title, Dunga was eliminated at the World Cup, and his gamble failed. Mano has even more weaknesses. He has never organized the defense properly, his attacking patterns are inconsistent, and he has never found a central figure. Everyone seems capable of contributing a little, yet nobody provides a core. That leaves the team entirely dependent on individual ability, which will always be punished against strong opponents.

entry.title: Lessons for Beginners After Beating Civilization V on Deity
entry.content:
I did not begin playing Civilization V this year, and it was also the first Civilization game I encountered. I remember choosing difficulty level six for my first game, on a small map with two continents. It did not feel too difficult, and I won on my first attempt... Then I challenged Deity immediately and was crushed. My skill level remained around difficulty seven afterward, and eventually I stopped playing.
This year I heard that Civilization V had received an expansion and picked it up again, determined to beat Deity this time. After reading some guides on the forum—especially i's split-path Archery strategy—I finally succeeded, which made me very happy.
Recently I have won three times, all by domination on Pangaea, without research agreements and after extracting money before each war: Babylon on small Deity at turn 298, Maya on standard Deity at turn 299, and Persia on standard Deity at turn 261. So slow...

In my experience, several points are crucial.

First comes technology. You cannot fall behind in research or military technology; everything else is negotiable. That is why I initially chose Babylon. I believed its early Great Scientist could produce a wave of technological advantage. Even if you cannot reach Industrialization first, you must unlock Gatling Guns before every AI. Then attack the nearby AI with the highest score, establish an advantage, unlock aircraft, and the game is essentially won.

Next is the location of your cities. I usually like to settle near a natural wonder, even if that requires walking a long way—I can place another city in between later—or directly in an opponent's face.

For social policies, I favor Tradition. I have read expert guides and session reports about wide expansion through Liberty and tried it myself, but diplomacy is genuinely difficult and military strength never rises enough. A traditional four-city empire makes happiness easy to manage, population easy to grow, and diplomacy reasonably good, which suits newcomers.

After Tradition, I choose Honor or Commerce according to the situation. Recently I have liked the two policies on Commerce's right side before going directly into Rationalism. I cannot open many policies, perhaps because my culture output is weak. A typical total is full Tradition, full Rationalism, the right two or three Commerce policies, and the first one or two on Freedom's right branch.

My building strategy is fairly mindless. Buy science and gold buildings as quickly as possible; the rest can wait. You can spend production on culture buildings. Forget factories and similar buildings: buy them if you can afford them and ignore them for now if you cannot. Whenever I do not know what a city should build, I usually produce a unit. You can build unlimited units, whereas each building can only be bought once... Once the AIs begin fighting each other, you generally cannot secure worthwhile wonders after the middle game.

I am terrible at managing city-states. Usually I can control only the nearest two and cannot be bothered with the rest.

I founded a religion in every game, and by the end it usually shared the world with one other religion. I have not researched religion much, so I will not discuss it. Early on I relied on natural wonders to secure a religion, which is hardly a universally applicable method.

PS: I always assumed the AI cheated on science output. After my latest Deity victory with Persia, I checked the demographics and found that, by staffing specialists, my per-turn research had actually surpassed the leading Korean AI in the middle game and ranked first. On Deity, apart from beginning with two settlers, are the AI's food, gold, culture, science, and production all calculated normally?

entry.title: My First Civilization V Deity Win: The Rebirth of Babylon
entry.content:
I recently read many expert guides and game reports on CivFanatics China. After several attempts, this novice finally beat Deity difficulty.

Before moving up in difficulty, I always felt that the AI developed unbelievably fast and I could never keep pace. Then I read I-Da's guide to a beeline for Archery, together with the new expansion's strategy of throwing successive Great Generals at the enemy. It seemed that there might still be a way to catch up.

The main idea is as follows:

Research Composite Bowmen as quickly as possible. Upgrade six Archers and use the brief advantage of the new unit type to overwhelm and eliminate one AI. Then research Philosophy, rush the National College, and beeline along the lower branch of the technology tree. Once Crossbowmen arrive, exploit another temporary advantage to eliminate a second opponent. At that point you control three capitals, wonders included, and have established an advantage large enough that you should be able to win.

The strategy exploits the fact that although the AI develops at divine speed, it researches technologies evenly without a clear focus. A human player can prioritize military technologies and create a sudden burst of strength by upgrading an entire unit class at once, using war to establish an advantage and gradually convert it into victory. The plan looked simple, clear, and thoroughly plausible, so I immediately tested it in two games. I abandoned both halfway through. In the first, I failed to eliminate anyone within eighty turns and gave up. In the second, I destroyed one opponent but fell too far behind militarily in the middle game. I had also pursued Industrialization before Machinery, decided the position was hopeless, and abandoned that game as well. I returned to the reports and found one describing a Babylonian science victory. Babylon's free early Great Scientist and the burst of research from planting an Academy seemed capable of reaching Machinery before the AI, so I tried again. As expected, the Great Scientist awarded after Writing created a scientific lead. After eliminating one opponent, I challenged Sweden, the universal enemy. But by the time I had finally driven Sweden from history, Austria had built a huge empire through diplomatic marriages and had already completed the Apollo Program. Faraway Empress Wu continued developing in peace, grew stronger by the day, and soon completed Apollo as well. After weighing the options repeatedly, I decided to eliminate the nearer Austrian empire first. Fate refused to cooperate: after I captured several Austrian cities, the great Empress had already launched her spaceship. Careful reflection revealed the key cause of failure: happiness management. Continuous conquest left my empire unhappy for most of the middle and late game, severely harming production. Yesterday I started over, again as Babylon. From the beginning, I prioritized happiness, kept it above five, founded new cities only then, avoided trading luxuries carelessly, and bought the friendship of one mercantile city-state. I withstood a powerful assault from the Iroquois Mohawk Warriors, a unique swordsman that requires no iron, coming from the north. Then I immediately sent my first Great General to establish a citadel and made the Iroquois my first target. I had to avenge the humiliation, especially since they had declared war on me; extracting a war indemnity seemed very possible. After sacrificing one Great General to stabilize the defense around my first expansion city, I used the second aggressively, captured the capital Onondaga, and—just as expected—the AI offered reparations and peace on the next turn. I gladly accepted.

Meanwhile, my second and third expansion cities were ready, and I was eyeing the powerful Austria next door. Why is it always Austria? Just as I prepared to attack, the AI married the city-state of Hanoi and blocked my route. I had no choice but to wait for Artillery and capture Hanoi first. That created another problem: after I took Hanoi, Austria attacked on two fronts, sending another force against my third city and giving me a considerable headache. I reloaded a save from several turns earlier and decided to drive between my second and third cities, abandoning the original route south through Hanoi. The hills here made movement difficult, but they also made it hard for the AI to approach. Machine Guns stood behind the Artillery, ready to destroy any enemy that climbed onto a hill. The position supported both attack and defense.

Capturing the vital city of Salzburg effectively opened the roads toward both the Austrian capital and India. Austria still led in score, but India had the technological lead and had completed the Apollo Program. The situation was nevertheless better than in the previous game because the distant Celts and Ethiopia trailed me scientifically and posed no concern. My immediate goals were to devote everything to science, unlock aircraft as quickly as possible, and capture Vienna fast enough to force peace. After planting a Great General's citadel, I took Vienna and secured the most important resource of all: oil. I devoted production to aircraft in preparation for an invasion of India. Artillery captured the frontline city of Vijayanagara and trapped seven early Indian aircraft there. The AI counterattacked with everything it had, and the city changed hands repeatedly. A metropolis that had once contained more than thirty citizens became a ruin with a population of one. When our Knights captured the city, their excellent mobility let them move back out, whereas enemy Infantry were trapped and destroyed inside. After several exchanges, the AI had no hope of retaking the city. My aircraft redeployed to attack Delhi.

The capture of Delhi and Mumbai sealed India's defeat. From then on, aircraft and tanks ruled the world. I rapidly fought my way to the gates of Ethiopia and achieved victory.

Looking back over the entire game, I managed happiness much better. The graph below shows that it was almost never negative. The traditional four-city build, together with circuses, colosseums, and theaters, deserves much of the credit. Later, I also captured many AI wonders that increased happiness.

PS: At the end, the strongest military still belonged not to me but to Austria. Good grief.

Final scores

Map replay video—the repeated struggle for Vijayanagara is entertaining.

entry.title: A WoW Quest Rant: Human Nature at Its Ugliest
entry.content:
This mechanically clumsy player has recently been playing WoW. Patch 5.2 added a weekly quest called Setting the Trap, which requires a group of at least four players. It has four stages, and each one requires a player to spend one of their own stones to activate it.

After recruiting in world chat, we finally assembled four people with stones, plus one freeloader. At the first stage, because it was my first time doing the quest, I did not understand what was going on. Everyone hung back and refused to activate it, which baffled me—I only learned the reason later. Eventually the group leader who had recruited us used a stone, and we cleared the stage quickly. For the second stage, I had figured it out and stepped forward to activate it.

After we finished the second stage, one of the people with a stone unexpectedly left the group. We could not recruit a replacement through world chat. Only a rogue in the party still had a stone, while two stages remained. The rogue refused to use it, saying that even if he did, we still could not finish the quest. He plainly wanted to save his stone and find another group later...

After a long wait with no recruits, the freeloader became impatient and said, “Either start it or leave.” The rogue immediately snapped back: “The two people who actually spent stones have not complained, so what the hell are you talking about?” Once things reached that point, I knew the run was doomed and left. Thinking about it afterward, I finally understood why everyone had hesitated at the beginning: they were afraid of encountering a jerk who would spend nothing and leave early...

There are too many things to criticize in that sequence. The ugliness of human nature was on full display.

entry.title: Mysterious Tibet in Photos
entry.content:
Jokhang Temple, Potala Palace, Mila Pass, Niyang River, Basum Tso, Lulang Forest, Nanyigou Valley, Namcha Barwa, Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon, Kadinggou Heavenly Buddha Waterfall, Yamdrok Lake, Karola Glacier, Duoqing Co, Mount Everest Base Camp, Yangbajain Hot Springs, and Namtso.

The beautiful scenery needs no introduction. Beyond that, my strongest impression of this journey through Tibet can be summarized in one sentence: the quality of the tourist infrastructure does not match the beauty of the landscape. From hotels to restaurants, the services fall far short of what a tourist destination should offer, yet prices are the same as in other tourist cities—and sometimes even higher.


Our itinerary, covering nearly 3,000 kilometers in total

Day 1: Jokhang Temple & Potala Palace

Our guide said that three kinds of people especially love Tibet: those who enjoy the meeting and exchange of different cultures, those with religious faith, and those searching for spiritual refuge.


Pilgrims bring the prayers of all living beings to Jokhang Temple and complete one hundred thousand full-body prostrations before entering. Their faces are the darkest and their clothes the dirtiest, but their hearts are the purest.

Lhasa is the center of Tibet, but Jokhang Temple is the true heart of Lhasa. The Tibetan Empire was imagined as a supine demoness, with Jokhang Temple standing over her heart to subdue her. The site was originally a lake, so building the temple first required filling it. Goats were the principal means of transport, carrying bags of earth and sand on their backs until the lake had been filled and the temple's foundation could be laid. The modern name Lhasa actually evolved from the Jokhang Temple. The city was not originally called LASA; old documents call it RASA. RA means goat and SA means earth, so the name meant “the place built by goats.” Later, after this sacred Buddhist hall was erected—with an image of the Buddha, scriptures, stupas, and worshippers arriving from every direction—people regarded it as the land of the Buddha and changed the name to Lhasa. LA means Buddha in Tibetan, and SA means land.


The golden roof of Jokhang Temple, bright enough to dazzle your eyes!


Unlike temples in central China, where incense is burned, Tibetan temples use butter lamps that remain continuously lit.

Like many temples, Jokhang does not permit photography inside. What makes it different is that pilgrims and tourists follow separate paths. Ordinary visitors cannot enter every inner chapel, which means they also cannot see the only surviving original life-size statue of the twelve-year-old Shakyamuni Buddha.


A distant view of Potala Palace from Jokhang Temple: the White Palace below and the Red Palace above

Built against the mountainside, Potala Palace is magnificent: a miracle of architectural history, a museum of the past, and a palace of art. Sixty percent of Tibet's treasures are said to be gathered here. It holds untold quantities of gold, jewels, thangkas, murals, and scriptures, along with the stupas of successive Dalai Lamas. The stupa of the Fifth Dalai Lama is the largest, sheathed in gold and set with innumerable gems. One of them is said to be a luminous pearl taken from an elephant's brain and to be beyond price.


The White Palace’s exterior is not covered with modern paint. It is coated with a mixture of yak milk, honey, Tibetan medicine, and a little lime. During renovations every five to eight years, the mixture is poured from above, producing this appearance.


To reduce the weight of the Red Palace, these “walls” are made from bundles of red branches. They reportedly take five years to prepare. When replaced, they are first fumigated with a Tibetan medicinal smoke and then changed one bundle at a time.


A thangka of the Four Heavenly Kings. This is also the last place where photography is allowed. Their pupils are painted in the final stroke—the literal finishing touch. PS: Their eyes are enormous.


Tibet’s Shoton Festival begins in two days, and these decorations hang from all the streetlights. Everyone drinks yogurt during the festival, and a giant Buddha thangka is unveiled on the first day.

 

Day 2: Mila Pass & Basum Tso

![](https://titanxxh-1259211834.cos.ap-shanghai.myqcloud.com/TenDaysInTibet/IMG_5469_zps8cff96e2.jpg) The first ray of morning sunlight in Lhasa


Many people had clearly set out early. The birthplace of the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo was crowded with photographers. Tibetan mastiffs and yaks stood nearby for photographs, but the moment you pressed the shutter, somebody appeared to demand payment. What a rip-off.


A typical Tibetan tent woven from yak hair. In rain, the fibers’ pores first become clogged with water and then keep more rain out. Yak hair is also said to protect against lightning strikes.


Although the mountains are bare, the blue sky and white clouds give them an imposing grandeur.


Cyclists from Xi’an Jiaotong University. The stone behind them marks the altitude as 5,013 meters. To be honest, when I got out and walked, I felt almost weightless.


A bridge reaching the opposite bank


“A steadfast pillar amid the current, dividing the waters in silent contemplation”—the phrase describes this great rock standing in the river.


“Lovely spring is no match for a dream, where fragrant grass grows; carry your dreams with you through blue skies, white clouds, green hills and clear water, while a gentle breeze crosses the setting sun.”


A dam—or perhaps a hydroelectric station?


Basum Tso means “green water” in Tibetan. After seeing the lakes later in the journey, this one seemed less remarkable. PS: tso means lake.


A peach tree embracing a pine


Nyingchi lies at a lower altitude and has the strongest economy in Tibet. If nothing else, its hotels are much better than those in Lhasa. PS: Flying into Nyingchi and then traveling gradually westward would probably be a sensible itinerary.

Day 3: Lulang Forest & the Great Cypress

![](https://titanxxh-1259211834.cos.ap-shanghai.myqcloud.com/TenDaysInTibet/IMG_5792_zps85a20da4.jpg) We had been traveling on mountain roads, where trees usually grow on only one side. A road shaded by trees on both sides is uncommon, and the trees here are not normally this tall.


A tilted photograph of the forest


Namcha Barwa, whose name means “spear piercing the sky,” has been rated the most beautiful mountain in China. It is the fifteenth-highest mountain in the world; the fourteen above it all exceed 8,000 meters. Clouds and mist surround it throughout the year, but today’s good weather revealed most of the summit. The best viewpoint is actually not Lulang Forest but the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon, where the mountain is nearest, the vertical difference greatest, and the sight most overwhelming. Seeing it from there requires extraordinary luck.

A poet once sighed: compared with Everest's solid mass, I am more enchanted by Namcha Barwa's graceful, upright cliffs soaring into the clouds; compared with Shishapangma's desolation and dryness, I prefer Namcha Barwa's organic union of swaying greenery with snow and ice; compared with Mount Kailash's isolation from the world, I feel more attached to the shifting clouds, movement, and vitality among Namcha Barwa's slopes. This may be the most perfect expression of the mountain's character.


Stone-pot chicken, Lulang’s signature dish. The pot is carved from stone from Mêdog; it does not crack when heated, and food tastes better the longer the pot is used.


The King of Cypress Trees, said to be 2,600 years old

Day 4: Nanyigou Valley & Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon

![](https://titanxxh-1259211834.cos.ap-shanghai.myqcloud.com/TenDaysInTibet/IMG_6032_zps6cf6d892.jpg) After reaching Nanyigou Valley, we first visited a Lhoba home. The Lhoba were the last ethnic minority officially recognized in China. When they were encountered, they still practiced slash-and-burn agriculture and then moved directly into socialist society.


A puppy followed our sightseeing vehicle for nearly a kilometer simply to beg for a bite of meat.


I wonder whether anyone lives in this thatched hut.


Love Stronger Than Stone: an enormous boulder split in two, with a peach tree growing from the crack. This remarkable sight inspired a local love story about the daughter of the Peach Tree King and a man from the tribe. When spring winds soften into rain, the blossoms within the giant rock sway in the breeze, revealing love’s miraculous power.


The Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon is 504.6 kilometers long, reaches a maximum depth of 6,009 meters, and averages 2,268 meters deep. It is the world’s largest canyon, filled with rapids and dangerous shoals as the river roars through it.

The day we visited was rainy and overcast, so we missed the chance to see Namcha Barwa up close from the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon. Then again, even on a clear day it might remain hidden.


A horse startled by our tour bus and fleeing without knowing where to go


The drizzle had just stopped as sunlight began to appear.

Day 5: Kadinggou Valley

That day's route took us from Nyingchi back to Lhasa, passing the Heavenly Buddha Waterfall in Kadinggou Valley.


A distant view of the magnificent waterfall descending from the heavens


A single-log bridge. The sign says no more than three people may cross at once, but nobody seems to pay attention.


Standing directly beneath the waterfall, with spray striking my face and fresh air filling my lungs, all the exhaustion of climbing disappeared.


A little plump is the ideal figure.


A path made from tree-stump slices. Why does their color make them look like pieces of sausage?


Back in Lhasa, today was the first day of the Shoton Festival. Worshippers poured into the holy city and caused traffic jams.

Day 6: Yamdrok Lake & Karola Glacier
