From today onward, our Tibetan journey reached its climax. The scenery before this had merely been the appetizers; we had to save room for the main course.


When a landscape enters the heart, even a foreign place becomes home.


Does it seem as though we are level with the clouds? PS: This photograph feels like a car advertisement.


Yamdrok Tso, usually called Yamdrok Lake, lies less than 100 kilometers from Lhasa. Together with Namtso and Lake Manasarovar, it is one of Tibet’s three sacred lakes. It is the largest inland lake on the northern side of the Himalayas, and its combination of water and mountains is unmatched in southern Tibet. Yamdrok is enormous and divided into several smaller lakes; no viewpoint reveals the whole of it.


“I want to fly higher.”


Snow-covered mountains on both sides of Yamdrok Lake


Karola Glacier stands more than 5,600 meters above sea level, the highest point on this journey. Glacier and white clouds merge into one. PS: Because of global warming, the snow line retreats a considerable distance every year. I do not know whether the glacier will still be visible many years from now.


We stayed in Gyantse that day. This is the Gyantse Dzong fortress. In 1904, British forces advanced on Gyantse and fiercely attacked the fortress. Chinese soldiers and civilians held their position for three months and repelled repeated assaults. Only after their ammunition and reinforcements were exhausted, leaving them hopelessly outnumbered, did the fortress fall.

Day 7: Duoqing Co

![](https://titanxxh-1259211834.cos.ap-shanghai.myqcloud.com/TenDaysInTibet/IMG_6778_zpsde21b247.jpg) Because our driver's Mandarin pronunciation was imperfect, we kept thinking the lake was called “Affectionate Lake,” a homophone of Duoqing Co. On the drive there, my mother became so excited photographing herds of horses, cattle, and sheep that she even dropped her phone. The driver said we felt far too much affection for this land.


A herd of cattle


A flock of sheep


A cracked road runs toward the horizon.


A panorama of Duoqing Co. Ordinary travel agencies rarely recommend this place, mainly because it is so remote; continue beyond it and you reach Nepal. Yet the scenery here is at least as beautiful as that of Ranwu Lake, which we had originally planned to visit.


A breeze began to rise. The water was no longer still and the reflection no longer sharp, but its blurred outline created a different kind of hazy beauty.


A sea of rapeseed flowers beside the road


Tashilhunpo Monastery is the largest monastery in the Shigatse region of Tibet. It stands on the eastern slope of Mount Nyima, west of Shigatse city. Since the Fourth Panchen Lama, it has served as the seat of successive Panchen Lamas and is comparable to the Dalai Lama’s Potala Palace. It is the leading tourist attraction in Tsang.

Day 8: Mount Everest Base Camp

This stop was not part of our original itinerary, mainly because we worried that my aunts would not be physically able to manage it. After several days of acclimatization, however, they unexpectedly asked to visit Everest themselves. We rose very early and spent seventeen hours on the road, finally returning to Shigatse just before midnight.


Beneath the morning glow, only Everest’s pointed summit appeared.


A winding mountain road. The final hundred-plus kilometers were all gravel like this, and reaching base camp took four hours.


Vegetation was even scarcer here, and the mountains were completely bare.


Bharal, or Himalayan blue sheep. They can eat only the grass growing between rocks, and every one of them is thin.


The best place to view Everest is not base camp, but a bend in the road shortly before reaching it.


This is base camp: essentially a ring of tents and several vehicles. Conditions are harsh, and fortunately we did not plan to spend the night.


“I came to your city and walked the road you once traveled.”


Rongbuk Monastery, the highest monastery in the world

Days 9–10: Yangbajain Hot Springs & Namtso

![](https://titanxxh-1259211834.cos.ap-shanghai.myqcloud.com/TenDaysInTibet/IMG_7193_zpse6b6f23b.jpg) Clouds hung like ribbons halfway up the mountains.


Yangbajain is a natural geothermal hot spring. Because the water is too hot, it must cool naturally through two pools before visitors can use it. PS: If you want to bathe here, I recommend spending one night at this location, because hotel guests can use the springs for free. Imagine soaking in steaming water beneath a starry sky at night—how delightful that would be. Watching snow fall in winter would be more poetic still.


Words left by passing travelers inside a temporary prefabricated building at Namtso


Namtso means “heavenly lake” in both Tibetan and Mongolian. The azure sky and blue lake merge into one, with the main peak of the Nyenchen Tanglha range visible in the distance.


The evening glow and a lone bird fly together.


Autumn water and the endless sky share a single hue.


Meditation beneath the moonlight


“Across the starry Milky Way, can I meet you? Distance does not frighten me; I only wish I could race to your side this instant.” The stars above Namtso. Many people saw a meteor cross the sky that night.


The sun rises in the east.


“Alone—just me, walking proudly; body and spirit leap as I gaze toward the heavens and embrace the kiss of stars and moon.”


All kinds of admission tickets; some can no longer be found.

entry.title: Resurrection of My Blog!
entry.content:
Rise Again, My Blog!


Vitruvian Meeple!

And so I began buying a VPS and domain again—the same choices as before, though fortunately they had returned to first-year pricing.
At Mo Zhuli’s recommendation, I compared Linode and DigitalOcean. Linode cost a little more, but it was faster and had been established for longer, so it seemed like a good choice.
Once I had bought a Linode instance, using it only for the blog would have been a waste. I set up Shadowsocks and PPTP myself, so when my VPNso Shadowsocks subscription expires I will not need to renew it.
The main task, however, was restoring my old WordPress backup and migrating all the content to Octopress. I worked on it for a while and it went fairly smoothly. My earlier decision to use Photobucket as an image host turned out to be wise, because the pictures survived intact. I recently discovered that Imgbox seems much faster. Some formatting problems remain, but never mind; they can mark the boundary between the old blog and the new one.

Steps for migrating WordPress to Octopress:

  1. Change WordPress’s permanent-link format to YYYY-MM-DD-title.
  2. Export the content as wordpress.xml and put it in the root of Octopress.
  3. Download this script and place it somewhere such as ./utils.
  4. Run ruby -r "./utils/wordpressdotcom.rb" -e "Jekyll::WordpressDotCom.process". The converted posts will appear in source/_posts.

There are plenty of Octopress setup tutorials, and the official documentation is good too. I recommend RVM rather than rbenv.
Here are two Chinese tutorials as well:

  • Deploying Octopress to Your VPS
  • Automatically Generating and Deploying Octopress

All right: Markdown syntax refreshed, mission accomplished, confetti everywhere.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Game Overview 1: HISTORIA
entry.content:
Essen 2014 has just ended, and HISTORIA received unanimous praise, taking first place on GeekBuzz. Yet most players who did not attend and try it in person—including me—may not know exactly what the game is about. Why is it so compelling? After reading the rulebook over the past two days, titanxxh decided to try a new series for the first time: titanxxh’s Essen 2014, covering games I purchased as well as introductions to several others. I welcome your feedback!

HISTORIA

Game Introduction

In HISTORIA, each player controls a civilization beginning in the late Stone Age, with the goal of carrying it from a tiny spark to glorious achievement. Your civilization will discover new technologies and expand into new territories. You can learn inventions by trading with neighboring, more advanced civilizations; exploit your own lands to obtain more resources for future development; or, of course, build military power and wage campaigns in every direction.
Building wonders will also elevate a civilization above its rivals and attract tourists later in the game. Leaders and national advisers assist you throughout.
The glory of victory belongs to the player who leaves the deepest mark on human history!

Components

  • 1 game board
  • 54 Power cubes
  • 45 Wonder cards (can you identify these three?)
  • 6 Development markers
  • 18 Leader cards (and these three?)
  • 16 Territory scoring tiles

  • 60 Action cards
  • 2 Time markers
  • 12 per-round scoring markers…
  • 30 Adviser cards
  • 7 Civilization cards
  • 6 Player aids

Game Board

Most of the board is self-explanatory after reading the rulebook, so I will not explain every element. The parts that do need explanation are:
The timeline: the inner ring represents eras and the outer ring represents rounds. There are three eras, each with four rounds. Why rounds vary in length will be explained later.
The Development Matrix: the vertical axis represents military strength and the horizontal axis technology.
Government bonuses: rewards are granted according to your type of government.

Setup

  1. Place the board in the center…
  2. Place one round marker on Era I and the other on Round 1.
  3. Separate the Wonder cards into three decks by era and shuffle them. Draw seven Era I cards to form the Wonder row; draw five in a two- or three-player game.
  4. Each player chooses a color, takes the four matching Power cubes, and places one in the Used Cube Pool.
  5. Each player takes ten Action cards and sets War and Tourism aside; they enter play later. The remaining eight cards form the player’s hand.
  6. Randomly assign a Civilization card and its five corresponding Adviser cards to each player. Each player shuffles their Adviser cards, places them face down, and draws one. (Players may also choose their civilizations.)
  7. Randomly determine turn order.
  8. Each player puts one marker on 0 of the score track and one in the lower-left corner of the Development Matrix.
  9. Randomly place the Territory scoring tiles on the world map.
  10. Separate the Leader cards into three decks by era and shuffle them. The player last in turn order draws a number of Leader cards equal to the player count, chooses one, and passes the rest to the next-to-last player. Continue until everyone has chosen, then reveal all Leaders together.
  11. Beginning with the starting player, each player places a Power cube in a territory and scores the points on its Territory tile.

Game Flow

The game consists of three eras, each with four rounds, for a total of twelve rounds.
At the end of a round, move the round marker clockwise to the next space and resolve its actions (described under End of the Round).

Victory Condition

At the end of the game, the player with the most points wins. Ties are broken in favor of the highest combined military and technology levels.

Game Rounds

Each round consists of several action cycles, depending on how many Action cards are played. In each action cycle, players decide which Action cards and/or Adviser cards to play from their hands.

Action Cards

To play Action cards, all players simultaneously choose one or more Action and/or Adviser cards, place them face down, and then reveal them together.
The maximum number of Action cards a player can play depends on the civilization’s technology level: initially one, two after discovering The Wheel, and three after discovering Medicine.

The following conditions apply when playing cards:

  • You must play at least one Action and/or Adviser card, even if it cannot be resolved.
  • Once revealed, cards cannot be withdrawn.
  • Some Action cards require Power cubes. You cannot use cubes in the Used Cube Pool; cubes spent from your supply enter that pool.
  • In turn order, each player resolves all cards they played.
  • During their turn, a player chooses the order in which to resolve their cards.
  • Some Action cards have an advanced effect, naturally at a higher cost.
  • Some Action cards have prerequisites; if they are not met, the card has no effect.

After an Action card is resolved, it is placed face up at the end of the discard queue. Adviser cards do not enter the discard queue; they are removed from the game.

Once every player’s cards have been resolved, begin a new action cycle. Continue until someone plays the Revolution Action card.

Action Descriptions

1. Military

Develop your civilization’s military strength. Spend one Power cube to gain one military level (move your marker one space upward on the Development Matrix).
Advanced effect (requires Metalworking): spend three Power cubes to gain two military levels.

  • If your civilization cannot increase its military level because of its technology level, the action has no effect. If you have reached the top of the Development Matrix (level 16), however, score 2 points.
  • A reward from a new military level may be used by your next action in the same action cycle.

2. Technology

Discover new technology. Spend one Power cube to gain one technology level (move your marker one space right on the Development Matrix).
Advanced effect (requires Science): spend three Power cubes to gain two technology levels.

  • If your civilization cannot increase its technology level because of its military level, the action has no effect. If you have reached the top of the Development Matrix (level 16), however, score 2 points.
  • A reward from a new technology level may be used by your next action in the same action cycle.

3. Art

Build a Wonder. Spend one Power cube to choose one Wonder from the Wonder row.
Advanced effect (requires Writing): spend three Power cubes to gain two Wonders.

  • A Wonder may be activated for its reward during the player’s actions, including on the next action of the same action cycle.
  • The Wonder row is not refilled immediately!

4. Exploit

Exploit your population. Return two Power cubes from the world map and/or your Used Cube Pool. If this makes you abandon a territory, lose points equal to that Territory tile’s value.
Advanced effect (requires Printing): lose 1 point to return four Power cubes.

  • If there are not enough cubes in the Used Cube Pool, simply return all available cubes.

5. Expansion

Expand your civilization. Place one Power cube in a territory adjacent to one you occupy.
Advanced effect (requires The Wheel): instead take one Power cube from your Used Cube Pool and place it on the world map.

  • A player with Navigation may expand into any territory.
  • When expanding into an empty territory, gain the reward on its Territory tile.
  • The United States and Russia are not adjacent (apparently the Bering Strait has vanished…), while Central and South America are adjacent! (The Panama Canal says hello.)

6. Trade

Trade with an adjacent civilization. It must have a higher technology level. You gain one technology level and it scores 2 points.
Advanced effect (requires Navigation): it scores only 1 point.

  • A civilization with Navigation can trade with any civilization.
  • Civilizations in the same territory count as adjacent…

7. Raid

Raid your neighbor. Your civilization may raid an adjacent civilization with a lower military level; remember that civilizations in the same territory count as adjacent.
Score 1 point and return one Power cube from the Used Cube Pool.
Advanced effect (requires Gunpowder): score 2 points and return two Power cubes from the Used Cube Pool.

  • If there is no adjacent civilization with a lower military level, the Raid has no effect.
  • You still score the points even if you cannot return every Power cube.

8. War

Declare war on another civilization in the same territory. War becomes available once your technology level is at least 2 (Agriculture).
The civilization with the higher military level wins and scores 2 points. The loser removes its Power cube from that territory and places it in the Used Cube Pool.
Advanced effect (requires Nuclear Power): the winner scores 4 points… (Is the game encouraging nuclear “peace”?)

  • Once a War action is played, it must be resolved even if that civilization can no longer win. (Once the arrow leaves the bow, there is no recalling it! Because actions resolve in sequence, a later player’s intended target may already have raised its military level.)
  • If military levels are tied, nothing happens; both sides stand down.
  • A player cannot lose their final territory.
  • If several civilizations share a territory, the attacker chooses which one to fight.

9. Tourism

Attract tourists to visit your Wonders. Tourism becomes available only after your civilization discovers Industrialization.
Score 1 point for every four Wonders you own.
Advanced effect (requires Internet): score 1 point for every three Wonders.

10. Revolution

This signals the end of a round. A Revolution Action card or an Adviser with a Revolution effect cannot be played if your discard queue contains fewer than three cards at the beginning of the action cycle. Revolution must be your final action.
Return the newest card in your discard queue (normally Revolution itself) and one other Action card to your hand.

When a player plays Revolution, move the round marker and begin the end-of-round phase.

End of the Round

At the end of each round, resolve every icon in that segment of the timeline ring. Icons in the large gray area are resolved individually by each player; icons in the small brown area affect other aspects of the game.
Resolve gray-area icons before brown-area icons.
Within the gray area, adding Power cubes must be resolved first; other icons may be resolved in any order.
Within the brown area, changing turn order must be resolved first.
Add Power cube: each player takes one Power cube from the common supply and places it in their Used Cube Pool.
Return Action cards: each player returns the two oldest Action cards from their discard queue to their hand.
Reset Wonders: each player readies any activated, sideways Wonder cards.
Return Power cubes: each player returns Power cubes from their Used Cube Pool; the number depends on how many territories they occupy.
Government bonus: each player gains the government bonus corresponding to their position on the Development Matrix.

Turn Order

Determine the new turn order from lowest score to highest. Among tied players, whoever acted later in the previous round acts earlier now. (A catch-up mechanism?)

Refill Wonders: discard all Wonders remaining in the Wonder row and draw seven new ones. When entering a new era, use that era’s Wonders.
Leader reward: every Leader has two conditions. If you satisfy either one, gain the reward; if you satisfy both, gain the higher reward. Whether or not the reward is earned, remove the Leader from the game.
Distribute Leaders: use the same process as during setup, but follow the newly determined turn order.
Territory reward: at the end of each era, if a territory contains only one civilization, that civilization scores the points on its Territory tile.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] La Granja Unboxing
entry.content:
Last year on my birthday, a package from a longtime friend unexpectedly arrived at the laboratory. I opened it and discovered La Granja, a game from my wishlist. I was so excited that an unboxing was essential.

The cover, with watercolor artwork that I really like.

The back of the box: one to four players, ninety minutes.

This is everything inside: a bag of wooden tokens, dice and language-reference sheets, punchboards, and the game board.

The rulebook uses excellent paper!

All the tokens punched out. Does anyone else get especially excited every time they do this?

The player board. Cards slide into the cutout sections. The fact that a single card can be placed in four different ways is one of the game’s defining features.

The main board.

I do not know what this is, and I could not make sense of it from the rulebook. Could an expert who understands German explain it?

Everything organized and packed away!

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Game Overview 2: Progress—Evolution of Technology
entry.content:
titanxxh’s Essen 2014 series is back! Once again, titanxxh brings an introduction to a civilization game, but this title focuses on exploring technology and contains none of the maps, warfare, and similar elements found in other civilization games.

Today’s game is Progress: Evolution of Technology.


Progress: Evolution of Technology

Introduction

As an expression of the progress of human thought, technology emerged very early in human history. Beginning with basic tools such as the wheel and plow, humanity invented increasingly sophisticated implements, used them to construct machines, and brought about the Industrial Revolution.
From nomadism, hunting, and tribal life to the modern society in which we live, humanity has devoted tremendous effort to understanding its own history. Arthur C. Clarke famously observed that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. Today we stand within a civilization built upon the knowledge and technology of those who came before us.

We are now ready to honor our past and review what we have learned. In Progress: Evolution of Technology, players immerse themselves in a universe of science and magic, retracing humanity’s technological path up to the first Industrial Revolution.

Game Overview

Progress: Evolution of Technology is a card-driven civilization game about technological development across history.
Players compete to become the nation that advances technology most successfully through the ages.
Each player guides their nation’s mysterious scientific research from the earliest signs of human invention, gradually passing through antiquity, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the dawn of the Industrial Revolution.
The goal is to accumulate victory points by researching technologies. Every technology benefits its owner and affects the entire player board. At the end, players also score according to their positions on one or more power tracks.

A friendly note from the designers:
Over tens of thousands of years, human societies developed countless technologies. After careful research, we selected those that had the greatest impact on society. Progress: Evolution of Technology primarily divides technological development into three fields: science, engineering, and culture. Government and military technologies are planned for later expansions. Some technologies are especially difficult to assign to one period or field because they profoundly affected many aspects of human life. In those cases, we favored gameplay over strict historical accuracy.

Components

  • 184 technology cards

Left side, from top to bottom:

- Technology type: science (atom), engineering (gear), or culture (column)
- The skill upgrade or knowledge token provided by the card
- Victory points at the end of the game
- Knowledge gained when the card is discarded

Right side, from top to bottom:

- The card's era and name
- Advancement by one space on one or more power tracks
- Illustration
- The cost or prerequisite technology required to discover it
- Applicable player count
  • 56 knowledge tokens
  • 5 player boards

At the end of the game, players score according to the development of each skill track.

  • 1 double-sided power board

The power board shows three tracks: prestige (crown), population (castle), and army (Roman helmet). Players score according to their rankings at the end.

  • 11 era tokens
  • 100 wooden markers

There are fourteen in each player color—red, green, blue, yellow, and white—and thirty shared black markers.

  • 5 technology trees
  • 5 player-aid cards
  • Rulebook

Note: every component except technology cards is considered unlimited.

Setup

  1. Select the technology cards corresponding to the player count.
  2. Separate them into three decks by era and shuffle each deck.
  3. Take a player board and wooden markers in one color. Put one marker at the starting position of each of the seven skill tracks.
  4. Place the power board in the center. Each player puts one marker at the starting position of all three power tracks. Set the knowledge tokens and black markers nearby.
  5. Put the Era I deck next to the power board and leave space for its discard pile. Set the Era II and Era III decks aside, also leaving room for their discard piles.
  6. Leave enough space for your personal play area. Choose a starting player; if you do not know how, choose the youngest.
  7. Beginning with the starting player and proceeding clockwise, everyone draws the indicated number of cards from the Era I deck:
    • Solo game: 6 cards
    • 2 players: 5/6 cards
    • 3 players: 5/6/7 cards
    • 4 players: 5/6/6/7 cards
    • 5 players: 5/6/6/7/7 cards
  8. The following illustration shows the starting layout for two players.

  1. Study the technology tree and devise a sound strategy.

Game Concepts

Skills

Skills reflect how efficiently a player performs different actions.
Every player board contains seven skill tracks, and the marker on each track defines the player’s current skill level.

  1. Actions: the number of actions a player may perform each turn; starts at two.
  2. Draw: the number of cards drawn when taking a Draw action; starts at three. After drawing, the player may perform no further actions and must end the turn.
  3. Hand limit: the maximum number of cards a player may retain at the end of a turn; starts at five.
  4. Shuffle: the number of times a player may shuffle a discard pile back into its deck and draw one card; starts at one.
  5. Development: the maximum number of technologies a player may have under development simultaneously; starts at one.
  6. Research: the number of markers placed on a technology put under development; starts at four.
  7. Quick Draw: the two numbers indicate, respectively, how many cards to draw and discard; starts at one/zero.

Technology Cards and Knowledge

Technology cards serve two roles in the game: both means and ends. A technology card can:

  • Become an active technology through a Discover action, or a technology under development through a Research action.
  • Be discarded to provide knowledge toward the cost of discovering another technology.

Knowledge is the game’s currency for paying discovery costs. There are three types:

  • Science (atom)
  • Engineering (gear)
  • Culture (column)

Universal knowledge can substitute for any one type.
Knowledge comes either from discarding technology cards from hand or spending knowledge tokens. When discarding a card, gain the knowledge shown in its lower-left corner. To spend a knowledge token, simply flip it to its gray side.

Current Deck

The current deck and its discard pile are the sources from which players draw.
The Era I deck is current at the beginning. The Era II and Era III decks become current later.

Sequence of Play

Proceeding clockwise, players take turns until the game ends. The active player is the player currently taking a turn. Each turn contains these phases, performed in order:

  1. Development phase
  2. Action phase
  3. Upkeep phase

After the active player completes upkeep, the next player becomes active and begins their turn. Experienced players may instead save time by beginning their turn during the previous player’s upkeep.

Development Phase

During development, the active player must remove one marker from each of their technologies under development. Details of developing technologies appear below.
If removing a marker leaves a technology with none, it immediately becomes active and its owner gains its benefit. See Benefits, New Eras, and Game End.
At the end of the Development phase, the active player may reclaim technologies they are developing.

Action Phase

During the Action phase, the active player performs as many actions as their Action skill allows.
Note: actions are not mandatory. You may forgo any number of them, though doing so is unlikely to win the game.
The active player must complete one action fully before beginning another. Available actions are:

  • Discover
  • Research
  • Draw
  • Quick Draw
  • Shuffle & Draw

Discover

A Discover action plays a technology card from hand as an active technology.
You must meet the card’s cost to play it.
Note: arranging active technologies in overlapping stacks by type is recommended.
Each technology may show one or two rows of costs or prerequisite requirements.
Every technology requires one type of knowledge and may list a prerequisite technology:

  • If that prerequisite is present in your play area, you do not pay the associated knowledge requirement.
  • If you lack the prerequisite, you must pay the listed knowledge requirement, or more.

Every row of costs or prerequisites must be satisfied separately.

Surplus knowledge may be used for another Discover action during the same turn. Any still unused at the end of the turn is lost. After playing an active technology, immediately gain its benefits; this may trigger a new era or the end of the game. See Benefits, New Eras, and Game End.

Research

A Research action plays a technology card from hand as a technology under development, which will later become active.
Its advantage is that you need not meet the technology’s cost or prerequisites, though several turns must pass before it becomes active.
Play the technology on the opposite side of your tableau from active technologies to avoid confusion. Put a number of markers on it equal to your Research skill. It is now under development.
Technologies under development do not count as active. They satisfy prerequisite requirements but provide no other benefits.
Note: a player may never possess two technologies with the same name, whether active or under development.

Draw

A Draw action means drawing cards from the current deck equal to your Draw skill, then giving up all remaining actions and entering upkeep.
Draw cards one at a time. After seeing each card, you may choose whether to draw the next from the top of the current deck or the top of its discard pile.

Quick Draw

For a Quick Draw action, first draw X cards, then discard Y cards.
Note: discard every card into the pile corresponding to its era.

Shuffle & Draw

A Shuffle & Draw action shuffles a discard pile back into its deck, then draws one card. It may be performed several times according to the player’s Shuffle skill.
The same deck may be chosen repeatedly. If no discard pile remains, simply draw one card.

Upkeep Phase

During upkeep, the active player prepares for their next turn while the following player may begin theirs. Perform these steps:

  • Discard down to the hand limit.
  • Flip knowledge tokens back to their colored side.

Benefits

Whenever you add an active technology, gain the benefits shown along the left side of its card.
At the top, improve a skill or gain a knowledge token.
In the middle, advance on the indicated power track.
At the bottom, receive victory points at the end of the game.
Note: all benefits apply immediately. If you gain an additional action, for example, you may take it at once.

New Eras

Some technology cards bear a new-era symbol. When active technologies in all player areas contain enough such symbols, the next era’s deck becomes current.

The number required to enter Era II is:

  • 1 symbol with 1–3 players
  • 2 symbols with 4–5 players

The number required to enter Era III is:

  • 1 symbol with 1–2 players
  • 2 symbols with 3–4 players
  • 3 symbols with 5 players

As soon as enough Era II symbols appear, Era I ends and Era II begins. Pause the game, add the Era II deck, and make it current.
As soon as enough Era III symbols appear, Era II ends and Era III begins. Pause the game, add the Era III deck, and make it current. Every player must also discard every Era I card in hand, including Era I technologies under development.

Game End

Era IV symbols trigger the end of the game. The number required is:

  • 1 symbol with 1–2 players
  • 2 symbols with 3–4 players
  • 3 symbols with 5 players

As soon as enough Era IV symbols appear, Era III ends and the game ends immediately. Remove every technology under development from the game, and all players calculate victory points.
Note: after adding expansions, Era IV symbols no longer end the game but begin a new era. If both the current deck and its discard pile are empty, the era ends immediately.

Scoring

Every player scores in the following categories:

  • Power tracks

Players score according to their positions on each power track. Tied players divide the points evenly.

  • Player board

For every skill track, score the victory points to the left of the player’s marker.

  • Technology cards

Add the points printed on technology cards in the player’s area.

The player with the highest total across all three categories wins. Break ties in this order:

  1. Universal knowledge tokens
  2. Culture knowledge tokens
  3. Science knowledge tokens
  4. Engineering knowledge tokens

If still tied, the players share victory.

titanxxh was lazy and did not translate the solo rules or quick-reference variants into Chinese.

The end of the rulebook also mentions three small expansions:

  • Personalities
  • Milestones
  • Progress: Industrial Revolution

Overview of the technology tree:

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Game Overview 3: Praetor
entry.content:
The third game overview introduces a worker-placement game: Praetor. My attention was first caught by the cool pose of the little figure on the cover. Since I also enjoy historical settings, the game naturally entered my field of view.
Praetor is not an easy word to translate into Chinese, and scholars themselves disagree about it. I will render it as “magistrate” here; textual critics, please go easy on me…


Praetor

Background

In AD 117, Hadrian—one of the famous Five Good Emperors of Rome, as was Trajan—succeeded to the throne of the Roman Empire. Early in his reign, Rome faced threats from barbarians in Britain, Egypt, and Judea. Unlike his predecessors, Hadrian did not focus on expanding his vast empire. He chose a different policy: defend its borders and spread its culture.
Southern Britain was under Roman rule, while the north was considered barbarian territory. After a major revolt in AD 119–121, Hadrian visited Britain. The Roman Empire stood at the height of its glory, and Hadrian no longer wished to wage endless campaigns against barbarians. To secure long-term Roman rule, he decided to consolidate the empire by building cities and fortifications.
By AD 122, Hadrian had begun constructing Hadrian’s Wall to defend against incursions from the north. (Yes, you read that correctly: it inspired the Wall in A Song of Ice and Fire; Westeros is essentially a mirrored Britain.) Alongside the Wall, Hadrian ordered several outposts built. Some soon grew into towns, supplying resources, workers, and fortifications for the Wall’s construction.
At the eastern end of the Wall, the outpost and trading station of Segedunum, at modern Newcastle, became a fort that supplied everything the construction effort required. It later developed into a city, reminding local people of the Roman Empire’s former glory.
Hadrian entrusted the task to five of his most trusted engineers, sending them from Rome to build the city together. In the end, however, only one could be appointed Praetor and govern the province in the name of Caesar and the eternal glory of Rome.

Objective

Each player seeks to accumulate the most Favor Points. At the end of the game, the player with the most Favor Points is appointed Praetor and continues leading the city toward prosperity. Players earn Favor Points by building new city tiles, sending workers to visit temples, and spending resources to meet Caesar’s demands.

Overview

In Praetor, you play a Roman engineer, working with the other players to build a magnificent city. You must manage your limited resources intelligently while finding new ones; recruit new workers as older employees retire; build settlements to keep the people happy while praising the gifts of the gods. And if you are willing to donate precious resources toward Hadrian’s Wall, Caesar will reward you and improve your chances of becoming Praetor.
Each round, you place workers on previously built city tiles to gain resources, Morale, new workers, and Favor Points. You may also send workers to construct new city tiles or spend resources to satisfy Caesar’s demands and earn Favor Points. At the end of your turn, you must pay your workers’ wages, or the city’s morale will deteriorate.
Most worker actions grant them experience—for example, they become increasingly skilled at gathering resources. Your most experienced workers eventually retire and give you Favor Points, but in the interests of solidarity, you must keep paying their pensions until the game ends.
The game ends when there are no more city tiles to build or Caesar has no more demands. The player with the most Favor Points is appointed Praetor and wins.

Components

  • 42 city tiles (labels in the image, top to bottom)

    • Resources required to build the tile and the Favor Points awarded to its builder
    • The tile action’s type (green, red, or gray), cost, and benefit
    • Plazas: the designs in the tile’s corners. When a player adds a new tile to the city, matching plaza designs earn additional Favor Points

  • 14 Wall tiles
    The front shows Caesar’s demand and the reward for fulfilling it.
    The back shows the extra Favor Points awarded when the same player completes later sections of the Wall.

  • 5 player boards (labels in the image, counterclockwise)

    • Indicates the standard/expert side of the player board
    • Citizens, the worker pool
    • Trainees, who must complete two stages of training after recruitment
    • Active workers; the lower-right shows the wage due at the end of each round
    • Retired workers; the lower-right shows the pension due at the end of each round
    • Resource exchange rates
    • Morale track; each level awards or deducts Favor Points at the end of the game

  • Scoring board (double-sided)
    Used to track Favor Points and turn order.

  • Resources (wooden tokens)
    112 coins, 25 wood, 25 stone, 20 marble, and 20 weapons. Resources are considered unlimited.

  • 4 reference boards

  • 8 worker dice and 15 disc markers in five colors: blue, yellow, white, black, and purple

Game Concepts

Praetor is a city-building game. Players use workers to gather resources, construct city tiles, and fulfill Caesar’s demands, always remembering to accumulate Favor Points in order to win.

  • Workers = dice
    A player’s workforce is represented by dice. Each worker is one die, and its value represents that worker’s experience. Workers gain experience by building new city tiles or taking actions. A worker who reaches six experience retires at the end of the round.
  • Resources
    There are five resources. Coins are the most common and are used chiefly to pay wages at the end of each round. Wood, stone, marble, and weapons are used to construct city tiles; wood is also used to make weapons. Any resource can be spent to fulfill Caesar’s demands and gain Favor Points.
  • Morale
    Your Morale level is shown on your player board. Keeping it high earns Favor Points at the end of the game.
  • Building the city
    Players build the city by placing city tiles. You spend resources to construct a tile and receive Favor Points in return. Whenever that tile is activated, its builder receives income. Workers build or activate city tiles to gain resources, workers, Favor Points, and more. Each city tile can be activated only once per round.
  • Fulfilling Caesar’s demands
    Players may activate the Imperial Outpost city tile to pay resources and gain Favor Points. After activating it, choose a Wall tile, pay the resources shown, and gain its Favor Points. Place that Wall tile in front of you; each later Wall section you construct awards additional Favor Points because of it.

Setup

  • Select city tiles for the player count—for example, in a three-player game, use tiles marked 2+ and 3+. Find the starting tiles marked 0 on the back and set them up as shown below.
  • Shuffle the Era I and Era II city tiles separately and form a face-down stack with Era I on top. Shuffle the Wall tiles into a face-down stack.
  • Reveal one more city tile than the number of players to form the available city tiles. Reveal the top Wall tile.
  • Choose a player board and place it before you. Depending on your experience, you may use side A or B; side A is recommended for new players.
    All A sides are identical, while every B side is different. Any combination of player-board sides is supposedly balanced (I have my doubts…), but side B provides an asymmetric experience and makes it harder for beginners to find a sound strategy.
  • Take the workers and markers of your color. Place one marker on 0 of the Morale track. Take 10 coins, 4 wood, 3 stone, 2 marble, and 1 weapon. Place three workers showing 1, 2, and 3 experience in your Active Workers area; put all remaining workers, showing 1 experience, in the Citizens area.
  • Set the scoring board and remaining resources nearby.
  • Place one marker on the gold mine closest to you.
  • The player who most recently visited Rome places a marker on 10 Favor Points. Moving counterclockwise, every other player places theirs one point lower. The player with fewer Favor Points acts earlier; place markers on the turn-order track accordingly.

Below is the setup for a three-player game. Note that the city in the center may become enormous—you need a large table!!!

Game Flow

The game lasts several rounds. Each round has three phases:

  • Turn Order Phase
  • Action Phase
  • Upkeep Phase

After the final round comes Final Scoring.

Turn Order Phase

Turn order is determined by each player’s position on the Favor Point track: the lower the score, the earlier the player acts. When scores are tied, the player whose marker is on top acts first. Once established, turn order does not change until the end of the round.

Action Phase

In turn order, players take turns performing one action or passing.

  • Place a worker from your Active area on an available city tile to construct it
    1. Choose an available city tile and check that you have enough resources.
    2. Place a worker from your Active area in the center of that tile and pay its resource cost.
    3. Add the tile to the city, adjacent to at least one previously constructed city tile.
    4. Place one of your markers on it.
    5. Gain the Favor Points shown on the tile.
    6. Gain one additional Favor Point for each corner whose plaza design matches the corner of an adjacent tile.
    7. Update your position on the Favor Point track.
  • Place a worker from your Active area on a constructed city tile to take its action
    1. Choose a worker from your Active area and place it on the city tile you wish to activate.
    2. Each city tile may be activated only once per round.
    3. If another player built the tile, pay its fee; otherwise, pay nothing.
    4. Gain the benefit.
  • Activate a special city tile
    You may also spend an action to activate a special city tile, whose action area is gray. Each player may activate each special city tile once per round.
    You must pay the tile’s owner to activate it. You do not use an Active worker; place one of your markers on it to record its use.

If a player has placed all Active workers, they must pass. Once a player passes, they cannot place any more workers that round.
A player may pass before placing every Active worker, but that is usually a poor decision. Before passing, review the Final Scoring section to see whether any action could still earn Favor Points.

Upkeep Phase

  1. Move every worker in your Trainee area one space to the right.
    • A Trainee in the second space becomes an Active worker.
    • A Trainee in the first space moves to the second. If you control the Academy, you may skip the second space and move it directly into the Active area. If you do not control the Academy but it has been built in the city, you may pay one stone to its owner to let all your Trainees skip the second space.
      If retired workers took actions through the Labor Camp, return them to your player board; they gain no experience.
  2. Return your workers one at a time in this order:
    • Workers used to construct city tiles gain 1 experience.
    • Workers used to activate red city tiles gain 1 experience.
    • All other workers gain no experience.
  3. Every Active worker with six experience retires; move it into the Retired Workers area. Gain 12 Favor Points for each worker retiring during Era I and 8 for each retiring during Era II. Determine the current era from the city-tile stack.
  4. Pay your workers.
    • Pay the wages of all Active and Retired workers as shown on your player board.
    • If you do not have enough coins, lose one Morale level for every missing coin. If your Morale is already at the lowest level, lose 5 Favor Points for every missing coin.
  5. If you have no Active workers after completing the steps above, you may lose 5 Favor Points to turn one Citizen into an Active worker with one experience.
  6. Maintain the city (skip this in the final round).
    • Reveal city tiles until the number available is one more than the number of players.
    • Remove every available Wall tile and reveal a new one.
  7. Check whether the next round will be the final round.
    • If the city-tile stack is empty, the next round is the final round.
    • If the Wall-tile stack is empty, the next round is the final round.

#Final Scoring

(Only after the final round.)

  • Active workers and Trainees
    • Each Active worker earns Favor Points equal to its experience.
    • Each Trainee earns 1 Favor Point.
  • Morale
    • Gain or lose Favor Points according to your Morale level.
  • Resources
    • Convert resources into coins at the Market exchange rates.
    • Score 1 Favor Point for every 10 coins.

Winning the Game

The player with the most Favor Points wins and is appointed Praetor. Break ties in this order:

  1. Morale level
  2. Number of Wall tiles
  3. Number of city tiles

If the tie remains, Caesar cannot decide and consults the gods; the gods favor the younger player.

#City Tile Details

(Left to right, top to bottom.)

  • Resources (benefit depends on worker experience)

    • Gold Mine—gain coins according to the worker’s experience
    • Lumber Mill—gain wood according to the worker’s experience
    • Quarry—gain stone according to the worker’s experience
    • Marble Quarry—gain marble according to the worker’s experience
    • Blacksmith—convert wood into an equal number of weapons according to the worker’s experience

  • Coins

    • Provincial Senate—gain coins according to the number of city tiles you control
    • Forum—gain 2 coins for each of your Active workers

  • Temples (activate to gain Favor Points)

    • Temple of Maia—gain 2 Favor Points for each of your Active workers
    • Temple of Apollo—gain 1 Favor Point for each city tile you control
    • Temple of Plutus—gain 1 Favor Point for each wood and 1 for each stone you own
    • Temple of Mercury—gain 2 Favor Points for each marble and 2 for each weapon you own
    • Temple of Venus—gain Favor Points according to your Morale level

  • Morale

    • Arena—gain one Morale level for every two city tiles you control
    • Oracle—gain two Morale levels for each Retired worker

  • Worker Camp, Market, and Outpost

    • Worker Camp—move one worker showing 1 experience from the Citizens area to the first space of the Trainee area
    • Market—exchange any number of resources using the Market rates
    • Imperial Outpost—choose an available Wall tile, pay its cost, and gain its Favor Points, plus additional Favor Points for each of your face-down Wall tiles. Then place it face down before you.

  • Special city tiles

    • Academy—use during the Upkeep Phase. You may pay one stone to its owner so that all your Trainees skip their second training space.
    • Labor Camp—use during the Action Phase without an Active worker. Once per round, pay its owner and treat one of your Retired workers as an Active worker with six experience to take an action.

  • City tiles with no action

    • Statue—exists purely for Favor Points
    • Triumphal Arch—exists purely for Favor Points

entry.title: After the First Defeat of Dunga's Second Spell
entry.content:
Eleven consecutive victories concealed many problems. With Oscar and Luiz Gustavo absent, they all erupted at once.

South American football has long since ceased to be dominated by Brazil and Argentina alone. The Copa América makes that especially clear. Every team is strong overall, and the gap between traditionally stronger and weaker sides has narrowed. Many players return to their national teams after a full season in European competition, so a decline in form is understandable and difficult matches should be expected. Dunga had already mentioned this before the tournament.

In the opening match against Peru, Brazil immediately put itself in trouble but eventually found a stoppage-time winner. The result was good, yet the process was deeply worrying. The old World Cup problem remained: Brazil had still not cured its dependence on Neymar.

Now to today’s match. Brazil’s World Cup victory over Colombia was already anything but easy; without David Luiz’s long-range free kick, nobody knows who would have advanced. With several players unavailable, a strong opponent desperate to respond after losing its first match, and a depleted squad, Dunga’s decision to prioritize defense in the first half was reasonable. The referee allowed plenty of contact, Neymar faced an old nemesis and became emotionally unsettled, and after Brazil conceded from a scramble, nobody calmed the situation quickly enough. The team’s tactical thinking became disjointed, just as it did when Dunga’s first Brazil side lost to the Netherlands at the World Cup. Brazil was extremely passive in the first half. After Douglas Costa and Coutinho came on in the second, more players could keep possession in attack and opportunities naturally increased. Colombia then sat back. Brazil attacked furiously for a while without scoring, and the match ended.

Overall, Brazil created few chances, but several were excellent: Neymar’s booked header, the opening caused by an opponent’s mistake, and Firmino’s near-post header were obvious to everyone. None was converted. Several other moves broke down at the final pass without producing a shot. Defensively, Thiago Silva was out of form, A22 remained reckless, and too many midfield fouls conceded too many free kicks. In my view, there were three main attacking problems. First, Neymar’s passing choices were poor; on at least three occasions he failed to release the correct teammate and wasted an opportunity. Second, the midfield and attack were badly disconnected, especially in the first half. Whenever Neymar received the ball in the final third, the entire midfield remained behind him. Both holding midfielders must take responsibility for their terrible positioning during attacks. The final problem was inefficient counterattacking. That should be easier to solve: counters are Dunga’s specialty, and with time he ought to fix them. Many people on the forums have complained about positional attack, but at this stage of football’s development, counterattacking remains the most efficient weapon. The fastest way for a weaker team—and yes, Brazil is now a weaker team—to rise is to master the counterattack. If you cannot counter efficiently, why discuss positional play? What powered Germany’s resurgence? Efficient counterattacking. Once your counters become dangerous, opponents no longer dare push their defensive line forward. You can then raise your own line and create the appearance of sustained pressure. In a sense, Luis Enrique understood how to use the extraordinarily efficient counterattacking of Barcelona’s MSN trio this year. He made the most important adjustment after Barça’s possession football declined, and the result was a treble.

Neymar will miss the coming matches. This is an ideal chance to train a tactical system that does not depend on him, instead of repeating the World Cup, when the team seemed unable to play after he was lost. To progress farther in this tournament—to beat strong opponents within ninety minutes instead of clinging on for penalties—I think Brazil must make the following changes:

  • Give Douglas Costa and Coutinho major roles. Douglas Costa has stood out in both matches and is physically strong enough to compete. Coutinho is also a capable dribbler, far better than starting Fred. Dunga probably left them out because he considered their defensive contribution inadequate, but attack and defense are inherently in tension. With so few options available, he must take the gamble.
  • Activate Filipe Luís’s overlapping runs. There is little more to say here. Dunga probably avoided this plan because Filipe had played so little recently. Without Neymar, however, the left-sided attack must rely on Filipe’s burst.
  • Push the defensive line higher, strengthen the midfield press, and bring in David Luiz to use his ability to step forward and create counterattacking opportunities.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Game Overview 4: Versailles
entry.content:
The fourth game in the series is Versailles. Like the two titles titanxxh introduced previously, it was one of NSKN Games’ 2014 releases. titanxxh saw that its rulebook was only four pages long and immediately chose it for an introduction…


Versailles

Game Overview

Versailles is an innovative family game for two to five players. Acting as architects and interior designers, players cooperate to build a magnificent palace for King Louis XIV while competing for the monarch’s favor.
On each turn, a player moves one or more workers to another location, activating every one of their workers at that destination. Actions provide resources, allow players to build the mysterious palace, create attractive decorations for its interior and gardens, and learn new skills. When His Majesty arrives, he will judge which of his faithful servants has performed best.

Components

When playing for the first time, punch out the tokens carefully and sort the wooden pieces! Seriously.

  • Game board

The board contains the construction site in the center and action locations around it.

Top row: King’s Favor, Marble Quarry, Gold Mine, Architects’ Guild
Bottom row: Alchemists’ Guild, Construction Site, Lumber Mill, Workshop

  • The king

King Louis XIV comes to inspect the architects’ work.

  • 45 worker meeples

The wooden meeples represent workers. At the start of the game, the workers that players will use are placed in predetermined positions on the board.

  • 5 activation markers

An activation marker records the location a player activated most recently.

  • 20 technology/scoring markers

Technology/scoring markers track each player’s three technologies at the Alchemists’ Guild and their victory points.

  • 90 resource cubes

Gold is yellow, marble white, and wood brown. Small cubes represent one resource and large cubes five.

  • 40 palace tiles

Palace tiles depict the palace’s interior and exterior areas.

  • 30 decoration tokens

There are six kinds of decoration, and their supply is limited.

  • 10 double-move tokens

Double-move tokens record how many special movements a player has left.

Setup

  • General setup
    • Place the board in the center. Put wood at the Lumber Mill, marble at the Marble Quarry, and gold at the Gold Mine.
    • Shuffle the palace tiles into a face-down stack. Reveal five and place them at the Architects’ Guild.
    • Sort decoration tokens by type and put them next to the Workshop.
    • Choose the starting player: whoever most recently visited Versailles or Paris, or decide randomly.
    • Put the king on the first space of the king track.
  • Player setup
    • Each player takes all workers, technology markers, the activation marker, and the scoring marker in one color.
    • Each player takes the matching double-move tokens and places them face up.
    • Each player puts two workers on the new-worker spaces at King’s Favor and puts their scoring marker at the beginning of the score track.
    • At the Alchemists’ Guild, put one of the player’s technology markers on the first space of each technology row.
    • Set each player’s starting worker positions according to the table. Return unused workers to the box.

Gameplay

A game of Versailles consists of consecutive turns, beginning with the starting player and proceeding clockwise until the game ends. On a turn, a player moves one or more workers to another location and may activate that location’s action.

  • Moving workers

On their turn, a player must move at least one worker from one location to another. Workers must follow the arrows printed on the board. The player chooses either a regular move or a double move, following the rules below.

  • Regular move

A regular move lets the player move one worker a single step in the direction of an arrow.

  • Double move

A player may flip one double-move token to replace a regular move with a double move. They may either:

Move two workers from the same location one step each as regular moves.
Move one worker once as a regular move while skipping over one location.

  • Activation marker

Regardless of movement type, a player may never move to a location containing their own activation marker. After completing a move, they transfer that marker to the location just activated.

  • Activating a location

After moving, the player may choose whether to activate the location’s action. When activating a location, each worker may be used only once. (That is basically a tautology…)

  • Location benefits

Each location offers one or more benefits according to the number of the active player’s workers there. In general, more workers produce a greater benefit. Other players’ workers do not count.

- Marble Quarry

With one, two, or three workers, gain one, two, or three marble.

- Lumber Mill

With one, two, or three workers, gain one, two, or three wood.

- Gold Mine

With one, two, or three workers, gain one, two, or three gold.

- Architects' Guild

The Architects’ Guild offers several options. The number of workers determines how many options a player may choose, and the chosen actions may be performed in any order.

    1. Pay the worker cost shown to the left of one of the five displayed palace tiles to take that tile. Do not refill the display while tiles are being taken. A player may hold no more than four palace tiles at any time; on taking a fifth, immediately discard one.
    2. Spend one worker to remove one palace tile from the display, or two workers to remove three. Slide every remaining tile down afterward.
    3. Spend one worker to flip one double-move token face up. Regardless of how many workers a player has here, this action may be performed only once per turn.

After the player completes every desired action, slide the remaining palace tiles down and refill the display to five from the stack. If the stack is insufficient, shuffle the discarded palace tiles. If fewer than seven palace tiles are available in total, the game ends immediately.

- Workshop

Spend the indicated workers and resources to buy one or more decorations.

- Alchemists' Guild

Spend the indicated workers and resources to advance technologies.

- Construction Site

When activating the Construction Site, a player may place one or more palace tiles in the center of the board. Every tile must satisfy these conditions:

    1. Each palace tile shows a required number of workers. The player must have at least that many workers at the Construction Site.
    2. Pay the resources and decorations. Return resources to their locations; decorations remain permanently on the palace tile.
    3. Place the tile adjacent to an existing palace tile or along the edge of the Construction Site. Outdoor and indoor portions must match those of adjacent tiles, or placement is illegal.

After placing a tile, score the victory points printed on it. A player may place multiple palace tiles during a single activation.

- King's Favor

The king  
Whenever King's Favor is activated or skipped over, advance the king one space. If he reaches the final space, the game ends immediately.  
A player may activate King's Favor to recruit new workers or refresh double-move tokens:

    1. Recruiting a new worker requires two or three workers to activate, according to the printed cost. A newly recruited worker appears at King's Favor and cannot be used immediately. A player may recruit two new workers in one action, or recruit the more expensive worker first.
    2. Spend one worker to flip up to two double-move tokens face up.

Technologies

The Alchemists’ Guild contains three technology tracks. Technologies grant players special abilities.

  • Improved Resource Collection

This technology gives the player extra resources.

Level 1: whenever the player gains wood, gain one additional wood.
Level 2: whenever the player gains marble, gain one additional marble.
Level 3: whenever the player gains gold, gain one additional gold. Note that activating the Gold Mine with one worker also gains one gold.

  • Improved Resource Locations

This technology lets a player collect resources when another player does. The amount gained depends on how many of their workers occupy that location. At least one of their workers must be present to use the technology.

Level 1: whenever another player activates the Lumber Mill, this player may also activate it to gain wood.
Level 2: whenever another player activates the Marble Quarry, this player may also activate it to gain marble.
Level 3: whenever another player activates the Gold Mine, this player may also activate it to gain gold.

  • Improved Special Locations

This technology lets a player activate the Architects’ Guild, Workshop, or Construction Site when someone else activates it. Benefits depend on how many of their workers occupy that location, and at least one worker must be present. If several players have the technology, resolve their actions one at a time, beginning with the player to the active player’s left.

Level 1: whenever another player activates the Architects’ Guild, this player may also activate it.
Level 2: whenever another player activates the Workshop, this player may also activate it.
Level 3: whenever another player activates the Construction Site, this player may also activate it.

Game End

The game ends as soon as any of these conditions is met:

  • The Construction Site has no space remaining.
  • The king reaches the end of his track.
  • The palace-tile stack is empty and fewer than seven discarded palace tiles remain.

The game ends immediately when a condition is triggered. Even if the active player has unused workers, they may take no further actions.

Final Scoring

At the end of the game, players add these victory points:

  • Every three marble, three wood, or two gold are worth one point.
  • Every palace tile still in a player’s hand is worth one point.
  • Every decoration is worth three points.

The player with the most victory points wins. Tied players share the victory.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Praetor Unboxing and Review
entry.content:
Yesterday—when this was written, that was last November—I went to an event at Club A for the third time, met the famous E in person, and shamelessly recruited several people there to help review Praetor. First, thanks to E, Mantou, and Caliph (I think it was Caliph…). The unboxing comes first, followed by my impressions after the first play.

The rulebook is thin, only a few pages. For the full rules, see [titanxxh’s Essen 2014] Game Overview 3: Praetor.

The backs of the player aids provide three promo city tiles. During our game, we discovered that these buildings were very important.

The front of the player aid shows every city tile. Note that the same city tile may have several copies depending on player count!

Player discs and worker dice in five colors. I recommend putting the starting resources in with them to make setup easier.

The remaining shared components. Why are the gold coins worth 1 while the silver ones are worth 5…?

All the Wall tiles. (Remember: the game’s theme is not building the Wall. This is important!)

The player boards are double-sided. I chose two at random to show here. In our first game, everyone used the identical A side; I do not know how well balanced the other side is.

The insert is ordinary. Both sides show several plaza patterns. (They are this obvious, yet E somehow could not tell them apart during the game…)

Three stacks of city tiles; 0 marks the starting tiles used during setup.

Finally, this. After one play, everyone agreed that “60–90 minutes” was a lie. A four-player game is definitely 180+ minutes, okay?

That concludes the unboxing. Next comes the session recap and review.

Final scores first.

E—white, 319; Caliph—blue, 224; Mantou—black, 174; me—yellow, 256.

Seeing that everyone was an experienced heavy-strategy player, I skipped the setting entirely, explained the rules, and launched straight into the game. Looking back, that was a serious mistake. It directly caused our friend Mantou to make a major strategic error and finish with a tragic score… Although the game is set during Emperor Hadrian’s reign, building the Wall is emphatically not its theme; the theme is building a city. Had Mantou understood that, he probably would not have gone on a Wall-building frenzy from the very beginning… In the opening, white and yellow steadily trained workers. E began training earlier than I did, but my Academy let me train workers faster. Blue developed slowly, while black set out on the one-way road of Wall construction.


Mantou’s Hadrian’s Wall…

After several rounds, black was scoring heavily from the Wall every round, but too few new workers caused a resource shortage and eventually a vicious cycle. Once I snatched one Wall tile, black was reduced to little more than a spectator… E and I alternated between stockpiling resources and constructing buildings. The difference was that E earned income from a powerful building with an entry fee of 3—which lets you use a retired worker—and could comfortably pay wages every round. I had to convert batches of resources into cash from time to time, wasting quite a few actions. I also retired two workers too early in one round and ended up with a gap in my workforce, though the Academy kept the damage manageable.

The calculations grew heavier late in the game. In our four-player game, there were only six strong point-generating buildings. Once the fifth appeared, turn order became exceptionally important. E realized this early, repeatedly seized first player, and ran several more scoring actions, gradually establishing a large lead. My strategy always kept plenty of resources on hand, several retired workers, and high Morale. Although I could use every scoring building and opponents could not lock me out, my terrible turn order meant I could score only once each round. I was forced to develop the Wall to compensate, but still fell far short.


The city at the end of the game

First-play review:
The game flows smoothly overall, makes point-scoring satisfying, and gives players ample ways to constrain one another. At heart it is a worker-placement game, but most of the scoring opportunities apart from the Wall appear late, and their order is not fixed. That demands well-rounded development; specialize too narrowly and you may find yourself unable to use any scoring building. Another issue is that constructing a scoring building does not mean you will get to use it—the most likely outcome is that you plant the tree and someone else enjoys its shade. The promo tile that adjusts turn order alleviates this problem to some extent. I watched Dice Tower’s review, in which Tom raised two objections. First, he considered the tiles unbalanced. I doubt that conclusion; I suspect they allowed the same player to exploit too many efficient scoring buildings without restraining them. Second, he said that considering the plaza patterns at the four corners when placing tiles “makes no sense.” I must say he is absolutely wrong. To me, this is precisely the kind of detail that shows the designer’s care. The reward naturally encourages players to place tiles together instead of creating bizarre shapes as they might in Eclipse or Carcassonne. Adjacent tiles necessarily share plaza patterns, encouraging the next player to make the same choice. As the image above shows, the city jointly constructed by the players ultimately forms a fairly regular square. In fact, it remained roughly square throughout our game. That both solves the problem of limited table space and truly feels like expanding a city piece by piece!

Finally, to quote E’s verdict: “Pretty good. 7.5 out of 10. A lot of calculation and a slightly overlong playtime.”

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Progress Unboxing and Review
entry.content:
This installment brings an unboxing and review of Progress: Evolution of Technology, which I introduced earlier. For the detailed rules, see the previous article.

Several of my recent games have come from NSKN Games. Many readers may know large publishers such as Z-Man, Rio Grande Games, and Pegasus Spiele but be less familiar with this company, which brought three titles to Essen that year. Before opening the box, let me briefly introduce it.
NSKN Games was a relatively young publisher founded in April 2011 by Andrei Novac, Agnieszka Kopera, Florin Neacsu, and Vlad Sladariu. Its name comes from the initials of their surnames. NSKN primarily designs and publishes family and strategy games.
The founders want entertaining strategy games that families and friends can enjoy together. Most of their titles are based on a historical period or an iconic event.

Here is the company’s website. It may require special network access.

The listed playtime is 45–90 minutes, which is fairly accurate.

The back of the box shows the setup. It occupies quite a lot of table space.

The rulebook has eight pages, though much of it repeats information.

Every player receives a technology tree.

A player’s ability board and the three power tracks

Four kinds of technology tokens

Some wooden components

Paper score sheets. Learning from Uwe Rosenberg?

Here are some technology cards. This is Agriculture from Age I.

Astronomy from Age II

Archaeology from Age III

Age IV is promotional content. This card should be Antibiotics.

Promo 2, the Great People expansion, with fifteen Great People in total

Promo 3, the Milestones expansion. These are not the only three cards.

First-play review:
After one complete four-player game of Progress, my overall impression is that it is merely an average light strategy game. The artwork is a major highlight; if it was all created specifically for the game, that was an impressive undertaking. Beneath the broad mechanisms of action-point allocation and hand management, several design problems were already obvious in our first play. The largest issue is that viable development paths feel too narrow.
First, the abilities in the game differ enormously in strength. In my view, hand size and number of actions represent the two extremes. Increasing hand size is almost meaningless to a player who manages cards well or draws fortunate cards, while gaining more action points fundamentally accelerates that player’s technological progress.
Second, the quality of your hand is crucial. If your cards consistently lack the prerequisite technologies, or never provide the power-track or ability improvements you want, planning your overall development becomes a headache.
Finally, interaction is too limited. Everyone mostly plays cards in silence. The only points of competition are the three power tracks, and you might not even draw the cards that affect them. This can also be considered an advantage, however. A player’s turn ends after taking the draw action, so the next player can begin while you examine your newly drawn cards and plan the following turn, reducing downtime.
I hope we can add the promos next time. Perhaps, as with Praetor in our previous session, they will solve some of these problems.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Versailles Unboxing and Review
entry.content:
This installment brings an unboxing and review of Versailles, which titanxxh introduced earlier. For the detailed rules, see the previous article.

First, the final scores: Feng 51, Xiaoding 46, me 45, and Weicheng and E 41.
PS: Recruiting workers at the beginning is genuinely a poor choice…

The rulebook is only four pages long…

The decorations were cut off-center

Double-move tokens

A stack of palace tiles

The figure representing the king

Various resources

Player tokens in five colors

The game board

The back of the box

45–75 minutes, and this time the claim is accurate…

First-play review:

Mechanically, Versailles centers on point-to-point movement with tile placement attached. Through a clever board design resembling a rondel, however, the designer makes the game feel fresh. As its rulebook claims, Versailles really is “innovative.”

Consider the board’s structure. It contains only eight locations. As shown above, the outermost ring forms a loop, while the construction site in the middle lets workers complete that loop more quickly. Versailles’s innovation grows directly from this arrangement.

There is relatively little direct player interaction during the game, yet players still affect one another in other ways. Depending on player count and strategic choices, different end conditions may be triggered, and the resulting pace feeds back into every decision. That may sound abstract, so consider the ideal route. Would it not be best for every worker to begin at the King’s Favor, advance one location at a time, exploit the full benefit of keeping three workers together, maximize the value of every action, accumulate enough resources, palace tiles, and decorations, and finally enter the construction site all at once?

The ideal is full, but reality is bony. During play, all kinds of reasons—perhaps you want to upgrade a technology first—force you to visit certain locations early. As the end approaches, every move requires greater care: the palace may be running out of legal spaces, the king may be about to inspect the work, and so on. Players must constantly observe and adjust their routes.

If that were the entire design, the game’s flow would still feel rigid and sticky. Each player also has two double-move tokens, however. They greatly enrich the possible routes and serve as the finishing touch to the core design.

Artistically, titanxxh believes the palace in the center of the board badly disrupts the overall harmony. Apart from that, the presentation is clean and refreshing.

As for playing time, the three end conditions constrain one another and ensure that the game never lasts too long, regardless of player count.

Finally, E’s comments:

The rules are simple and the playing time is short, yet the game still has some depth. It is probably best not to play with five, though, and it could use more ways to score.

entry.title: [Board Game Life] Issue 5: On Strategic Depth in Board Games
entry.content:
This article first appeared on Baidu’s Board Games forum. The circumstances behind it are complicated, so I will omit them here.

When it comes to strategic depth, I have not played as many board games as the experts on the forum, nor can I claim to have mastered more than a handful. Even so, I believe I am capable of drawing a few conclusions.
This expands on a reply I posted yesterday.

Can a game’s strategic depth be quantified? Personally, I believe it can, but the problem is complicated enough that even a full paper would not be sufficient to explain it in detail.
First, I must point out that directly comparing strategic depth across different types of games is difficult, though indirect comparison is possible. To keep this article from becoming so long that it loses focus, everything below concerns comparisons between games of the same type.

A game’s strategic richness can be divided qualitatively into breadth and depth.

Let us begin with breadth. Put simply, it is the number of meaningful decisions available to a player each turn in the current state—considering their own player board or hand and, when information is public, the other players’ situations. Because these are board games, designers generally do not approach them as they would video games, so a player rarely has many meaningful options at a decision point, usually somewhere from zero to ten. Games with higher weight ratings may increase that number to some extent. The important point is that breadth is driven primarily by the options the designer provides; the player then combines those options with the rules to make a decision. Consider Agricola. Its worker-placement spaces are the ones the designer created, with new ones added each round. To take an action, players must pay certain resources or satisfy certain conditions. How might we increase the game’s strategic breadth? Easy: add more action spaces, introduce more types of resources—as in Ora et Labora—or impose additional conditions. But there is a limit to useful breadth. As noted above, designing a board game is not the same as designing a video game; endlessly adding options or restrictions is not necessarily beneficial. Designers’ notes often reveal that early prototypes contained very concrete, abundant detail, which designers gradually refined as development proceeded.
In summary, breadth as one aspect of strategy depends largely on the designer. The player’s own thinking accounts for a relatively small part here: they merely check whether their current state satisfies certain conditions, and with computer assistance even that step could be skipped.

Depth, on the other hand, is what I believe has the greater influence on a board game’s strategic richness. Depth is less intuitive to define than breadth. Broadly, it determines how many layers a player must consider when making a decision. “Layers” has a rich meaning here and generally includes, but is not limited to, the following aspects:

  • A player’s own medium- and long-term planning

This is clearly reflected in most games. Players need to establish a medium- or long-term plan; many games, for example Tzolk’in, require you to build a point-scoring engine. In strategically rich games, a player with a plan will generally gain an advantage over one who treats every turn in isolation, or will at least think more efficiently. If it is more difficult for a player to establish a clear plan in one game than in another, we can say the former has greater strategic depth.

  • How to make trade-offs when conflicts arise

Many games feature competition for resources, one of the relatively few forms of player interaction in Eurogames. This easily creates situations where you cannot have your cake and eat it too.
