Conflicts over resources then affect short-term and even long-term plans. “Resources” here means anything concrete or abstract that helps a player win: wood or stone in Agricola; the choice between settlements in Ora et Labora—different settlements can shift the entire focus of your later strategy; or even the alliances you forge and enemies you make in negotiation games. The more conflicts a game asks players to balance, and the harder it is to determine the basis for those trade-offs, the greater its relative strategic depth.

  • How to control randomness

Games with shared decks, bags of tiles, dice, and similar elements introduce randomness, but the amount of randomness does not directly determine strategic depth. A well-designed game can include substantial randomness while giving players mechanisms to control it; The Castles of Burgundy and Troyes are classic examples. A poorly designed game instead leaves players feeling helpless before fate. I will avoid naming examples for fear of provoking outrage. If a game’s mechanisms keep random events from causing wild swings in a player’s position, we can say that game has greater strategic depth.

  • Identifying your principal opponent, especially with hidden information

This issue generally arises when victory information or other key information is hidden or only partly public, forcing players to identify their opponents. Even in games with fully public information, however, identifying the right opponent is not necessarily simple. A few examples make both points clear. Legends of the Three Kingdoms contains hidden identities, yet identifying opponents is fairly easy: after one round, most roles are clear and do not change as play continues. In Modern Art, the key resource—money—and the composition of other players’ hands are hidden, making the principal opponent difficult to identify and causing that opponent to change continually. Then there is Ora et Labora, a zero-randomness game with completely public information. Even after more than forty plays, I still find it hard before Phase D to judge whether players of comparable skill are slightly ahead of me or slightly behind. The harder it is to identify one’s opponent and the more frequently that opponent changes, the greater a game’s relative strategic depth.

  • How to constrain your opponent

In traditionally American-style games, methods of constraining opponents are often direct. In traditional Eurogames, they tend to be less direct, and their design generally discourages players from focusing so much on interference that they neglect their own development. This point is closely related to the one above. If you identify the wrong opponent, or fail to notice that your principal rival has changed, you may target the wrong person with the wrong disruption. That not only harms their experience but can, more seriously, unbalance the entire game. In general, the less obvious a game’s methods of constraining opponents, the higher their cost, and the harder it is to identify the correct opponent, the greater the game’s strategic depth.

  • How to avoid being constrained, and how to keep your second-best options from becoming too poor when you are constrained—in other words, raising your floor

This last item is the only one listed here that requires interpreting another person’s thoughts. As the saying goes, you may know a person’s face but not their heart; human intentions are hard to fathom. It also interacts with the previous point: how you think about constraining an opponent largely determines how that opponent thinks about constraining you. The topic is too complex for me to explain clearly because it involves judging your opponent’s level of reasoning. But I do have experience with the latter question: keeping second-best options acceptable after being blocked. As an undergraduate, I had a close friend who played often. In pure tactical calculation, I admit he was better than me, though he also fell into analysis paralysis far more often. But he tended to focus excessively on his own development and overlook how others might affect him. This was less obvious in two-player games and especially pronounced in multiplayer ones. Sometimes his move depended entirely on whether the other two or three players blocked his intended action. If anyone did, his entire plan collapsed; if nobody did, he executed an optimal decision smoothly. Remember that you are playing with people. You cannot fully understand every player’s reasoning or model everyone as a perfectly rational decision-maker. Therefore, when making decisions, it is necessary not only to maximize the expected value of your future positions but also to reduce their variance. I will refrain from judging which games are strategically deeper on this final point…

The discussion above shows how difficult it is to analyze strategic depth, even qualitatively. Only after mastering a game—which usually requires a major investment of time—can one confidently attempt a full quantitative analysis.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Game Overview 5—Zhanguo
entry.content:
For the first installment after the return of my Essen 2014 series, I decided to translate the game that readers currently anticipate most and that I personally considered the most promising title of 2014: Zhanguo. At this point, I have to complain about foreigners’ understanding of Chinese language and history. According to the setting, the chaos of the Warring States period has already ended, and Qin Shi Huang has begun implementing measures to consolidate his rule and unify the empire. The game clearly should not be called Zhanguo; “Great Qin” or “Unification” would seem far more appropriate. Anyone expecting rival Warring States powers to fight one another may therefore be disappointed. Judging from the rules, however, Zhanguo continues What’s Your Game?’s tradition of heavy strategy titles. Fans of Eurogames should love it.


Zhanguo

Front of the box

Historical Background

Between 230 and 221 BCE, the ambitious young King Ying Zheng of Qin unified China and brought all the other Warring States under his rule.
The game takes place after this conquest. Although the King of Qin has proclaimed himself emperor, many occupied regions still do not consider themselves part of his empire. The peoples of the newly annexed states continue to regard their lands as independent kingdoms with their own traditions and laws, which they are unwilling to lose.
To prevent political disorder, Qin Shi Huang abolished the feudal system, introduced a system of commanderies and counties, divided China into several provinces, and personally appointed officials. He also decreed that differing cultural elements should be standardized to bind society together more effectively.
Domestic policy was not the only concern of the newly unified China. The Xiongnu posed a constant threat from the north, and Qin Shi Huang understood that the only way to remove that danger was to construct a great wall—one of the most extraordinary structures in human history.
In Zhanguo, players contribute to Qin Shi Huang’s project of unification. By completing a series of demanding tasks, they transform the divided states into a single empire.
The game lasts five rounds. In each round, players must make the best use of the cards they receive. A card may be placed on a player board to increase its owner’s personal influence within the empire, or played to the main board to recruit officials, construct palaces, move officials, appoint governors, or help build the Great Wall.
At the end of the game, the player who contributed most to Qin Shi Huang’s unification wins.

Components

  • 1 game board
  • 4 player boards
  • 120 cards: 40 ivory, 40 orange, and 40 brown
  • 40 worker tiles
  • 6 wall tiles
  • 12 task tiles
  • 1 round marker
  • 30 governors: 8 in each of four colors
  • 20 wall pieces: 5 in each of four colors
  • 24 palaces: 6 in each of four colors
  • 32 discs: 8 in each of four colors
  • 20 unrest markers
  • 60 officials: 20 red, 20 gray, and 20 white
  • 4 score tiles showing 100/200
  • 39 unification tokens in ivory, orange, and brown: twelve worth 1 point and one worth 3 points in each color

Setup

The illustration below shows the setup for a four-player game. With fewer than four players, remove the unused components.

  1. Game Board

    • Place the board in the center of the table. It is divided into several areas: rewards, tasks, court, provinces, and the Great Wall.

      • Provinces: the five provinces are identified by the following symbols.

      • Great Wall: the three Great Wall construction sites are identified by the following symbol.

  2. Player Supplies

    • Each player chooses a color—blue, red, purple, or yellow—and takes:
      • 8 discs
      • 8 governors
      • 6 palaces
      • 5 wall pieces
      • 5 unrest markers
      • 5 white officials
      • 5 gray officials
      • 5 red officials

  3. Cards

    • Separate the cards into three decks by the color on their backs and shuffle each deck.
    • Place the decks face down beside the board.

  4. Round Track

    • Place the round marker on space 1 of the round track.

  5. Three-Point Unification Tokens

    • Place the three tall octagonal columns in the court area of the board.

  6. First Player

    • Choose the first player randomly. Play proceeds clockwise.
    • In clockwise order, every player places one disc on the reward track, with the first player’s disc at the top.

    Note: The order of these discs changes every round. The player whose disc is at the top becomes first player, but turns still proceed clockwise from that player rather than following the order of the discs. The disc order matters only for breaking ties during the Unification Reward phase, described below.

  7. Victory Points

    • Every player places one disc on space 0 of the victory-point track.
      Victory points shown on a black background are awarded at the end of the game. Points shown on red are scored immediately.

  8. Task Discs

    • Every player places their remaining six discs beside the task area.

  9. Walls

    • Shuffle the six wall tiles and place one face up at each Great Wall construction site.

  10. Tasks

    • The task area is divided into two sections. Each section contains one Great Wall task, one palace task, and one governor task.
    • Shuffle the Great Wall tasks and place two face up in the task area. The other two are not used.
    • Repeat this procedure for the palace and governor tasks.

  11. General Supply

    • Place the worker tiles and one-point unification tokens beside the game board.

  12. Player Boards
    There are four player boards, identified by a circle, square, triangle, or star.
    Each board is double-sided. The symbols on side A are outlines, while those on side B are solid.
    All side-A boards are identical; every side-B board is different, as explained later.

    • We recommend using side A for your first few games.
    • If you decide to use side B, you may choose the boards through an auction or another method. Each player begins with 15 points.
      Note: Leave space above the player boards for cards.
      Each board is divided into five provinces, using the same symbols as the main board.
      Within every province, the government area is above and the worker area below.

  13. Officials

    • Every player takes the three officials indicated in province 1 of their player board and places them in province 1.

Note: With the exception of worker tiles, all resources are limited. Every component is visible to all players.

Round Overview

The game lasts five rounds. After the fifth, the player with the most victory points wins. Every round contains the following three phases:

  • Phase 1: Draw Cards
  • Phase 2: Play Cards
  • Phase 3: Unification Rewards

Draw Cards Phase

At the beginning of each round, every player draws two cards from each deck, giving them a hand of six cards with two of each color.

About the cards

During Phase 2, players use cards to perform actions.

Card fronts:
Every card has an ability, an activation number from 1 to 120, and a unification type: writing, currency, or law.
The ivory deck represents the unification of writing and contains cards 1–40.
The orange deck represents the unification of currency and contains cards 41–80.
The brown deck represents the unification of laws and contains cards 81–120.
Detailed card abilities are listed at the back of the rulebook.

Card backs:
The symbol in the center shows the card’s unification type.
The numbers below show the range of card numbers in the deck.
Players must allow their opponents to see the back of at least one card in their hand.

Play Cards Phase

Beginning with the first player and proceeding clockwise, each player plays one card to perform one action. Continue until everyone has played all six cards.

How to play a card
On a player’s turn, they may:

  • Perform a Unification Action by playing a card into one province of their player board.

or

  • Perform a Court Action by playing a card face up to the court area of the main board, covering the previously played card and forming a stack.

Unification Action

The player chooses a province and slides one card beneath the bottom edge of their player board, leaving the ability on its upper half visible.

Each province can hold at most three cards. Once placed, a card cannot be moved.

Unification tokens: the player takes one to three one-point unification tokens matching the type of the card just placed. The number depends on whether it is the first, second, or third card placed in that province.
If there are not enough one-point unification tokens, the player scores 1 victory point for each missing token.

Unrest markers: certain actions during the game increase unrest in a province. Every province has an unrest track that records its current level.

  • No unrest marker on the track represents unrest level 0.
  • Whenever the unrest level changes, move that province’s unrest marker.

Unification Actions and unrest: when performing a Unification Action, placing the second card in a province raises its unrest by 1, while placing the third raises it by 2. A player may not perform an action that would increase the province’s unrest beyond its maximum.

Court Action

The player places a card in the court area of the main board and performs one of the following six Court Actions.

Important! Any card may be used for any action.
Important! A player may choose only an action they can perform, and they must complete that action.

  • Recruit an Official

Every player’s personal supply contains five red, five white, and five gray cubes representing officials.
The player chooses one cube and places it in the government area of any province on their player board.
There is no limit to the number of cubes in a government area.

  • Move Officials

Officials may work in a government area or a worker area.
In a government area they carry out administrative duties; in a worker area they hire laborers for the emperor.
The Move Officials action lets a player move their officials to another province or between areas of the same province.
One movement point moves one official:
- From a government area to the government area of an adjacent province.
- From a worker area to the worker area of an adjacent province. A worker area may contain at most two officials.
- From a worker area to the government area of the same province.

Adjacent provinces share a solid border rather than a wall on the game board.

Important! Moving an official from a government area into the worker area of the same province costs no movement points and may be done at any time during your turn.

  • Appoint a Governor

The player chooses a province in which to appoint a governor, then:

  1. Removes one set of officials from that province on their player board and returns them to their personal supply.
  2. Places a governor in that province on the game board. The player may choose any unoccupied bonus space and immediately receives its bonus. If every bonus is occupied, place the governor beside them and receive no bonus.
  3. If the province’s unrest level is not 0, reduce it to 0.
  • Hire Workers

The player chooses a province, then:

  1. Hires workers according to the number of officials in that province’s worker area. Each official hires one worker.
    Because a worker area can contain at most two officials, this action can hire no more than two workers.
  2. Regardless of the number hired, increase that province’s unrest by 1. This action cannot be performed if the province is already at maximum unrest.
  • Build a Palace

The player chooses a province, then:

  1. Removes two workers from that province and one worker from a different province, returning them to the general supply.
  2. Places a palace in an empty palace space in the chosen province.
  3. If possible, takes one three-point unification token.
  4. Scores 1 point for every card currently tucked beneath their player board.

Important! A player may not build a palace in a province whose unrest level is too high.

  • Build a Wall

Three Great Wall construction sites are marked by flags on the map. Each site contains two wall sections, and each section has a wall tile assigned to it.
The player chooses a wall section, then:

  1. Places one wall piece in one of the section’s three wall spaces. A player may have no more than one wall piece among the three spaces in the same section.
  2. Removes one, two, or three workers according to the chosen wall space. Those workers must come from different provinces.

Activating Card Abilities

As noted earlier, any card can be used for any action. After completing the chosen Court Action, however, the card played may activate abilities on cards in the player’s board.
The player chooses the order of activation and receives the reward shown in the upper-right corner of each activated card.
Two conditions must be satisfied to activate an ability:

  • The number on the played card must meet the relevant requirement. For Hire Workers, Build a Palace, or Build a Wall, its number must be higher than the card previously on top of the court stack. For Appoint a Governor or Recruit an Official, its number must be lower than the previous top card.
  • The action performed must match the symbol on the left of the ability card.

Note: For the first Court Action of a round, the active player may choose any value for the nonexistent previous top card X.
Note: The Move Officials action does not trigger card abilities.
Important! Abilities in a province at maximum unrest do not activate.

Unification Reward Phase

After every player has used all cards, the Play Cards phase ends and the Unification Reward phase begins.
Resolve the reward for writing first, then currency, and finally laws. Each reward goes to the player who contributed most in that field.
The exact reward depends on the round and the type of unification.

First, every player totals the value of their writing-unification tokens. The player with the highest total decides whether to accept that round’s reward:

  • If they accept, the player returns all ivory unification tokens, gains the reward, and moves their disc onto that reward.
  • If they decline, the player keeps the ivory tokens and does not move their disc. After that player passes, the player with the second-highest total decides whether to accept.

Resolve the currency- and law-unification rewards in the same way.

If players tie for the highest total value of unification tokens, determine their priority as follows:
First come players still on the reward track, from top to bottom, followed by players who have already taken a reward in the current round, again from top to bottom.
In the example below, the order is blue, yellow, red, then purple.

After resolving all three fields, return the player discs to the reward track in the order above. The player at the top becomes the new first player.
Note: Unification tokens score points at the end of the game, as explained below.

Tasks: the task area is on the right side of the game board. When a player meets the conditions of a task, they place one disc on the leftmost unoccupied space of that task.
Note: Tasks score points at the end of the game, as explained below.

End of the Game

The game ends after five rounds. Players calculate victory points as follows:

  1. In each province, the player with the most governors receives a base of 9 points plus 3 points for every governor there. If several players tie for the most, they divide these points equally.
  2. The players with the most unification tokens receive 5, 6, or 7 points for the three respective types. Ties are broken by the current disc order.
  3. Score the two task sections separately.
    Add the values beneath a player’s discs.
    Multiply that total by the number of the player’s discs in the section: ×2 for two completed tasks or ×3 for three.
  4. Score points according to the wall tiles.

Variant Rules

  1. In rounds 1–4, players draw three cards from each deck, keep two, and shuffle the discarded cards into the bottom of the relevant deck.
  2. The order on the reward track determines player order instead of clockwise order.
  3. Increase a province’s unrest by 1 for each worker hired there.

Strategy Tips

One of the most important considerations is balancing the number of cards played to your personal board against those played to the game board.
The more cards you place in your personal board, the more powerful your Court Actions become, but you also have fewer opportunities to trigger those abilities.
For a first game, we recommend placing three or four cards in your player board during the first round before taking Court Actions.
Likewise, if you plan to activate card abilities, pay attention to the colors of cards in other players’ hands. For example, if you want to activate abilities linked to Build a Palace, it is better to save high-numbered cards rather than place them in your player board, especially while opponents still hold brown cards.
Your goal is to activate as many card abilities as possible, but do not become trapped by that objective. Victory does not require it at all costs. Sometimes you need to perform an action even when it activates no abilities.
Task requirements are also crucial because they determine where you appoint governors and construct walls and palaces. The more of your discs you place within one task section, the more victory points you receive. We recommend concentrating on one section.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2014] Game Overview 6 and Unboxing: Fields of Arle
entry.content:
Fields of Arle

This Essen 2014 installment features another new money pit from Uwe Rosenberg: Fields of Arle, sometimes described as a two-player Agricola on a grand scale. Arle is a small village in East Frisia, northern Germany—a place almost nobody outside the area would know. The game is somewhat autobiographical: Arle is where Uwe’s father was born, while Uwe himself was born twenty kilometers away in Aurich, which also appears in the game.
The setting returns us to the Middle Ages and the glory days of the village of Arle. Though Arle was not large, its high-quality flax contributed to Frisia’s prosperity. Players begin from nothing in a “one-horse town” with only one flax field—and literally one horse in the setup—then gradually develop it into a major textile town.


Front of the box

Introduction

Welcome to East Frisia!

Arle is a small village in East Frisia. Today, only the scale of its cathedral reminds people of its former importance.
In centuries past, Arle stood out because of the fertile farmland around it. The finest flax in northern Germany was said to grow there. As demand for the resource rose, local farmers quickly became wealthy and lived better than other East Frisians. Growing prosperity also gave people freedom to decide whether to cultivate flax personally or pursue other needs.

You may grow wheat, raise animals, harvest peat, colonize moorland, or build dikes. You may cultivate forests, travel by vehicle, or construct workshops and inns. Your most important task is to build the renowned cathedral mentioned above.
The game consists of nine “half years,” alternating between summer and winter. Different actions are available in the two seasons. A season-specific inventory occurs after each half year, and final scoring determines who achieved more over four and a half years.

For those who come from the sea,
East Frisia is not at the end of the world,
but rather at its very beginning.

Ewald Christophers

Components

  • One large main game board
  • 2 home boards
  • 2 “travel destination/barn” storage boards
  • 1 supply board
  • 9 travel destinations per player
  • Building materials:
    • 24 clay/bricks
    • 24 wood/timber
  • Clothing:
    • 24 linen/summer wear
    • 24 leather/leather wear
    • 24 woolen cloth/winter wear
  • Replacement pieces:
    • 1 5× linen
    • 1 5× woolen cloth
    • 1 5× leather
  • 1 scoring pad
  • 2 overview sheets
  • 1 sticker sheet
  • Tiles:
    • 5 forest/park
    • 7 stall/depot
    • 3 stable/double stall
    • 14 wheat field/flax field
    • 3 cart/horse cart
    • 3 carriage/droshky
    • 2 handcart/wagon
    • 6 peat boat/plow
    • 10 dikes
    • 2 paths
    • 6 moor/drained moor
    • 31 buildings
  • Wooden indicators:
    • 10 tool indicators per player
    • 1 wheat indicator per player
    • 1 flax indicator per player
    • 1 hide indicator per player
    • 1 wool indicator per player
    • 2 food indicators per player
  • Wooden tokens:
    • 4 workers per player
    • 40 peat
    • 20 sheep
    • 20 cattle
    • 20 horses
  • 1 half-year marker
  • 1 starting-player marker

Setup

  1. Put the supply board between the players and arrange the supply piles as shown. If the table is not large enough, simply leave this board in the box.

    For pieces in the top row, a player may freely choose either side when receiving one during the game.
    Pieces in the bottom row may be used only on their front side; the reverse is the upgraded version.

  2. Place the large game board next to the supply board. Put the orange half-year marker on space one of the round track. Each player chooses a color and places their tool indicators on the leftmost spaces of the ten work tracks.

    Tool indicators show how many tools you own, and that quantity can increase during play.

  3. Familiarize yourself with building costs, which are printed on the board.

  4. Choose the starting player randomly and give them the starting-player marker. Put one worker from each player on every space from July through October, with the starting player’s worker on top.

  5. Place buildings according to their colors on the board. Some colors have more buildings than spaces; remove the extras from the game.

    There are two sets of green buildings. For a first game, use the four light-green buildings. Once familiar with the game, use four of the seven dark-green buildings instead.

  6. Take a home board and arrange every component on it as shown.

    The travel-experience track is on the left, empty land in the center, and goods tracks on the right.
    In addition to the home board, take a “travel destination/barn” storage board and the set of travel destinations in your color. Place them on the storage board. The barn is beneath the destinations and begins empty.
    You receive:

    • One overview sheet
    • 4 wood, 4 clay, and 3 peat

    The result should look roughly like this:

Because Uwe’s rules are so verbose, I improvised the material that follows. This installment is therefore not really a rules translation; at most, it is a detailed introduction.

The objective is to develop your village as much as possible over nine rounds. The player with the highest final score wins. Numbers inside compass roses indicate points. The main ways to score are:

  • Advance your dikes. As they move forward, they unlock more land; in the final row, they also prevent certain penalties.
  • Points from buildings.
  • Points from stables and stalls, as well as from animals.
  • Travel experience.
  • Draining moors reduces penalties, and harvesting all their peat reduces them further.
  • Cloth and clothing.
  • Forests and parks.
  • Goods, whose points can be doubled with a depot.
  • Plows, peat boats, and vehicles.

Gameplay

The game lasts nine rounds. Each represents half a year, alternating between winter and summer, and the game ends after the fifth summer.
Every round has three phases.

Preparation Phase

Players put their four workers on the corresponding months—July through October in summer, January through April in winter—with the starting player’s workers on top.

Work Phase

From left to right, players perform actions one at a time, with the starting player acting first.
Summer actions are available only in summer rounds and winter actions only in winter rounds. Each season has fifteen different actions. They are all printed on the board, so I will not translate them here. Content inside the blue-and-white Frisian pattern represents a cost; actions generally require payment.

Only one player may perform one special action—an action from the other season—in a round. Their opponent receives the starting-player marker afterward. If nobody uses a special action, the starting-player marker still changes hands.

At any time, a player may:

  • Load goods onto vehicles. Loading flips an item to its other side. If it is a travel destination, goods may be sold for food. One large vehicle space cannot hold two small goods, but two small spaces can hold one large good.
  • Rearrange animals.
  • If they own a peat boat, exchange goods at a 1:1 rate.

Inventory Phase

After both players complete the Work phase, conduct the season’s inventory.

Summer inventory:

  1. Unload vehicles. Players receive the goods or travel experience they contain.
  2. Milk animals. Owning 2/5/7 sheep or 1/3/5 cattle yields 1/2/3 food.
  3. Harvest. Every wheat field on a home board produces one wheat, every flax field one flax, and every forest one wood.
  4. Subsistence. Pay three food and two peat—winter is coming!

Winter inventory:

  1. Unload vehicles as above.
  2. Breed animals. Only animals in stalls and stables reproduce, and there must be room for the offspring, since young animals live with their parents. Every pair of the same animal produces one new animal.
  3. Shear sheep. Owning 1/4/6 sheep yields 1/2/3 wool.
  4. Subsistence. Pay three food.

Game End

After nine rounds, the game ends. Players may use their peat boats to exchange goods, then score:

  • Clothing and building materials, with halves rounded down.
  • Items in the barn.
  • Travel experience.
  • Tool levels on the main board.
  • Each good scores according to its quantity on the goods track. If the player owns a depot, double the points in this category.
  • Points and penalties on the home board.
  • Animal points equal twice the number of the least numerous animal plus the number of the second-least numerous animal.
  • Failing to meet subsistence during an Inventory phase causes penalties here, although anyone who has played Uwe’s other games is unlikely to let that happen.

Solo Variant

The player cannot use special actions. A score of 110 is considered highly commendable!

Unboxing


Front of the box


Back of the box


Rules and overview sheets


Wooden tokens


Everything…


From another angle


Travel destinations


Starting-player marker


Buildings, fabrics, and other pieces from the supply


The only cow bearing Uwe Rosenberg’s name

entry.title: Answering Zhihu: Are Board Games Doomed in China?
entry.content:
This article originated as an answer on Zhihu.

The question was: Are board games in China destined to reach a dead end?
The argument was: compare the inconvenience of board games with the convenience of video games, and board games seem inherently disadvantaged as an organized activity.
The questioner appeared inclined to believe that board games in China would ultimately reach a dead end.

“I would like to hear veteran players’ views on the future of board games.” The questioner did not define a veteran, so as someone who has been in the hobby for six years, I will shamelessly offer an answer. I am purely a player of German-style strategy games, so my perspective on filler games and American-style games is inevitably incomplete. Please forgive that limitation.

My conclusion first: Board games in China are not destined to reach a dead end, but they are unlikely to become truly popular. My threshold for “popular” is actually low: the average person would need to take part in board-game activities more often each year than they go to the cinema, attend a live match, or engage in similar entertainment—assuming they are not already film or sports fans. At that point, the concept of board games would be widespread among the public and would have surpassed at least some other forms of entertainment.

The reason for this conclusion is simple. Zhang Jiawei once discussed “light appreciation” and “deep appreciation,” and I think that distinction is especially visible in board games. Board games tend to require deep appreciation, which makes it hard for them to become popular. Yet society will never lack the minority who seek that kind of experience, so the hobby will not reach a dead end.

The answer itself is now complete. Everything below is simply prompted by my own feelings.

The questioner compared board games and video games, so let me expand on that first. “Video games” is an enormous category encompassing mobile, PC, and console platforms and many genres. As a whole, video games are currently extremely popular. Divide them by genre, however, and you find that many have never been popular, while others enjoyed popularity for a long time and are now declining. Examples abound: the pinnacle of turn-based strategy, Heroes of Might and Magic III, was popular only briefly; the real-time strategy game Warcraft III remained popular for a long time but has declined in recent years. If the questioner still plays Dota, they should also know what a downward trend looks like. The decline of these games and the possible decline of board games share certain similarities. Why they declined has much to do with changes in the pace of people’s lives, but that is not the focus of this answer, so I will not elaborate.

Back to light and deep appreciation: why are board games hard to promote? Why are they niche entertainment both in China and abroad? In my view, it is closely connected to their tendency to demand deep appreciation. Players can certainly experience some of the fun and charm of board games very quickly through simple filler and party games. But that is only the tip of the iceberg, far removed from a complete understanding of the medium, so it counts as light appreciation. At the stage of light appreciation, people need little prior knowledge. You do not need deep artistic training or cultivation to decide whether a painting looks beautiful; if it feels right, you naturally respond. Deep appreciation, however, requires a reasonably thorough understanding of the thing itself. Consider watching football. If you not only find beauty in a goal or a skillful dribble, but also recognize the beauty of every brilliant save by the goalkeeper; a defensive shape maintained at all times; an accurate long pass from deep by a modern holding midfielder or defender with excellent vision; a manager’s emergency positional adjustment to restore control after losing the midfield; and home fans who never stop singing—then congratulations, you have entered the realm of deep appreciation. Without a substantial understanding of football, that is difficult to achieve.

Board games likewise support deep appreciation, but unlike football, they have few immediate thrills such as goals or dribbles that let outsiders discover their charm through light appreciation. In the mainstream board-game world—by which I mean German-style strategy games, and I ask fans of American-style games to go easy on me—it is difficult to provide sustained moments of excitement even for players, let alone spectators. Most of my board-game sessions take place in a store inside a shopping mall. The outer wall is glass, so people passing in the corridor can see us play, and some stop to watch. Ninety percent watch briefly and cannot understand what we are doing. The remaining ten percent enter and ask what we are playing; only five percent are willing to hear me explain what it is. How many ultimately fall down the rabbit hole, I do not know. This shows that board games struggle to attract someone at the level of light appreciation. The exact reasons are probably complex and lie outside my field, so I cannot explain them clearly.

At this point, many people may still wonder: after all this talk, what does deep appreciation of board games actually look like? To explain it well, I must use several specific games as examples. I prefer analyzing concrete cases because broad generalizations about board games are complicated. Players with little exposure to the hobby may find the examples hard to follow. If they interest you, find a local board-game group and experience these titles yourself.

(Beginning with simple board games.)

  1. Carcassonne

    Rules: players take turns drawing tiles and joining them together, scoring according to how the tiles connect—a scoring rule I will not spell out here. When all tiles have been used, the player with the most points wins.
    After hearing those rules as a spectator, can you tell what makes it fun? At most, the game’s light appeal may be: “Oh, the completed castle is enormous,” or “The artwork is attractive; that looks great.” After several games against an expert, however, you may begin to ask why you always lose. Why does every move your opponent makes score more on average? Why can your cities so often not be completed, halving their score? Why are all your meeples committed and impossible to recover? And so on. Watch several more games between experts and you may notice that their decisions differ greatly from yours, leading to a realization: every tile placement involves a great deal of judgment. Beyond maximizing your own score, you must limit your opponent’s score, and doing that well requires knowing how many copies of every tile remain.
    This example shows that deep appreciation of a board game may arise from refining one’s strategy toward perfection. Most German-style board games consist of decision after decision, so there are many similar examples; I chose the simplest.

  2. Chinatown

    Rules: the board contains dozens of numbered spaces. Players draw numbered shop-location cards and tiles representing different kinds of businesses. The game lasts several rounds. In each, players trade shop locations, shop tiles, and cash, then build shops together and calculate income. Connecting more shops of the same type increases their revenue. After the final round, the player with the most cash wins.
    What might light appreciation look like here? Assume the player has already been initiated through Carcassonne and knows to design a strategy around the rules. They realize that adjacent shops produce more income and work toward that goal, feeling pleased when they complete a large business. More often, however, random draws leave their shop locations and tiles poorly matched. When a trade is needed, the situation may not offer an obvious win-win exchange. The player cannot accurately estimate the value of costs and returns during negotiation, deals repeatedly collapse, and other players isolate them, producing a miserable score. After two more games, they may discover that negotiations work better if they do not state every benefit too bluntly or reveal too much of their position; that three-way trades can increase the chance of success; and that verbal promises can make future possibilities part of the transaction. And so on.
    This example shows that deep appreciation of a board game can come from moving beyond the literal rules and incorporating real-life experience and thought into play. Many role-playing games, cooperative games, and negotiation games have strong immersion. Players naturally begin talking, and with the right atmosphere, imaginative participants enrich the setting and collectively perform a vivid story.

  3. Twilight Struggle

    Rules: a world map contains many countries divided into regions. Two players represent the United States and Soviet Union through several decades of the Cold War—ten turns corresponding to its early, middle, and late periods. By playing cards, they increase their control of the world. Certain cards score according to control of a region. If one side’s score passes 20, that side wins. The score track is a tug of war, so points gained by your opponent subtract from yours. Otherwise, the higher score after ten turns wins.
    It must be noted that, at the time of writing, this is the highest-ranked game on BGG, the largest board-game website. I do not personally like it very much, but that does not diminish its greatness. Let me describe what I have seen many players experience. Beyond the thrill of controlling the whole picture as the leader of a superpower, every time you play a card, it describes an event, and the rulebook explains that event. You learn a piece of history. You are astonished, impressed, or amused; you look up captivating topics on Wikipedia in an attempt to reconstruct what happened; you sense the perfect harmony between the mechanics and history; you marvel at the labor the designers invested; you applaud and give the game your highest praise: a 10 on BGG. All of this depends on being willing to try the game more deeply—and meeting the right opponent.
    This example shows that deep appreciation of a board game can arise from curiosity about a buried period of history, a distant place, an ancient craft, or a departed soul. The player follows the game’s subject outward until it becomes a way of life. Many board-game settings draw on history, culture, art, and economics. Players encounter new knowledge that sparks curiosity and reflection.

Every board game has something distinctive and could support an essay of its own. I have used familiar classics here. If reading this makes people willing to learn more about board games and experience them, my goal is achieved. To return to the beginning, I do not expect board games to become a mass craze; I only hope more people will know them and that the hobby will become a little more widespread.

entry.title: Answering Zhihu: Did One Star Make You Fall in Love with a Team? What Is Your Story?
entry.content:
This article began as an answer on Zhihu.

Ronaldo made me fall in love with Brazil, and afterward it became difficult to love a second footballer or a second team. Here is the story of Ronaldo, Brazil, and me. The first half is mostly about Ronaldo; the latter half is about Brazil.

I first watched football in 1998 and understood nothing, but there is no doubt that Ronaldo revealed its magic to me. Just as Hannibal won battle after battle and reached the gates of Rome only to lose the Second Punic War, how wonderful it would have been if the story had stopped before that night at the Stade de France. Unfortunately, this world has no “if.”

Then came the endless injuries. How many people sighed that heaven envied such talent as the Phenomenon fell to earth? Yet the story unfolded like a Hollywood film: a hero becomes famous in youth, endures hardship, loses his way—and then comes the triumphant return. The 2002 World Cup came to Asia, the first and only major tournament I could watch without turning day and night upside down. Brazil had stumbled through qualification and was not favored beforehand. Ronaldo scored eight goals, equal to the entire Spanish team’s total when it won the 2010 World Cup—and no, I am not trying to mock Spain. Brazil also won all seven matches, an unprecedented achievement that has not been repeated. When captain Cafu climbed the platform and lifted the World Cup trophy, Ronaldo, with his little fringe of hair, smiled like a child. I smiled like an idiot.

At the 2006 World Cup, the defending champions arrived amid enormous hype with their “Magic Quartet,” only to lose once again to their destined nemesis France in the quarterfinal. Ronaldo had just become the World Cup’s all-time leading scorer and now experienced defeat again. It was the first and only time football made me cry. Even so, I remained full of confidence in that Brazil side. I could never have imagined that his historic goal against Ghana would be his last for the national team.
After leaving European football and returning to Brazil with Corinthians, an overweight Ronaldo kept running and fighting for a place at the 2010 World Cup. He even completed the final hat trick of his career. Sadly, the stubborn Dunga never gave the veteran a chance. Whenever I remember this, I think of how fortunate Klose was. With my terrible graphic-design skills at the time, I even made this image.

As Brazil won the Copa América and Confederations Cup, I gradually became accustomed to a national team without Ronaldo. My focus shifted from admiring stars to appreciating matches, and I slowly changed from a Ronaldo supporter into a pure Brazil fan. It still puzzles me that I did not become one in 2002, when Brazil reached its peak. I can still remember the 2009 Confederations Cup final. Brazil trailed by two at halftime, then scored four in the second half, though one was disallowed. I celebrated without restraint. The image of veteran captain Lúcio weeping after heading the winning goal moved countless Brazil fans.

The 2010 World Cup was the first I watched without Ronaldo. Brazil sailed through the group, demolished old rival Chile in the round of sixteen, and dominated the Netherlands in the first half of the quarterfinal. Felipe Melo played a perfect through ball for Robinho to score, and for a while I thought the result was secure. Somehow, however, an own goal seemed to throw the entire team into confusion after halftime. Brazil lost 2–1 and was eliminated. The World Cup that I believed offered the best chance of victory ended in the quarterfinals. One could only lament football’s randomness and the tricks of fate.

On Valentine’s Day 2011, Ronaldo held a press conference and announced his retirement. As the television program Total Soccer put it, football fans around the world said goodbye to their footballing valentine that day. “Time, do not hurry me. I do not resist what must come; time, do not hurry me. I will still pursue what has gone far away.” I think those classic commentary lines will remain permanently in every Ronaldo fan’s heart. Total Soccer also did something unprecedented, devoting three consecutive episodes to its Ronaldo retrospective, Legend.

The rest of the story concerns Brazilian football alone. After the failure of the 2010 World Cup, Dunga stepped down. His stubborn selections had denied young players enough experience, leaving Brazilian football short of personnel for a long time. Brazil lost to Paraguay at the beginning of the knockout stage of the 2011 Copa América and entered a complete slump, but after years of watching football I could accept that calmly. By the 2013 Confederations Cup, Brazil could barely participate only because it was the host, and I did not expect the young Seleção to win. Once again, I was proven spectacularly wrong. In hindsight, however, the 3–0 destruction of a declining Spain in the final may only have encouraged the returning Luiz Felipe Scolari to persist with an outdated tactical system.

Countless Brazil supporters awaited the 2014 World Cup at home, hoping that beneath the gaze of Christ the Redeemer, their team would reach the final at the Maracanã. Fate played another cruel joke. The score of 1–7 struck every Brazilian face inside the Mineirão again and again. At 0–5, I pounded the desk in anger; my little finger hurt for more than a month afterward. After the match, I saw David Luiz—who earlier had looked so grown-up while comforting James Rodríguez—now desperately needing somebody to comfort him. The meaningless third-place match brought a 3–0 defeat, and even the victorious Dutch players did not appear particularly happy. Judged purely by strength, fourth place was probably a good result.

As four years earlier, Scolari stepped down. Failing to win the title may not have been his fault, but ending with ten goals conceded across two matches had a great deal to do with his aggressive strategy of trying to seize the initiative immediately. I later watched an episode of the travel documentary series On the Road, Season 2: Samba Never Surrenders. It showed that Brazilians quickly recovered their love of football after the 1–7 defeat, with children again playing everywhere in the streets. That warmed my heart.

Dunga returned for a second spell and won ten consecutive friendlies. Just as everyone began to believe that a great revival of the samba dynasty was at hand, the Copa América arrived—and Paraguay struck again, delivering a wake-up call to the Brazilian Football Confederation. If it continued doing nothing, another four years might pass and end in emptiness. That led to the remarkable sight of every living former Brazil coach gathering for a consultation. Notice Zagallo in the distance; even at his age, he still cannot stop worrying about the team.

Time passes. Brazilian football long ago lost the constellation of stars that shone at the end of the twentieth century and beginning of the twenty-first. The situation has become so absurd that the country cannot find even one serviceable specialist center-forward. Think how many Brazilian strikers once occupied that position and could only lament being born in the same era as an even greater rival. But so what? Having fallen in love with you at your most glorious, how could I bear to abandon you in decline and loneliness? Juventus supporters who watched their team reach last year’s Champions League final must understand. And although our World Cup results have disappointed over the past decade, we still won three consecutive Confederations Cups and two consecutive Copa América titles. Compared with our neighbor, we have been fairly fortunate.

I will end with a recent featured image from the Brazilian Football Confederation’s official website.

entry.title: It Is an End; It Is a New Beginning
entry.content:
From July 22 to September 12, I worked for almost two months and finally finished it. Apart from an extremely irregular daily routine, my ability to concentrate seems to have improved a little. Keep it up!

There appears to be even more ahead. Job hunting means grinding LeetCode, and Essen 2015 is approaching, so I would like to write a preview. At this rate, however, I probably will not have time to continue the Essen 2014 series…

Here is the punch card from Bitbucket. It looks very regular, does it not? Unfortunately, it uses UTC, so shift everything eight hours to the right to see my actual commit times…

I will use the final commit to commemorate the days that have passed, and to thank everyone for their help!

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] Preview 0: 51 Games After the First Cut
entry.content:
Essen is coming—is this how everyone feels?

Before We Begin

titanxxh resumed updating the blog just one week after finishing a paper submission. How diligent is that…? With Essen 2015 approaching, we are entering a new Essen 2015 cycle! (In other words, the Essen 2014 series has been abandoned T_T.)

Main Text

From all the games currently announced in BGG’s Spiel 2015 Preview, I made a preliminary selection of 51 based on their “faces”—my first impression of the art, player count, mechanisms, and so on. I put them into a GeekList I created.

The games are in no particular order, and the choices are highly subjective. In addition to the preferences below, I excluded everything without preview images, non-standalone expansions, and wargames, though reprints of older games were eligible.

Plain text = preference; italics = prejudice.

  • Player count: two-player games; games for more than five players
  • Style: German-style; American-style
  • Theme: Rome, civilization, economics
  • Strategic weight: heavy strategy; filler games
  • Mechanisms: worker placement, multiple paths; negotiation
  • Publishers: WYG, DoW
  • Designers: Uwe Rosenberg, Martin Wallace

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] Preview 1—You and Me
entry.content:
Two People, One Drama


In tribute to a pinnacle of Chinese cinema

My Essen 2015 previews begin with this installment and will continue across several chapters. Each chapter will examine several games from the list in my previous article in greater detail. This chapter focuses on my beloved two-player games, so I have titled it You and Me.

The amount of public information varies between games. When a detailed introduction is impossible, I can only fill gaps through inference and written descriptions. In the “BGG Resources” field below, Abundant means both rules and a video explanation are available, Moderate means either rules or video is missing, and Scarce means neither is available.

Haru Ichiban

  • Art: Fresh
  • Insert: Unknown
  • Time: 20 minutes
  • Text: None
  • BGG Resources: Abundant

One glance at Haru Ichiban tells you that the name is Japanese. Haru means spring, while ichiban means first. According to the designer’s translation, it refers to the first gentle breeze of spring. Despite the Japanese title, the designer is the famous Bruno Cathala, creator of Cyclades, Five Tribes, and Abyss. Trust me, however: nobody scanning a list of more than five hundred Essen releases checks the designers. Most of us are drawn by descriptions and artwork, and this game’s fresh, delicate art is especially eye-catching.

The rules are simple. Each player has flowers numbered 1–8 and one frog. Every round, both secretly choose a flower and reveal them together. The player with the lower number becomes the Little Gardener and the other becomes the Senior Gardener, and both place their flowers on lily pads. They then manipulate the spring breeze and frogs according to the rules to move the pads. Players score for patterns formed by flowers: a 2×2 square is worth 1 point, four consecutive flowers horizontally or vertically are worth 2, four diagonally are worth 3, and five consecutive flowers in any direction are worth 5 and immediately win the game.

At heart, this is an abstract game in which two players influence the positions of flowers within a set of constraints and score for forming patterns. The designer gave this otherwise dry mechanism an appealing setting: two players use the spring wind and leaping frogs to arrange their flowers. The artist’s image of two gardeners seated on opposite sides of a pond, matching wits among scattered lily pads, adds a trace of Zen.

Fog of Love

  • Art: Simple
  • Insert: Unknown
  • Time: 45–90 minutes
  • Text: Heavy
  • BGG Resources: Scarce

This Essen brought the emergence of several games focused on romantic relationships, and Fog of Love attracted considerable attention for that reason. The silhouettes of a man and woman on the cover contain the title and a line: “A game about romance, relationship and … bluff.”

Because BGG resources were scarce, I could introduce it only through the designer’s description. Fog of Love tells the story of an intense romance. The couple begins with love at first sight, then passes through awkwardness, arguments, parties, thoughtful gifts, secret affairs, children, and reconciliation in the hope of reaching a happy ending. Each player portrays a character with several personality traits and learns how to keep the relationship alive, develop mutual understanding, and determine whether the other person’s feelings are sincere. As in the real world, players face major events and make crucial decisions. You must decide which choices are best for yourself and which benefit the couple, while also considering your partner’s thoughts, because both players’ decisions shape the final outcome. In this romantic game, maintaining balance, trusting intuition, and making precisely calculated choices are keys to success. You may win together, lose together, or…

In short, it looks like a small game for couples, but its 45–90 minute duration suggests hidden depth. I look forward to seeing how it performs at Essen.

…and then, we held hands.

  • Art: Fresh
  • Insert: Unknown
  • Time: 30–45 minutes
  • Text: None
  • BGG Resources: Abundant

Saving the best for last is my habit, so the final title here is the two-player game I anticipated most that year. Like the previous game, …and then, we held hands. focuses on a romantic relationship—or perhaps simply a relationship. The difference lies in the subtitle shown above: “fix what is broken.” This game follows two people whose relationship is approaching its end as they try to repair it and eventually hold hands again.

The image above shows a prototype player board, so it looks a little rough. The artist is the familiar illustrator of Dixit, however, and the final version should satisfy everyone. The rules are very simple. Using a card from your own hand, representing an event, or from your partner’s hand, you resolve emotional problems belonging to yourself or the other player and move around the board. When each player has resolved all four of their problems, the relationship advances to a new stage, allowing both to enter the next inner ring. If the relationship advances through three stages and the players meet in the center, they have successfully joined hands again and win.

This seemingly simple and somewhat abstract game moved me deeply through a series of excellent details. First, because the setting concerns two people whose relationship is in trouble, verbal communication about strategy is forbidden. Both players must constantly notice the other’s state and address problems with empathy. Second, this is a game about balance. Each player must monitor their emotions throughout the game, remain as balanced as possible to replenish their hand, and avoid a deadlock in which movement becomes impossible; if either player cannot move, both lose. Finally, the left and right sides of every event card represent two different emotional changes. A player on the left side of a ring can see only the emotion on the card’s left, and vice versa. The designer explains this as changing the angle from which you view a problem so that you can adjust your response to the event.

Although I had not played the game, simply thinking through these details made me admire how coherent they made the whole design. …and then, we held hands. is both a game and a metaphor for the real world. I thank the designers for bringing us a small game whose meaning extends beyond play.

Conclusion

Two is my favorite player count. Strategically, two players simplify the decision space and make strategy purer. In terms of time, two-player games are usually much shorter. Playing with one other person is also the best way to teach something new because the experience is more direct and intimate. The three new games chosen for this installment use the distinctive charm of two-player play, inviting players to sit quietly and experience the designers’ sense of Zen in a calm environment, creating something unique.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] Preview 2: Many Hands Make Light Work
entry.content:
Kickstarter


Kickstarter’s crowdfunding model

Beginning with this installment, titanxxh’s Essen 2015 preview will run through several chapters. Each one will select a few games from the list in the earlier article and introduce them in greater detail.

As Kickstarter’s crowdfunding model has become familiar, people in every industry have participated by either backing or launching projects—just as the title says, many hands make light work. Board games are among the industries best suited to this model. A designer needs only a good idea and can avoid handling traditional fundraising and market research; meanwhile, tiered stretch goals fit the logic of board-game publishing, and increasingly elaborate components can attract still more backers. This chapter therefore focuses mainly on successful board games from Kickstarter over the past year.

The quantity of public information varies from game to game. Where a detailed introduction is impossible, titanxxh can only fill the gaps through inference and prose. In the “BGG resources” field below, abundant means both rules and video introductions are available, moderate means either rules or videos are missing, and scarce means neither is available.

Between Two Cities

  • Art: clean
  • Storage: unknown
  • Playing time: 25 minutes
  • Text: none
  • BGG resources: abundant

This year Stonemaier Games—the publisher behind Viticulture—has two new releases. One is Between Two Cities, introduced here; I prefer the short Chinese nickname “A Tale of Two Cities.” The other appears to be a war-game-like design called Scythe, with highly realistic artwork.

Between Two Cities supports three to seven players, with one- and two-player variants added later. The game’s website offers Chinese rules, but the translation is almost beyond criticism. Each player helps the neighbors on their left and right build a city. At the end, the lower-scoring of those two cities becomes the player’s score, and the highest score wins.

The game has three rounds in which players place, respectively, six single-space tiles, two double-space tiles, and six more single-space tiles. Each city ultimately forms a 4×4 grid, scored according to the types of buildings it contains. The highlight is its intense interaction—or, more accurately, negotiation. Compared with 7 Wonders, its table-talk factor rises by several levels. A player may even refuse to place their own tile until someone else places theirs. The rulebook discourages that behavior because this is a cooperative game; if it happens, resolve placement with a random-order card.

Among Nobles

  • Art: realistic
  • Storage: none
  • Playing time: 90–120 minutes
  • Text: light
  • BGG resources: abundant

Among Nobles is set in feudal Europe. Players build their own families and expand their dynasties through marriage and childbirth.

Players control some of the most iconic and influential figures in European history, cleverly exploiting their unique abilities to compete for victory. They wage wars, arrange political marriages, and contend for influence at court. Each player begins with one married couple and uses them to build an extensive family.

The game lasts three rounds. Players allocate action points to activate their characters’ abilities from left to right; after marriage, the abilities of husband and wife trigger together. At the end of each round, when a character deck runs out, the oldest generation dies. Once all three decks have been exhausted, the game ends.

The rules are not complicated. The game probably takes so long because the character decks are thick, which is necessary to express the essence of this engine-building design. Its theme is more tightly integrated than in most Eurogames, apart from the rather implausible fact that players choose which people are born… Looking at your family tree at the end should also be a distinctive experience.

Spirits of the Rice Paddy

  • Art: fresh
  • Storage: unknown
  • Playing time: 90 minutes
  • Text: light
  • BGG resources: moderate

In Spirits of the Rice Paddy, the designer explains that ancient Balinese people believed poor farmers could prosper only with help from powerful spirits—surely their mature irrigation systems deserve some credit too…

Players compete to build the best rice paddies. They use cattle to construct walls and remove rocks, ducks to eat pests and fertilize the rice, and workers to clear weeds. Most importantly, they must control water flow intelligently to irrigate the fields. Fortunately, powerful spirits grant blessings and cast spells. After seven exhausting rounds of cultivation, whoever harvests the most wins.

Thanks to Uwe Rosenberg, titanxxh fell in love with games about farming and economics. What first drew me here was the title, because I had always assumed only China cultivated rice; instead, the setting is not Chinese at all…

As a Kickstarter project, Spirits of the Rice Paddy unlocked every stretch goal. Even the meeples gained a custom shape, becoming little people in straw hats. BGG offered no session information, however, so the game’s overall strategic depth remained unclear. The rules appear to contain many objectives that players race to complete, potentially creating sudden swings in scoring. There should be other sources of points besides objectives, so perhaps the problem is not severe. Spirit-card strength is another major factor. One video review suggests that the cards are very powerful, meaning every player’s experience should differ considerably and replayability should be strong.

Tesla vs. Edison: War of Currents

  • Art: clean
  • Storage: perfect
  • Playing time: 90 minutes
  • Text: light
  • BGG resources: moderate

Tesla vs. Edison: War of Currents is exciting from its title alone. Players can take the role of Edison or Tesla—technically the chief inventor of one’s company. Three other figures are also available, but the designer probably believed these two names would attract more attention. During play, you can hire other nineteenth-century celebrities to work for you.

Your actions determine the fate of your company, and four areas require attention: electrical projects on the map, research into new technologies, investment in public relations, and trading shares on the market. To win, you may concentrate on one or two areas or develop them evenly.

The game lasts six rounds, with a celebrity auction after every two. In company-prestige order, players take actions through celebrities or scientists. At the end, whoever owns the most valuable stock portfolio wins; cash does not count.

The game should appeal to at least three groups: people interested in science, history, or business. After watching someone else’s rules video, I felt there were many details and that remembering everything in one sitting would be difficult. Overall, the theme appears tightly integrated and the game should be worth trying.

PS: Who would volunteer to play Edison? Tesla is obviously ten streets ahead…

entry.title: A Quantitative Analysis of Ora et Labora
entry.content:
This article reorganizes an older post. I was bored one day and started a solo game. While playing, I thought of some ways to analyze a building’s effectiveness, ran the numbers again, and reached several conclusions.

Note 1: Every figure below is an estimate and is not precise. The method matters more than the values.

Note 2: The method is not limited to solo play. It also applies in multiplayer games, although the data will change. In a four-player game, for example, a resource action probably yields only about four goods.

Ora et Labora is an unconventional worker-placement game. It focuses on building a multilayered economic system in which players complete a chain of conversions on the way to victory. Its many scoring methods make the game as a whole difficult to evaluate, while naturally giving players more choices.

Today we want to study the effectiveness of a particular building in a solo game. How should that effectiveness be evaluated? The simplest approach is obviously to calculate the return from placing a worker. To simplify the problem, I analyze only buildings that directly produce points. As noted above, however, Ora et Labora is a multilayered economy. Most buildings do not produce points directly, and the conversion performed by a scoring building often depends on several preceding steps. What then?

A building effect generally consumes some raw materials and produces some points. We count the number of actions, t, required to collect every input, then divide the resulting score by t. This gives the average return per action from using the building. Comparing that figure with a standard return reveals whether a building is strong or weak.

First, I take the 518 points from my afternoon solo game under the Irish rules and divide them by the total number of actions: 64 + 15 + 4—32 rounds × 2, plus 15 uses of my prior’s effect and 4 uses of the neutral prior. The standard return per action is therefore 518/83 = 6.24.

Next, let us analyze a simple building: Cloister Workshop.

Note: in a solo game, assume that taking goods from the production wheel yields an average of six, based on experience.

The total return is 3×3 + 4 = 13. Placing a worker costs one action. Taking three clay—remember that the number of times the effect can be used is limited—costs 3×1/6 of an action. Taking one stone costs 1/6, and taking four fuel, or two peat-coal, costs 2×1/6. The total is thus two actions for thirteen points, an average return of 6.5. That looks respectable.

Now let us examine a more complicated building: Chapel.

The total return is 3×8 - 3 + 2 - 0.4×7 = 19.2, because every whiskey is worth one point and two coins, while five coins equal two points. Placing a worker costs one action and taking one coin costs 1/6. The remaining question is how to calculate the actions needed to acquire beer and whiskey.

Clearly, the only efficient way to obtain large quantities of both goods—the alternative of collecting them one by one is much too slow—is the following production chain:

Brewery:

Because this building’s conversion has no quantity limit, the calculation is more complicated. One Malthouse action converts half the grain into malt, and one Brewery action converts sets of malt and grain into beer. Those two actions are fixed. Obviously, the more goods converted at once, the fewer actions each beer requires on average. Suppose we take grain x times. That produces 6x grain, or 3x beer. The average actions required for each beer are therefore (x+2)/3x.

Whiskey Distillery:

This building’s conversion also has no quantity limit. Notice that the malt conversion already comes from the Malthouse above, so we need only count the actions spent collecting grain. One Whiskey Distillery action converts sets of malt, wood, and peat-coal into two whiskey. That action is fixed. Suppose we take grain, wood, and peat y times each; we obtain 12y whiskey. The average actions per whiskey are therefore (3y+1)/12y.

Because Chapel requires equal quantities of beer and whiskey, 3x = 12y, and thus x = 4y.

The total number of actions is therefore (1 + 1/6 + 3×(4y+2)/12y + 3×(3y+1)/12y) = f(y), producing an average return of 19.2/f(y). Substituting realistic y values shows that this is actually worse than Cloister Workshop. The value of y cannot be very large: the game lasts only 32 rounds, and six rounds are required before you can take six grain again. Without another way to gain grain, you can do so only four or five times; even counting the joker, perhaps eight or nine. In other words, y cannot exceed two, leaving the average return at only about 6.015.

Fortunately, Chapel is not the end of the conversion chain. Players can use other methods to convert its output into a thirty-point wonder. I wonder whether continuing the calculation would produce a higher average return.

entry.title: [A Life in Board Games] Episode 6: A Brief Look at Uwe Rosenberg's Design Philosophy
entry.content:
This article first appeared last year on Yikeguan’s WeChat public account and was also posted on the Board Games Tieba forum. I had barely played Caverna or Fields of Arle then, so I did not write much about them. This is a good opportunity to update it.

Uwe Rosenberg!

Uwe Rosenberg is rendered on Chinese BGG as Wu Rose Mountain, but Chinese players more affectionately call him “Teacher Uwe.” Far too many introductions to Uwe already exist online, so I will not repeat them; interested players can search a wiki. Whenever his designs are discussed, opinions vary widely. Those who dislike them can usually produce a long list of reasons, and “recycling old ideas” would probably appear on every list. Those who love Uwe—especially devoted fans like me—always recognize something beloved in each new game and become excited by every surprise created through a change in his design. Whatever individual players think of him, Uwe’s status in board gaming is beyond dispute. Consider the BGG rankings: Agricola was 6th, Le Havre 15th, At the Gates of Loyang 190th, Ora et Labora 47th, Glass Road 176th, Caverna: The Cave Farmers 3rd, and Fields of Arle 106th. Even the two-player versions of Agricola and Le Havre achieved respectable rankings, at 108 and 604. Rankings do not represent everything, but so many highly placed works at least demonstrate an outstanding design philosophy maintained at an exceptionally high level over many years. When thinking about that philosophy, I have sometimes wondered whether Uwe studied the Chinese Book of Changes. Something always changes within what remains constant, while something constant is always concealed within change. The proportion is consistently just right, and many of those changes genuinely improve the games enormously.

Across Uwe’s designs—from Agricola, Le Havre, and At the Gates of Loyang, jokingly called the “hunger trilogy,” to Ora et Labora, Glass Road, and Caverna—every title bears his distinctive style regardless of its specific mechanisms. They support solo play, provide a good experience at different player counts, offer several strategic paths, and use related economic themes. Seven years passed, yet Uwe’s central philosophy remained unchanged. At the level of detail, however, each title introduced many admirable changes. Let me select several games I know relatively well and analyze them.

Agricola

Agricola was not Uwe’s first design, but many players probably discovered him through it. As his breakthrough work, its arrival in distant 2007 ended Puerto Rico’s long reign, removing that game from first place and elevating itself to the pantheon. Even today, any veteran discussing Agricola will almost certainly praise it highly. Agricola is a classic worker-placement game, but it incorporates several then-novel details that greatly enrich play: available action spaces increase as the game progresses; occupation and minor-improvement cards are unique to each player; resources accumulate from round to round; and so forth. These details are also interconnected, so the design feels cohesive rather than patched together. Actions introduced later in the game should naturally be more attractive, for example, but allowing resources to accumulate ensures that early spaces do not become useless. Occupations and minor improvements give players individual approaches, preventing competition for shared resources from becoming too fierce. Most praiseworthy of all is resource accumulation. This greatly simplifies balance because it is self-balancing: when the resources on an action space are insufficiently attractive, nobody chooses it, and the amount eventually grows until it becomes worthwhile. Conversely, a player may take a space even before its resources meet their own expectations, anticipating that another round of growth would make it irresistible to somebody else. You can rarely wait for the perfect moment to collect exactly the right resources. The whole game therefore contains a beauty of imperfection. Is life not the same? Yet what makes a design can also undo it. Occupations and minor improvements enormously increase replayability, but excessively powerful cards and combinations inevitably damage balance. Concentrating many decisions at the beginning of the game, as Seasons also does, has caused considerable controversy and is unfriendly to newcomers. Feeding feels slightly too tense and its penalties too severe, leaving players frustrated. Resource accumulation is excellent, but replenishing every space becomes tedious late in the game. Many groups have surely tried to speed things up by having several players replenish resources together, only to add something twice or omit it entirely. Overall, Agricola remains an unsurpassed masterpiece for many players, the foundation of Uwe’s whole body of work, and a source from which countless later designers have borrowed.

Le Havre

In 2008, Uwe went a step further with the second title in his harvest trilogy, Le Havre. Agricola and Le Havre once stood together in BGG’s top five, a glorious achievement that Uwe’s fans loved to mention. Agricola’s influence is obvious in Le Havre, but so are many noteworthy changes. The number of workers falls to one; players can borrow their primary resource, money, from the bank; buildings enter play randomly within certain limits; and more. Uwe seems to have recognized several obvious shortcomings in Agricola and optimized them. Feeding is no longer as oppressive, since in the worst case a player can take loans. The most conspicuous change is resource replenishment. Rather than adding large quantities of resources at the start of a round, two fixed resources are added at the beginning of each player’s turn. This avoids the duplicates and omissions of Agricola. Replenishment also becomes a metronome for the game. Because this metronome has seven beats, every player follows the same feeding rhythm but receives a different number of actions, giving each a distinct tempo. This design helps stagger the players’ strategic plans. A fixed replenishment rhythm has its own limitations, such as making it difficult to introduce new resource types and keeping accumulation speeds constant. For those reasons, some players rank Le Havre above Agricola, while others consider it far inferior.

Ora et Labora

In 2009, Uwe concluded the harvest trilogy with the somewhat lighter At the Gates of Loyang, which I will not discuss in detail. After two quiet years, he appeared at the fair with a new design: my personal favorite, Ora et Labora, which my friends and I simply call Ora. If I had to summarize its design in one word, that word would be elegance. When teaching the game, players unfamiliar with Uwe may see its small rondel and feel curiosity or even confusion. Veterans of his work, however, will surely applaud the brilliance of the design. A circle truly is a perfect shape. People learn to handle life smoothly after being polished by experience, and this rondel seems similarly refined by Uwe’s years of work, eventually becoming such an elegant solution: move the pointer gently, and everything is done. Tzolk’in later borrowed something of this idea. The mechanism solves Agricola’s tedious replenishment, incorporates Le Havre’s metronome, and makes introducing new resources simple. The rondel does have limitations. Agricola can give resources of the same type different growth rates, for example, whereas this system cannot. That does not prevent us from praising its elegance. Ora also introduces the relative positions of buildings, substantially changes scoring, and raises the level of thought required. Players must decide not only when to buy which building but also where to place it, maximizing the score of their settlements. This demands stronger overall strategy. Perhaps because of the added complexity, Uwe removed every random element and fixed the exact quantity of all buildings, reducing the cognitive burden.
