The familiar feeding phase from earlier designs also disappears, replaced by a subtler and more flexible settlement-building phase. Players no longer become frustrated by insufficient food, and they have choices when building settlements. If a high-scoring settlement is temporarily unaffordable, they can build one worth slightly less, conserve resources, and prepare earlier for the later game. Since a settlement scores mainly through surrounding buildings, its own value does not affect the final total too severely, making the system friendlier. Another strength is player interaction. When another player constructs a building before you, that is not necessarily bad: you may still use it, perhaps even gaining its benefit before its owner, while saving the resources required to build it. On the other hand, using it lets your opponent cycle their worker sooner while slowing your own worker rotation. Finally, Ora’s finest quality, in my opinion, is its kindness to trailing players. In many games, someone whose early development goes wrong—because a building is taken or a route disrupted—has effectively left the competition. Here, until the final phase, that player still has a chance to allocate resources intelligently, convert them into points, and catch up. For all these reasons, Ora et Labora became my favorite game and the one I have played most, without exception. It is also one of the few games I rated a perfect ten on BGG. A high rating may result from original design, polished mechanisms, or an excellent play experience. A perfect score, I think, has only one cause: the player’s deep love. If loving the right person at the right time is called happiness, then meeting the right people and playing the right game at the right time must be another kind of happiness.

Glass Road

The following year, Uwe released two-player versions of Agricola and Le Havre. They streamlined the originals without losing their strategy and make good choices for a casual game with your partner. In 2013, Uwe released two titles at once, Glass Road and Caverna. Because Glass Road was shorter, my friends and I played it more often. Uwe adopted a simplified form of Ora et Labora’s building system, dividing buildings into three types: conversion buildings, one-use buildings, and scoring buildings. He also retained Ora’s concept of resource conversion to drive progress. The principal innovation is that players no longer stack resources in front of themselves. Instead, a rondel similar to Ora’s records each quantity. The deeper reason for this design is that obtaining an advanced resource consumes one of each basic resource, precisely represented by moving the pointer one space. Is that not elegant? The rules for playing character cards are equally clever. Each round, a player chooses five of fifteen characters but may actively play only three. The other two must be triggered by another player’s action or are wasted. You must therefore choose the characters you need while anticipating what others may choose, and pay attention to the order in which you play them. This also balances turn order: someone who plays a character first has the advantage of choosing a desired building before others, but runs a greater risk of opponents sharing the action and reducing its benefit. Glass Road’s design is very clean—perhaps Uwe devoted most of his energy to Caverna—and its strategic depth is not especially high. This lighter title is genuinely a good introduction to his style for new players.

Caverna

Third! Third! I am not obsessed with rankings, but watching Uwe’s Caverna climb steadily still made me a little excited. Its design is fundamentally based on Agricola. It removes occupations and minor improvements, then makes many buildings available for purchase from the beginning, as in Ora. Several details, including fencing and feeding, are simplified. It introduces expeditions, which effectively give players a more flexible action space; to keep them balanced, the dwarf with the lowest weapon level must act first. Scoring is also more exhilarating. Agricola’s scoring caps disappear, and even unusual development paths can produce high scores, helping distinguish players’ strategies. These details show that Caverna inherited the ideas of Uwe’s earlier designs and truly brought them together. It is therefore unsurprising that it replaced Agricola as his highest-ranked game.

Summary

As this article approaches its end, I want to quote a line I once read that expresses how I feel about Uwe’s game design. “Game design is an art, and every art has its own language. In game design, mechanisms are the main elements of that language. They are like words: ordinary people can use them only to write ordinary prose, but Shakespeare in literature, or Uwe Rosenberg and Stefan Feld in board games, can use them to create masterpieces.” What makes Uwe even more remarkable is his continual refinement. He gradually distills and innovates upon a simple mechanism until it approaches perfection and elegance. Looking back, it may no longer resemble the original idea, yet its roots can always be traced.

Afterword

I had long wanted to write about Uwe’s games but never acted on the idea. First, I truly had not played every one of them deeply. I had only read an introduction to At the Gates of Loyang and never played it at all. Nor am I a prominent figure in the board-game community, merely an ordinary player, so I never felt qualified. Second, Uwe’s games form such a distinctive school that a poorly written article could draw fire from both supporters and detractors. Last month I saw Yikeguan’s call for writers and, after much thought, decided to try. A recent family move had left little time for writing, but looking at the wall of board games in my new study finally gave me motivation to record my modest view of Uwe’s work. I deliberately omitted Ora et Labora’s weaknesses because I simply could not bear to criticize my favorite game. I must thank the friends who loved Ora as much as I did and whom I met during my relatively free junior and senior years at university. I still remember how, at the end of many sessions, we somehow tied. Repeated ties are astonishing in a game where scores reach into the hundreds. I also feel fortunate not to have missed such an excellent game. (As far as I knew, Ora had never been reprinted and was almost impossible to buy. Good news! Game Harbor has licensed a Chinese edition of Ora et Labora, expected early next year. Its quality should be improved in the same way as the second German edition.)

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] Preview 3: Old Favorites, New Games
entry.content:
Old Favorites, New Games

Beginning with this installment, titanxxh’s Essen 2015 preview will run through several chapters. Each chapter will offer a more detailed introduction to several games listed in the previous article.

Every game in this installment is a new work from a designer or publisher I favor. Uwe Rosenberg has been distinctly unproductive this year, offering only the ultralight Hengist. Presumably he spent all his time on next year’s release; the rhythm of Uwe’s development cycle is impossible to decipher. Martin Wallace’s Ships and WYG’s Nippon, by contrast, initially appear to maintain a high standard.

The amount of public information varies from game to game. When the available material does not support a detailed explanation, I can only fill in the gaps with inference and text. In the BGG Resources field below, abundant means both rules and video introductions are available, average means either rules or video are missing, and scarce means neither is available.

Hengist

  • Art: clean
  • Insert: none
  • Time: 15–30 minutes
  • Text: none
  • BGG resources: average

The premise of Hengist is that Hengist and his brother Horsa sail a longship in search of treasure because, astonishingly, their boss does not pay them enough… Uwe’s productivity has declined in recent years, so he fills gaps in the development of large games with two-player titles. You know what that means: another heavy Uwe game next year. Compared with that heavy game still brewing, this two-player title is decidedly light.

The main mechanism is collecting cards and then playing them according to terrain to obtain treasure. Road tiles cover the treasure areas beneath each section of the board, leading randomly to treasures below that section. They begin unrevealed. Players can explore or play a card to peek—scout—before deciding which path to take. Every time a Scout card is played, the leftmost board section moves to the right and everyone on it is lost.

At first glance, the game’s strategic depth seems quite low. The main decisions are whether to remain on an earlier board section to pursue higher scores—points are arranged in descending order, while remaining farther back risks disaster—and how to use your hand. Since the game relies on drawing cards, however, randomness is substantial.

P.S. The longship is nicely designed. More and more board games seem to be moving toward papercraft models…

Ships

  • Art: realistic
  • Insert: unknown
  • Time: 120 minutes
  • Text: light
  • BGG resources: average

Ships is Martin’s release this year. Its title recalls his earlier Automobile and Aeroplanes, but its scope is far broader. From ancient Phoenician galleys to modern steamships, players build vessels, place merchants, and control cities to score points. At the beginning of the rulebook, Martin says that if you like complex economic games, you will enjoy this one.

(The game board is centered mainly on Europe.)

The game lasts several rounds, with players taking turns until it ends. It spans three eras—galleys, sailing ships, and steamships—and each era introduces new cards, effectively additional actions. On a turn, players mainly spend action points to take actions. There are eight kinds, and the same action can be taken repeatedly. The most important action is building ships, for which Martin drew a dedicated flowchart. There also appear to be many scoring paths; the rulebook contains at least seven sources of points.

The game’s style is typical Martin Wallace: plain, robust, and deep. At the end of the rulebook, Martin explains that he realized many civilization games focus on continents even though the sea is often the true object of competition, which prompted this design. It is difficult to understand a heavy game merely by reading its rules. According to another player’s review on BGG, even three experienced players took three and a half hours for their first game, suggesting considerable complexity. That reviewer also mentioned the variety of scoring paths. In short, Ships is a definite purchase for titanxxh.

Nippon

  • Art: clean
  • Insert: unknown
  • Time: 90 minutes
  • Text: none
  • BGG resources: average

Four enormous Chinese characters on the cover of Nippon—“Meiji Restoration”—state its theme. Japan was then a closed feudal society seeking transformation into an industrial nation. The emperor sent envoys west to study, brought back technicians and scholars, and completed a rapid industrial revolution through railway construction. He relied most heavily on support from the four great zaibatsu, which played a decisive role in Japan’s fate. Each player represents one zaibatsu, investing in industry, advancing technical knowledge, and exporting goods to increase its influence. Nippon is a fast-paced economic game filled with challenging decisions.

Three scoring triggers occur before the game ends. Players take turns choosing between two options: select a worker from the board and take an action—the worker’s color is unrelated to the action—or Consolidate. This choice resembles the design of Zhanguo. When consolidating, you receive money, coal, and the emperor’s reward. Like WYG’s earlier games, Nippon should have rules of moderate complexity but substantial strategic depth.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 1. Among Nobles Overview, Unboxing, and Review
entry.content:
Xiaoda’s new Essen games finally arrived. In the middle of the week, E—who actually ambushed Xiaoda at home, absolutely deranged—I, and Bowl King could not wait any longer and went to Club A to play several new titles. The first installment of Essen 2015 will take a detailed look at what has been called the year’s most underrated game: Among Nobles.


Among Nobles

Overview

Among Nobles is a card game in which each player leads a family in feudal Europe. You expand your family and use marriage, war, and intrigue to pursue victory. Players control some of the most influential and iconic figures in European history, including Napoleon, Charles I, and Catherine the Great, activating sequences of abilities on their cards. When a female character marries, she joins her husband’s family, after which the couple can be activated together. The right—or wrong—marriage can decide the game. The player with the most Prestige Points at the end wins.

Components

  • 1 rulebook
  • 60 character cards
    • 6 starting Lady cards
    • 6 starting Lord cards
    • 16 Era I characters
    • 16 Era II characters
    • 16 Era III characters
  • 9 Province cards
  • 1 Starting Player card
  • 45 coin tokens
  • Prestige Point tokens
    • 50 one-point Prestige tokens
    • 50 five-point Prestige tokens
  • Player tokens in five colors—black, white, orange, purple, and gray. Color-blind friendly; excellent!
    • 3 Action tokens (discs)
    • 10 Army tokens (cubes)

Character Cards

Male characters have brown backgrounds and female characters light backgrounds. The colors of the bars above and below each card indicate the character’s traits; a couple’s traits determine those of their children.

  • Red: Commander, skilled at military affairs and actions in the first row.
  • Blue: Devout, skilled at piety and actions in the second row.
  • Yellow: Merchant, skilled at commerce and actions in the third row.
  • Green: Negotiator, skilled at intrigue and actions in the fourth row.

A character’s abilities appear beneath the portrait.

  • (Crown) Noble: the ability applies to this character permanently.
  • (Stork carrying a bundle) Baptism: the ability triggers when this character is born.
  • (Church) Alliance: the ability triggers when this character marries.
  • (Grim Reaper) Legacy: the ability triggers when this character dies.
  • (Scroll) Intrigue: a special ability triggered when the character takes an Intrigue action.

Setup

  1. Lay out the nine Province cards in a 3 × 3 grid. In a three-player game, remove Holland, Normandy, and Vienna—marked 4+ in the lower-right—and arrange the remaining Provinces in a 2 × 3 grid.
  2. In a three-player game, remove all green cards.
  3. Shuffle each era’s character cards separately.
  4. Reveal seven Era I characters, or five in a three-player game. These represent children who may be born in the future.
  5. Place the Prestige Points and coins nearby.
  6. Each player chooses a color and takes its Action tokens—use only two per player in a five-player game—and Army tokens. Not all ten Army tokens are available at the beginning; additional tokens must first enter your personal supply through certain effects.
  7. Each player takes a reference card.
  8. Each player receives two Armies and one coin.
  9. Determine the starting player: all players simultaneously reveal one to five fingers. The player showing the greatest unique number becomes starting player; if the highest numbers tie, use the next lower unique number. For example, with 5, 5, 4, 4, and 3, the player showing 3 starts.
  10. Distribute the starting families. First separate the six starting couples into three groups, A, B, and C, according to their card backs:
  • Three players: because green cards are unused, each group contains only one couple. Player 3 chooses a couple, Player 1 chooses one, and Player 2 receives the remaining pair.
  • Four players: Player 4 chooses a couple and gives the other pair in that group to Player 2. Player 1 chooses a couple and gives the other pair in that group to Player 3.
  • Five players: Player 5 chooses a couple and gives the other pair in that group to Player 3. Player 1 chooses a couple and gives the other pair in that group to Player 4. Player 2 chooses either couple from the remaining group.
  1. Each player places their Lady card underneath their Lord card so that only her action area remains visible.

Tips

Coins matter! Sons matter! Marriage matters! Remember these facts before your first game, or your actions will become very awkward.

Game Flow

The game lasts three eras.

Each era contains several rounds. Players first take actions during every round, followed by an Upkeep Phase. When the final character of the current era appears, a generational change occurs during the next round’s Upkeep Phase. The game ends after the third generational change.

Action Phase

Beginning with the starting player, players take turns performing one action and placing an Action token on the character card being activated, continuing until every Action token has been used. Note: in the first round of the game, each player has only one action.

  • Activate: activate an unmarried man, unmarried woman, or couple that has not yet been activated. Choose one of the four action rows and resolve its icons strictly from left to right.
  • Reactivate: after every unmarried man and couple in your family has been activated, you may reactivate an already activated character. You may resolve only one action icon from the first column of one row. Note: if a character lacks an icon in the first column of a row, that row cannot be used for reactivation.

Action icons:

  • (Crossed swords) Military: choose one of the following.
    • Pay one coin to move one Army from your personal supply to any Province.
    • Move one Army from one Province to any other Province for free; the Provinces need not be adjacent.
  • (Cross) Piety: gain 1 Prestige Point.
  • (Coin) Commerce: gain one coin.
  • (Gender symbol) Procreation: choose a character from the display to become this couple’s child. A boy costs one coin. Place the newborn character one row beneath the couple to show that it belongs to the next generation. Note: this action is mandatory unless you cannot pay its cost, the display contains no child with suitable traits, or the icon was triggered by one of your third-generation couples. If the newborn character has a shield icon in the upper-right, add one Army token to your personal supply.
  • (Pair of rings) Marriage: pay two coins for a wedding. Choose an unmarried man in your family as the groom. Every other player must offer an unmarried woman. Return the unchosen women; the selected bride’s family gains 2 Prestige Points. Move the bride’s card into the groom’s family and place it beneath him to form a couple.
  • (Scroll) Intrigue: resolve the character’s Intrigue ability. For a couple, use the husband’s ability. The icon has no effect on a character without an Intrigue ability.
  • (Trading hands) Hire: pay two coins, then take either a Military, Piety, or Marriage action.

Upkeep Phase

  1. Determine control of the Provinces. Resolve each Province in turn. If it contains Army tokens of more than one color, every player present removes one Army at a time until at most one player has any Army there. That player controls the Province.
  2. Gain Province income. Each Province’s controller receives the Prestige Points and/or coins it provides.
  3. Reset characters by removing Action tokens from character cards.
  4. If no displayed character was taken, discard all of them.
  5. Generational change: if one was triggered in the previous round’s Upkeep Phase, the oldest generation of every player’s family—the top row—dies, triggering any Legacy abilities. If a player has no male heir, reveal cards from the top of the deck until a male appears. He automatically becomes that player’s male heir and marries an unmarried woman of the oldest generation, if available. Shuffle all other revealed characters back into the deck.
  6. Refill the character display to its starting size. If the final character of the current era is revealed, a generational change will occur during the next Upkeep Phase.
  7. Pass the Starting Player card clockwise.

End of the Game

After the third generational change, the game ends. Players may exchange every three coins for 1 Prestige Point. The player with the most Prestige wins. If tied, the player controlling the most Provinces wins; if still tied, play again!

Unboxing Photos

Front of the box!

The rulebook, only a few pages long; the rest introduces the characters.

The player aid is detailed enough that this alone is almost all you need.

Simple components, and no obnoxious red-and-green pairing, haha.

Nine Province cards and one Starting Player card. The Grim Reaper side means that a generational change has been triggered.

The starting Lords and Ladies. I am not sure whether an illustrator created these portraits.

Now let us examine several characters from the game:

  • Felipe II de España — Philip II of Spain

    Philip II was Habsburg king of Spain from 1556 to 1598 and king of Portugal—as Philip I—from 1581. His reign marked the height of Spanish power. Historians often describe this period as the era of Habsburg domination of Europe. Ambitious, Philip tried to maintain a vast Catholic empire but ultimately failed.

    But why is his Intrigue ability designed to remove an unmarried woman in exchange for two coins and two points?

  • Henry VIII of England

    Henry VIII (June 28, 1491–January 28, 1547), the second son of Henry VII, was the second Tudor king and succeeded to the throne on April 22, 1509. He was also Lord of Ireland and later King of Ireland. Seeking to set aside his wife and marry a new queen, Henry quarreled with the pope and launched the English Reformation. Important acts allowed him to remarry, made the English bishops leaders of the Church of England, separated the English church from Rome, and established Henry as England’s supreme religious authority. He dissolved the monasteries, bringing royal power to its peak, and incorporated Wales into England. Although some say Henry became an Anglican before his death, he promoted Catholic rites and doctrines throughout his life. His descendants Edward VI and Elizabeth I continued the Reformation, while his daughter Mary I restored Catholicism during her reign. Henry VIII married six times and ordered two of his wives beheaded.
    Beyond the Reformation, he actively encouraged humanist scholarship. His union of England and Wales brought royal power to its height. State power expanded, as did middle-class participation in politics. Henry successfully involved England in continental diplomacy, but exhausted the treasury in doing so and left problems for later monarchs.

    His Intrigue ability is entirely fitting: remove his own wife to gain three coins and three points.

  • Henriette Marie de France — Henrietta Maria of France

    Henrietta Maria was a French princess, daughter of Henry IV and Queen Marie de’ Medici, sister of Louis XIII, and aunt of Louis XIV. She was born at the Louvre. Her father was assassinated before she turned one, and her mother was banished from court in 1617.
    Considered as a bride for the English crown prince in the 1620s, she married Charles I—already king—at St Augustine’s Church in Canterbury on June 13, 1625, becoming queen of England, Scotland, and Ireland. Their marriage was initially far from harmonious. As a Catholic, she brought many Catholic servants and clergy from France and practiced Catholic rites openly, provoking distrust throughout England and displeasing the king, who eventually forced her to send most of her French attendants home. The king was also exceptionally close to the Duke of Buckingham—rumors described their relationship as homosexual—leading to continual marital disputes.

    Is that why her card can produce children without a man?

  • Napoléon Bonaparte

    Does he really need an introduction?

    His abilities are nothing but swords—and every time he moves an Army into a Province containing someone else’s Army, he gains a point! What an ability! Worthy of one of Europe’s four greatest commanders!

First-Play Session Report

First, the game’s best player count should be four. Unfortunately, my two experiences were a three-player game and watching a five-player game. I still need to arrange a four-player session later.

My first game was with E and Bowl King. Two rounds after the rules explanation and start of play, E flipped the table because his colors could not produce a son, blocking his actions. But E had chosen a starting couple first, and I had emphasized the importance of sons beforehand, so he has only himself to blame…

After restarting, I was second in turn order and had to take the remaining couple. As a result, one of my actions was blocked during both the second and third rounds. Bowl King controlled two Provinces early while marrying off a daughter, creating an enormous scoring lead. E and I earned relatively little by marrying off daughters, and with no meaningful source of income, I headed straight for last place.

Since the game includes opportunities to attack one another, the leader naturally becomes a target. In the middle game, E married one of my daughters, instantly reviving my economy. As everyone accumulated more couples, action quality became critical. Bowl King foolishly married one of my useless daughters simply because she was pretty, and gradually lost his advantage.

Late in the game, several Armies produced earlier by Charles I—who adds an Army whenever a son is born—let me control more Provinces. I also assembled one couple that could score four points per round, raising my scoring efficiency, plus a character who generated three coins each round to keep the economy running. Even when E repeatedly used Intrigue to smash several of my Armies at the end, I retained control of two Provinces. The first game ended with me on 53, Bowl King on 50, and E on 46.

First Impressions

Whether judged by its mechanisms or card design, the game integrates its setting very well. Players constantly discover thematic connections during play, which is delightful. The rules are not complicated. The main questions are which player to target, which children to choose, how to arrange marriages, and what your scoring path will be. Individual actions are generally easy to decide, giving the game medium strategic depth but high interaction. The character portraits are also attractive.

Three-player games omit some characters, while five-player games give each player only two actions and feel awkward. Poor flexibility across player counts is one of the game’s major flaws.

Some lessons from play:

  • Coins are important! To maximize action efficiency, you need marriages, and marriages cost money. Early in the game, you also need Armies to secure the income from one or two Provinces, and placing Armies costs money too.
  • Too many Armies are useless. In the middle and late game they enter and leave the board frequently; roughly five is enough.
  • Producing too many children is equally useless. Focus on the quality of the couples in your family and improve the value of each action.

Among Nobles suits players who enjoy historical settings—especially European history—or who enjoy immersive Eurogames and do not mind a little direct aggression.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 2. 7 Wonders: Duel Overview and Review
entry.content:
First, some cosplay by overseas geeks to set the tone

After finishing the busy work on my thesis, I chose for the second installment of my Essen 2015 series a very popular game that I had missed during the previews: 7 Wonders: Duel, commonly called the two-player version of 7 Wonders. Overall, Duel makes numerous design improvements and provides an excellent play experience. Its three victory conditions are very well judged. Military and scientific victories are difficult but not impossibly distant, making this one of the finest two-player games.

“The beginning does not hint at the end.”
Herodotus

The designers placed this sentence from Herodotus, the “father of history,” at the very beginning of the rulebook. It seems both a verdict upon the ancient civilizations that created humanity’s greatest wonders and a message to the players: every game of 7 Wonders: Duel is full of uncertainty. I could not find the source of the quotation, however. Did the designers invent it?


Designers Bruno Cathala and Antoine Bauza

7 Wonders: Duel was designed by Antoine Bauza and Bruno Cathala. Bauza designed the original 7 Wonders and Tokaido, while Cathala created Abyss and Five Tribes. Both clearly have considerable experience with light strategy games. Their two-player collaboration worked extremely well, and I look forward to their future designs.

Game Overview

7 Wonders: Duel uses the setting and many mechanisms of the original 7 Wonders, but adapts them to the particular nature of two-player games, increasing competition and interaction.

Each player leads a civilization through three Ages, using cards to acquire coins, strengthen the military, develop science, and construct buildings and wonders.

During play, a player may win immediately through military or scientific supremacy. If nobody achieves either by the end of the third Age, the player with the highest total score wins.

Components

  • 1 game board
  • 23 Age I cards
  • 23 Age II cards
  • 20 Age III cards
  • 7 Guild cards
  • 12 Wonder cards
  • 4 Military tokens
  • 10 Progress tokens
  • 1 Conflict pawn, shown below after being painted by an overseas player
  • 31 coin tokens
    • 14 worth 1
    • 10 worth 3
    • 7 worth 6
  • 1 rulebook
  • 1 score pad
  • 1 player aid

Setup

  1. Place the game board to one side of the play area.
  2. Place the Conflict pawn in the center of the board.
  3. Place the four Military tokens in their corresponding spaces.
  4. Shuffle the ten Progress tokens, reveal five on the board, and return the rest to the box.
  5. Each player takes 7 coins.
  6. Players choose Wonders.
    1. Choose a starting player.
    2. Shuffle the twelve Wonder cards and reveal four at random. The starting player chooses one, the second player chooses two, and the starting player takes the remaining card.
    3. Reveal four more at random. The second player chooses one, the starting player chooses two, and the second player takes the last. Return the remaining four Wonder cards to the box.
  7. Build the three Age decks. Remove three cards face down from each Age. Choose three Guild cards face down and add them to the Age III deck. Shuffle all three decks separately.

Game Flow

The game lasts three Ages. It ends immediately if a player achieves scientific or military supremacy; otherwise, it ends after Age III.

At the beginning of each Age, arrange its twenty cards as illustrated for Age I, II, or III. The bottom row is always face up, and each higher row alternates between face up and face down.

Players alternate turns, with the starting player acting first in Age I. On a turn, choose one card that is not covered by any other card and perform one of three actions:

  • Construct a Building
    Pay the resources shown at the upper left of the chosen card, or use a prerequisite building’s chain symbol to build it for free. As in the original 7 Wonders, resources may come from your own city or be purchased from your opponent. The difference is that a resource costs 2 coins plus the number of matching resources on your opponent’s brown and gray cards, and the payment goes to the bank rather than the opponent.
  • Discard for Coins
    Discard the chosen card and gain 2 coins plus 1 for each yellow building in your city.
  • Construct a Wonder
    Pay the resources shown at the lower left of the Wonder card, then place the selected Age card face down beneath one of your unbuilt Wonders. Important: only seven Wonders may be constructed during the entire game. One player’s eighth Wonder will always remain unbuilt.

After a player uses a card, reveal any face-down card that is no longer covered.

When all twenty cards have been used, the Age ends. Set up the next Age, then the player with the weaker military position chooses its starting player. If the Conflict pawn stands exactly in the center, the player who took the final turn of the previous Age becomes the starting player.

Military

Every crossed-swords symbol on a building or Wonder moves the Conflict pawn one space toward the opponent. When it enters a zone containing a Military token, discard that token and force the opponent to lose the number of coins shown; if they have fewer, they lose all their coins. If the pawn reaches the final space, the opposing capital, that player immediately loses and you achieve military supremacy.

Science

The game contains seven kinds of scientific symbols. Whenever a player acquires a pair of identical symbols, they choose one Progress token from the board. A player who collects six different scientific symbols achieves scientific supremacy.

End of the Game

If neither player achieves military or scientific supremacy, the game ends after three Ages and scores are calculated.

  • Score points according to the position of the Conflict pawn.
  • Score blue, green, yellow, and purple cards.
  • Score Wonders.
  • Score Progress tokens.
  • Score 1 point for every 3 coins.

In a tie, the player with the most points on blue cards wins.

Review

7 Wonders: Duel solves many problems found in the original:

  1. Chain symbols for prerequisite buildings are now conspicuous at the top of each card rather than hidden beneath a pile, and later buildings show the same symbol within their costs.
  2. Interaction increases enormously. The criticism players most often make of the original 7 Wonders is insufficient interaction—really, the inability to interfere with distant players. Duel retains competition over military strength, resource purchasing, and scientific buildings, but adds even more important competition over card selection and turn order. Those two outstanding ideas lift the whole design to another level.
  3. It balances military, science, and points well, maintaining a delicate equilibrium between the three.

As for weaknesses, several Progress tokens feel rather useless. The Wonders are mostly well balanced, though one or two seem slightly weaker. I will not name names.

Overall, 7 Wonders: Duel genuinely offers everything a light strategy game should: attractive art; a perfect insert, even with sleeved cards; an appropriate sense of theme—the Conflict pawn makes a satisfying impact as it crashes across the board, and the limit of seven Wonders is clever, while civilization is honestly a difficult theme for a light game; and, most importantly, an experience that is simple yet deep. As mentioned earlier, players must consider not only what each card does but also the order in which cards are taken. Should you let your opponent reveal a face-down card? Can an extra-turn effect deny them a crucial building? You must also think about who begins each Age.

Some gameplay tips:

  • Production buildings—brown and gray—are important. The game strictly limits the supply of resources. If a player cannot produce a particular resource in Age I and fails to correct that in Age II, the rest of the game will be extremely difficult.
  • Commercial buildings—yellow—are important. First, players will often lack a resource. If the relevant production building was also removed from the game, a commercial building providing favorable trade for that missing resource becomes enormously useful later. Second, discarding cards for coins is common, and commercial buildings greatly increase the return from that action.
  • Wonders are important. In terms of raw card design, the standard return for a Wonder is 9 points, represented by the Pyramids of Giza. In actual games, few Wonders generate the equivalent of 9 points, so the Pyramids are a strong choice. Differing construction costs make direct comparisons difficult, however. Extra-turn effects on Wonders are excellent, but poor use can also backfire badly. The player who constructs fewer Wonders must find points elsewhere.
  • Watch science and military strength. Do not let your opponent use an extra turn to reveal a face-down card and then win immediately through scientific or military supremacy.
  • Choosing the starting player is crucial, especially after both players have exhausted their extra-turn effects.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 3. Codenames: Overview and Review
entry.content:
Game Overview


Vlaada Chvátil is truly a prodigy; no genre escapes him

Uwe Rosenberg has moved ever further along the path of medium-to-heavy worker-placement games. Vlaada Chvátil, by contrast, overwhelms other designers with the diversity of both his mechanisms and game weights. From Through the Ages to Galaxy Trucker, from Mage Knight to Codenames, VC has demonstrated the full force of his extraordinary design talent.


Apparently it is fashionable for designers to cosplay their own covers

Codenames is a word-guessing game. Players split into two teams, each led by a spymaster. Every round, the spymaster offers one word as a clue, and teammates try to identify all of their team’s agents. If they accidentally select the assassin, they lose immediately.

Components

The components are extremely simple:

  • 8 red agent cards
  • 8 blue agent cards
  • 1 double-sided agent card
  • 7 innocent-bystander cards
  • 1 assassin card
  • A deck of key cards
  • A stand for the key card
  • A deck of double-sided word cards
  • A one-minute sand timer

Setup

  1. Randomly select 25 words and arrange them in a 5×5 grid.
  2. The red and blue spymasters sit on one side, and their teammates sit opposite.
  3. One spymaster draws a key card and places either side in the stand. Only the spymasters may see the colors corresponding to every word.
  4. The color around the border of the key card determines which spymaster receives the double-sided agent card. That team goes first and must identify one additional word.

Gameplay

  1. The starting team’s spymaster gives a clue, then must maintain a poker face.
  2. Their teammates discuss and indicate a guess by touching one word card. According to the color on the key, the spymaster covers it with the corresponding agent card. If it belongs to their team, they may continue guessing and repeat step two.
  3. When the team guesses incorrectly, chooses to stop, or reaches its guess limit, the opposing spymaster gives a clue and play returns to step one.

Giving a Clue

A clue has two parts:

  • One word: the words on the table are related to this clue by meaning, not merely by structure. For example, you may not say “S” to indicate that your team’s words begin with S. You may spell a word if you or your teammates think it is necessary. The rulebook later explains in detail what qualifies as a legal single word.
  • One number: the number tells teammates how many words on the table relate to the clue, and means nothing else. It cannot become part of the clue—for example, saying “eight” because “octopus” is on the table.

Guessing

  • Teammates must guess at least one word.
  • They may guess at most X+1 words, where X is the number given by their spymaster.

Game End

  • As soon as a team identifies all its agents—nine for the first team and eight for the second—the game ends and that team wins.
  • If either team identifies the assassin, the game ends and the opposing team wins.

Review

Although Codenames has a BGG weight of only 1.4, after many plays I do not believe its strategy is shallow at all; the strategy section below explains why. Sometimes one team gains such a large lead in revealed words that it can win by guessing only one at a time. For a more enjoyable experience, I still recommend that both teams try to connect multiple remaining words whenever they give a clue.

In most games, however, the trailing team does not fall too far behind. Even if the opponent has only one word left, a burst of imagination can still identify three or four at once and reverse the result. Such games often become classics.

For the spymaster, early clues can be direct, but many words must be considered. Later, more words are covered and fewer need consideration, yet the remaining words are much harder to connect. Operatives initially face many words but little prior information. As the game continues, they face fewer words but must account for clues and missed guesses from several earlier rounds, both their own and the opponent’s. The tension therefore lasts throughout the game.

BGG classifies Codenames as a party game, but in our experience four is the ideal player count. With six or eight players, teammates need to discuss their guesses, which both increases downtime and risks revealing information to the opposition. If the purpose is simply a cheerful party experience, of course, neither issue matters.

The game also has an extraordinary dependence on language—perhaps translation into Chinese makes this contradiction especially conspicuous. Word-guessing games always depend on language to some degree, but Codenames does so more severely. My friends unanimously felt the fan translation was unplayable and looked forward to Yih Guan’s localization, because a genuinely successful Chinese edition of Codenames would amount to half of a redesign.

Strategy Notes

Here I will discuss some of the game’s strategy. It also demonstrates that this “small” game has considerable depth: easy to learn, difficult to master.

For spymasters:

  1. Trust your teammates at all times!
  2. Avoid the assassin by every possible means!
  3. Connect words through polysemy, or connect to polysemous words on the table.
  4. Watch for opposing words similar to your own, then decide whether to wait for the opponent to clue them first or find another way around them.
  5. Try to connect at least three words with the first clue.
  6. Try to connect two words with later clues.
  7. Decide whether to give a precise clue for fewer words first, or a more ambiguous clue for more words.
  8. Learn to use abstract nouns, adjectives, and verbs as clues.
  9. Whenever possible, connect a word with only one obvious meaning to another word instead of leaving it alone until the end.

For operatives:

  1. Trust your spymaster at all times!
  2. Inspect every word before guessing.
  3. Rank related words by strength of association and guess the strongest first.
  4. If you realize that you missed a word, prioritize it on the next turn instead of guessing an uncertain word from the new clue.
  5. Remember every clue your own team has received.
  6. Remember every opposing clue and analyze which words they may have missed.
  7. In the middle and late game, when choosing among several weakly related words, think from the spymaster’s perspective and ask why that clue was given.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 4. Pi mal Pflaumen Overview, Unboxing, and Review
entry.content:
Game Overview


Pi mal Pflaumen, German for “pi times plums”

Pi mal Pflaumen is an abstract game wrapped in a theme. After reading the rulebook, however, I have to complain: this is the most ridiculous background story I have ever encountered.

According to the rulebook, the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries were centuries of science—which is almost too obvious to say—and produced two great figures: Leonhard Euler, whom you may know from Euler’s formula, and Maria Sibylla Merian, a naturalist and artist whose work appears below. The rulebook never explains why these two people were chosen. Instead, it adds that they really were connected. In my searches, every webpage associating them pointed back to this rulebook. Only a German Wikipedia article mentioned that Euler’s second wife was Merian’s granddaughter. Naively, I had expected some earth-shattering story.


Maria Sibylla Merian’s work characteristically combines several stages of a caterpillar’s transformation into a butterfly within a single picture.

The game has three stages, represented by the caterpillar, chrysalis, and butterfly on the card backs. In each stage, players play and select cards, scoring by completing sets of fruit. The player with the highest score wins. It supports three to five players and takes only about half an hour, making it a good choice while waiting for someone to arrive.

Components

The components consist of only 119 cards and English and German rulebooks.

  • Bilingual English/German rulebook

  • Cards for the three stages

  • Turn-order cards

  • Plum cards, the watchdog, and pi cards


A closer look at the card illustrations

Setup

Setup is very simple. Shuffle the cards for each of the three stages separately and place the other cards nearby.

  • In a three-player game, remove cards 19–25 from each stage. Use turn-order cards 1–3, with the plum version of card 3.
  • In a four-player game, remove card 25 from each stage. Use turn-order cards 1–4, with the plum version of card 4.
  • In a five-player game, use turn-order cards 1–5.

Deal an equal number of Stage I cards to every player. The person who most recently ate fruit becomes the starting player.

Gameplay

The game contains three stages. In each stage, every player plays six cards, or five in a five-player game.
Each trick proceeds as follows:

  1. Beginning with the starting player and proceeding clockwise, everyone plays one fruit card face up. Later players can see earlier cards before deciding what to play. A player with pi cards may add one or more of them to the fruit card.
  2. After everyone has played one fruit card, assign turn-order cards according to card value. Each pi card adds 3.14 to the fruit’s printed value. The player with the highest total receives turn-order card 1.
  3. In ascending turn order, every player chooses one of the fruit cards played in the current trick and places it in their personal display.
  4. If the chosen card has a special action, resolve it immediately. The player may then use fruit cards in their display to complete a set, as explained below.
  5. The final player to choose, who in practice has no choice, takes one plum card from the common supply. Plums are an additional type of fruit.
  6. The player with turn-order card 1 becomes the new starting player. Set all turn-order cards aside and begin the next trick.

Three special actions:

  • Take the watchdog from the common area or another player.
  • Steal one fruit card from the personal display of another player who does not have the watchdog.
  • Take three pi cards from the common supply. They may be played alongside a fruit card on a later turn.

Completing Sets

Choose one scoring fruit card in your personal display and combine it with other fruit cards to meet the requirement printed on that scoring card. Then turn the scoring card face down and set it aside; remove the other fruits used in the set from the game. ABC means one each of three different fruits. AABB means two each of two different fruits. The scoring card itself may count as one of the required fruit cards, but it does not have to, in which case you spend one additional card.

End of the Game

The game ends after three stages. Players reveal their completed scoring fruit cards and add their points. The highest total wins. In a tie, the tied player with the most fruit cards remaining in their display wins.

Variant

After taking a fruit card, you may complete only one set. No sets may be completed after the game ends. Under this variant, deciding which set to finish at what moment becomes crucial.

Review

This small game from Pegasus Spiele provides production quality and artwork worthy of its 68-yuan price. It is fundamentally abstract and its attached theme makes little sense, but its overall quality is good.

We played several games at counts from three to five. As expected, three players produced the best experience. With four or five, the player who has the second-lowest selection priority each trick occupies a foolish position: they get neither a good card nor a plum as compensation, making card luck much more important. In addition, stealing can unbalance a multiplayer game when players act irrationally or hold awkward fruit combinations, because the trailing player may end up being robbed. Five-player games also finish quickly, making difficult objectives excessively risky.

The three-player game, by contrast, is excellent. Only the player with second selection priority is slightly awkward, while first and third are both valuable. If one of three players has the watchdog, the other two can simply steal from each other. Most importantly, plums are more plentiful relative to the player count—an average of one-third of a plum per player per trick. Everyone therefore holds more fruit overall, making the timing and composition of sets a much more strategic question.

entry.title: Ora et Labora Chinese Edition Unboxing
entry.content:
Ora et Labora, titanxxh’s single favorite game, now has a Chinese edition! This article presents unboxing photos and compares the component quality of the Chinese edition with the 2011 English edition.

Unboxing Photos


Front of the box; the awards it received are visible along the bottom


The back contains a game summary, with the Lookout Games and Wanderer’s Wharf logos below

All the components inside

After punching out every token

Comparison Photos

  1. Comparing the fronts of the boxes

    Beyond adding many awards along the bottom, the central illustration has also changed slightly: it adds an eagle and a sheep, puts “MMXV” on the wagon, and uses somewhat darker colors.
  2. Comparing the rulebooks

    There are still four rulebooks, all translated.
  3. Comparing wheel assembly

    The English wheel uses two plastic pieces, one pressed into the other and difficult to remove. The Chinese edition uses a metal screw that can easily be unscrewed.
  4. Comparing player aids

    The English edition provides only a thin sheet of paper and even places the Ireland and France variants on the same page, which is rather unreasonable. The Chinese edition separates them onto cardboard, so each player needs only one small board during a game.
  5. Comparing token cutting

    The English edition’s cutting is beyond criticism—and mine is actually one of the better copies. The Chinese edition is cut cleanly.
  6. Comparing heartland boards

    Another much-criticized English component: its heartland boards are far too thin. The Chinese edition thickens them to match the tokens.
  7. Comparing cards

    The cards differ little.

entry.title: A Journey Through Tanzania in 37 Photographs
entry.content:
From Kilimanjaro to Lake Manyara, and from the Serengeti to Ngorongoro Crater, I did not want to revisit this journey as a simple chronological diary. Instead, titanxxh selected 37 photographs from the more than 2,000 I took. Through them, this article returns to the moments that moved me most.

“Baba Yetu” is written in Swahili, the local language. It is the theme song of Civilization IV and the first piece of video-game music to win a Grammy. To my surprise, our driver had heard it too.

  1. The Longest Night

    On the flight from Shanghai to Addis Ababa, we traveled in the same direction as the sun at roughly the same speed. We had boarded at midnight, yet experienced another twelve hours of darkness in the air. It felt as though this sleep should never end. Shortly before landing, I finally used my phone to record day and night changing places at an altitude of 40,000 feet.

  2. Uhuru Summit

    Mount Kilimanjaro—Kilimanjaro in Swahili, meaning “shining mountain”—lies in the Kilimanjaro Region of northeastern Tanzania near the Kenyan border. It is Africa’s highest mountain and is often called the Roof of Africa or King of Africa. Its highest point is Kibo, also known as Uhuru Peak, at 5,895 meters or 19,341 feet. Part of the mountain is protected as Kilimanjaro National Park and is listed as a World Heritage Site.[^1]
    My heart sank when we arrived at Kilimanjaro Airport. The day was overcast, so there was a good chance we would never see the mountain. Clouds concealed the entire massif as we drove toward Kilimanjaro National Park. Because our itinerary did not include entering the park, we soon turned back. Yet shortly before sunset, the tip of Uhuru Peak emerged. It was not very clear—perhaps my photography was simply poor—but I could not contain my delight and took this picture.

  3. Students in Tanzania

    We drove past a school just as classes ended and taught the children to say “Happy New Year.” They were very excited to see foreigners. Our driver later explained that Tanzania provided seven years of compulsory education, with hopes of extending it to eleven under the new president.

  4. The Road Uphill

    Most roads here are unpaved; only major routes receive a surface like this. I hope life here can gradually follow an uphill road too.

  5. Quadcopter

    A quadcopter, also called a quadrotor, is a multirotor aircraft with four rotors for hovering, maintaining attitude, and level flight. Unlike a fixed-wing aircraft, it rises through thrust from its rotors. All four are the same size and arranged almost symmetrically. In a simple design, changing the relative speeds of the rotors adjusts thrust at different points and counters each rotor’s torque, allowing the aircraft to hold an attitude or perform different maneuvers. This differs from a helicopter. A conventional helicopter has two rotors, and its tail rotor merely offsets torque from the main rotor and controls yaw.[^2]
    The film crew was highly professional and brought a quadcopter for aerial footage, though some countries apparently prohibit them. These were the first animals we encountered: zebras and giraffes beside the road. The crew launched the aircraft for the first time.

  6. Exhausted

    You understand…

  7. Half Dead, Half Alive

    I took this casually and happened to capture an acacia that was half withered and half flourishing. The contrast fascinated me. I wonder what misfortune befell its right side.

  8. Farm House Valley Lodge

    Our hotel on the second day was much better than the first. Every room had two beds, a child’s bed, and mosquito nets, while the grounds resembled a farm. Tanzania and Kenya take completely different approaches to conservation and tourism development. Tanzania strictly limits the number of incoming tourists, and the entire Serengeti contains only five hotels, so each hotel has excellent surroundings. This picture shows the swimming pool at the entrance, and pools are virtually standard equipment in local hotels. The natural consequence is higher prices.

  9. Grazier

    I captured this scene with my phone mainly because I was surprised to see a donkey here. Later we discovered camels too. Apparently a scientist introduced them and entrusted them to local people to see whether they could survive.

  10. Nature versus Science

    We came across an antelope carcass beside the road. Professor Wang stepped out of the vehicle to take a sample. Our driver said the distant stork would also eat carrion, so I photographed the moment.

  11. Helping Hand

    Throughout the trip, we met many European and American visitors. Most were elderly couples traveling by themselves, although someone this old was genuinely rare. At the rest area entering the Serengeti stood a small rocky hill. Everyone climbed it to look for lizards, myself included, and I happened upon this scene on the way up.

  12. Wandering

    This large stork strutted around the rest area without paying anyone the slightest attention. Animals here are not afraid of people. Protection is effective, no visitor or other person attacks them, and so they show no wariness toward humans.

  13. The Great Migration

    We had seen antelopes, wildebeest, buffalo, and zebras all along the route into Serengeti National Park, but this was the first time we found vast herds grazing together. Zebras eat the tops of the grass, wildebeest consume the lower parts, and gazelles eat the tender shoots that grow afterward. The whole ecology is wonderfully harmonious.

  14. Sunrise in the Serengeti

    On the third day, we stayed at Serengeti Lobo Wildlife Lodge. The hotel is distinctive, perched across several giant rocks, while its wooden corridors and staircases have a strikingly Chinese character. Best of all, two paths lead to separate high points from which visitors can photograph sunrise and sunset. I rose especially early the next morning and waited for dawn. At first, I thought the sun would remain hidden behind the clouds and be impossible to photograph, but nobody was willing to leave. At last it appeared, allowing me to capture this unforgettable image: sunrise over the Serengeti.

  15. May Peace Prevail on Earth

    A pillar stands outside Serengeti Lobo Wildlife Lodge, with this wish written on its four sides in four languages.

  16. Give Me Some Space

    Serengeti Lobo Wildlife Lodge is home to many rock hyraxes. They are round and adorable. Shortly before leaving, we found three pressed tightly together. The expression in this picture seems to say, “Move over—you are squashing me.”

  17. The Sleepy Family

    Lions hunt infrequently, so anyone who is not a documentary crew waiting in one place is unlikely to photograph them in motion. We were no exception. Even so, a whole family sleeping this sweetly on a rock was an engaging sight.

  18. Why Are You Here?

    What is that—a turtle? Yes, it is a tortoise. The Serengeti’s biodiversity is astonishing, and this unexpected creature is only the tip of the iceberg.

  19. Yawn

    Almost every small river here contains a community of hippos. Like lions, hippos are lazy and spend nearly the entire day soaking in water. When one finally opened its mouth wide, I captured the instant at once. We were told that a tourist from Shanghai once left his vehicle, whereupon an enraged mother hippo defending her calf rushed over and bit him in half.

  20. Arrogance

    Lizards usually walk with their heads down. Their bodies are so flat that photographs do not show them well. This phone image is not very sharp, but the colorful lizard raised its head proudly and made the scene far more vivid.

  21. A Weaving Weaver

    A male weaver bird’s nest is one way of attracting a mate. When a female arrives, she tries to damage the nest and test its stability. If she cannot break it, the nest is sturdy and dependable, so she stays; otherwise she abandons that male. While we waited at the rest area, this tree held many weaver nests, and this yellow bird happened to be building one.

  22. Loneliness

    A dead tree, solitary bird, and dark clouds compose a perfect scene of loneliness.

  23. Leopard

    We were extraordinarily fortunate to see all of Africa’s Big Five. We had already encountered many elephants, buffalo, and lions, but continued searching for a leopard and rhinoceros. Just before leaving the Serengeti, someone finally located a leopard resting in a tree. We could not approach, so I photographed from far away the only leopard we saw as a keepsake.

  24. All for One

    When one vehicle discovers something interesting, the driver usually spreads the news through various means. Some use radio; others exchange information verbally as vehicles pass. One cannot help admiring the drivers’ command of the grassland’s geography: in the Serengeti, with no road signs, they navigate entirely from memory. After this leopard was found, more than twenty vehicles arrived from every direction merely to catch a glimpse.

  25. Umbrella

    As acacias grew taller, giraffes’ necks grew longer too. Solitary acacias decorate the vast grassland. This specimen had an exceptionally classic shape, and the sky that day was perfectly clear, producing this photograph.

  26. Hourglass

    While we were driving, I suddenly noticed that a distant hill and the clouds beyond the window mirrored one another vertically. I quickly captured this “hourglass.”

  27. Outline

    From a hot-air balloon, we could look down over the grassland. Trees “protect” a small river along both banks, while only short grass grows beyond the water’s reach.

  28. Flames

    Our hot-air-balloon pilot was of mixed Canadian and Tanzanian heritage. He explained that a balloon cannot control its direction directly. Pilots instead learn the wind direction at different altitudes and adjust height to make small corrections. Intermittent bursts of flame kept us floating at a stable level.

  29. A Living Encyclopedia

    This was our driver. The job demands a great deal: besides driving for more than ten hours a day, drivers must identify the local animals. Most importantly, they possess eyesight far beyond that of ordinary people—vision like an eagle’s. While driving, they notice every distant irregularity: which bird is perched on a branch, or which animal hides in the grass. I cannot imagine developing those abilities without ten or twenty years of experience.

  30. What Are You Looking At?

    A weaver bird tilted its head and stared at me. I wanted to reply, “You. What about it?”

  31. Defense Mechanism

    When zebras sense danger, they gather together so each can watch another’s back. It is a defensive mechanism. Does it not feel like two people venturing deep into danger, then fighting back to back and entrusting their blind side to a companion?

  32. The Maasai

    We visited a Maasai village. The women sang and danced, while the men welcomed us by jumping vertically from a standstill. Maasai homes consist of only a few branches. They are so low and small that one must crouch to enter. Inside is room for only a bed and a fire, with no natural light. It is difficult to imagine how they survive. PS: their body odor was extremely strong…

  33. Simba

    It was rare enough to find a lion that was awake—and a male lion at that. I was thrilled.

  34. Scared Witless

    A zebra beside the road urinated in fright when it saw us approach.

  35. Geometric Aesthetics

    After touring Ngorongoro Crater, the slopes on both sides of the uphill road formed a perfect V, creating this photograph full of geometric beauty.

  36. The Starry Night of Ngorongoro Crater

    Every previous day, I had forgotten to photograph the African night sky. On our final night at Ngorongoro Crater, I took out the camera. Without a tripod, I used my phone as a support and recorded this perfect last night.

  37. Panoramic View of Ngorongoro Crater

    Save the best for last. If a trip to Africa leaves you only one day in Tanzania, do not hesitate: go directly to the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. Wildlife here is extraordinarily dense, and its diversity loses nothing to the Serengeti. We saw rare flamingos and the last member of the Big Five we had not yet encountered, the white rhinoceros. Ngorongoro Wildlife Lodge is the area’s oldest hotel. The next morning, I used my phone on the hotel balcony to capture this panorama of Ngorongoro Crater.

[^1]: Wikipedia: Mount Kilimanjaro
[^2]: Wikipedia: Quadcopter

entry.title: Ora et Labora Overview and Rules
entry.content:
Ora et Labora, titanxxh’s single favorite game, now has a Chinese edition! So I am going to give a proper introduction to this culmination of Uwe Rosenberg’s work.

Overview

Ora et Labora—Latin for “pray and work”—is a game about medieval monastic economics. Uwe truly loves medieval settings. Medieval monasteries naturally included prayer, but even more of their life consisted of hard labor inside and outside the monastery. Each player manages a monastery, sending a prior and two lay brothers to work in buildings that produce goods. At the beginning, each player has only a 2 × 5 heartland board, but may purchase additional landscapes as the game progresses. Play pauses five times, and after each pause players can build settlements, ideally placing them where the surrounding settlement values are high. Ora et Labora offers two variants, France and Ireland, and players choose which one to use.


A handmade clergyman created by an overseas geek

Setup

  1. Production wheel and hand: choose the production wheel appropriate to the player count—three players; four players; the three- or four-player short game; or one or two players—and the correct side of the wheel hand. Use the slower-growth side for two players and the other side otherwise.
  2. Buildings: first decide whether to use the France or Ireland variant.
    • In a three-player game, remove buildings marked 4 in the lower-right. In a two-player game, also remove those marked 3+.
    • Turn the buildings to their France or Ireland side.
    • Sort buildings by the symbol at the center-left: a book or the letters A, B, C, and D. Display the book buildings on the table and place each other group beside the matching space on the wheel.
  3. Place the goods indicators on space 0 of the wheel and the settlement indicator on A.
  4. Stone and grapes: place the stone and grape indicators outside their corresponding wheel spaces. They are unavailable at the start and enter later. The Ireland variant has no grapes.
  5. Each player receives:
    • 1 heartland board
    • 3 clergy
    • 8 settlement cards
    • 1 reference card
    • 1 of each basic good: clay, wood, peat, coin, grain, and livestock
  6. Landscapes: sort both the long districts and square plots by the price in the lower-right, cheapest first, to form two stacks. Players must purchase the cheapest available tile of either type.

Game Flow

Only the three- and four-player rules are described here. The one- and two-player and short-game rules differ slightly. Once the Chinese edition is released, players who understand the three- and four-player game should be able to read the other rules quickly.

At the beginning, choose a starting player. That player takes the Starting Player marker and turns its one-coin side face up. The marker passes clockwise after every round.

Round Sequence

Each round contains five phases, resolved in order:

  1. At the beginning of the round, every player checks whether all three clergy are on buildings. If so, return all of them.
  2. Move the wheel hand one space counterclockwise, increasing the production of every good. If an indicator is already on the final space, the hand pushes it forward, so its production stays unchanged. In the France variant, grapes enter in Round 8 and stone in Round 13. Place their indicators on 0; at that point, the joker indicator may immediately be used to obtain stone or grapes.
  3. Whenever the hand passes a settlement-phase letter—A through E—pause play and insert a Settlement Phase, during which players build settlements.
  4. Beginning with the starting player and proceeding clockwise, each player takes one action. The starting player then takes one additional action.
  5. At the end of the round, pass the Starting Player marker clockwise.

Action Options

Choose one of the following three options as your action.

  • Place clergy: place one available clergyman—not currently on a board—either the prior or a lay brother, on an unused building and resolve its function.
    • You may place your own or another player’s clergyman. To use another player’s, pay that player 1 coin, increasing to 2 after the Whiskey Distillery in the Ireland variant or Winery in the France variant has been built. Alternatively, return one wine in France or whiskey in Ireland to the common supply as payment. In that case the other player receives nothing; the alcohol was a gift, which they happily drank on the spot.
    • You may place clergy without using the building’s function.
  • Fell trees or cut peat: remove one Forest or Moor card from your board, then take wood or peat equal to the number shown beside that good’s indicator on the production wheel.
    • This action uses no clergyman.
    • You may use the joker indicator to gain wood or peat.
    • You may take this action even if you have no Forest or Moor, and even if the indicator’s value is 0.
    • Removing a Forest or Moor exposes a landscape space on which you may later construct a building.
  • Construct a building: choose a currently displayed building, pay the resources in its upper-left corner, and place it on an empty space of your board.
    • Yellow monastery buildings must be adjacent to an existing yellow building.
    • The placement must satisfy the terrain requirement in the upper-left.
    • Buildings cannot be moved after construction.
    • If your prior is available, you may immediately place him on the newly constructed building and use its ability.

Bonus actions may be taken any number of times at any point during your turn.

  • Turn grain into straw: flip any number of grain goods to their straw side. You cannot reverse the conversion.
  • Exchange money: exchange five one-coin goods for one five-coin good or vice versa. You may also exchange wine for one coin or whiskey for two coins.
  • Purchase a landscape: during each turn or Settlement Phase, you may purchase one landscape. Pay the coins shown in the lower-right, choose a side, and place it. Long districts may extend only above or below your heartland. A square plot’s coast side may extend only at the upper or lower left of your heartland, while its mountain side may extend only at the upper or lower right. The tile must be adjacent to a landscape you already own.

Production Wheel

When a player gains resources from the production wheel through certain buildings, take the number of goods shown by the corresponding indicator—or the joker—then move that indicator to 0.

Settlement Phase

Whenever the wheel hand passes A, B, C, D, or E, insert a Settlement Phase. Players may each purchase one landscape at this time, proceeding clockwise from the starting player if more than one wishes to do so.

  1. Move the settlement indicator to the next letter.
  2. Each player may choose one settlement from their hand to build. Pay the food and energy in its upper-left corner, then place it on an empty space of your board.
    • Excess food and energy are wasted.
    • Observe the settlement’s terrain requirement.
    • Settlements cannot be moved.
    • You may construct only a settlement from before the current phase. In the first Settlement Phase, for example, you may build only one of the four book settlements; in the second, A settlements become available.
    • You may decline to construct a settlement.
  3. Add the buildings corresponding to the letter just passed to the display.

Bonus Round in a Three- or Four-Player Game

Once the hand passes E on its second circuit—Round 25—the game enters its final Bonus Round.

Each player returns their prior, then takes one bonus action in player order. That action may be constructing a building, after which the prior may be placed on it to use it, or activating any player’s building without paying a fee and regardless of whether it has already been used.

Scoring

Add the following three categories. The player with the most points wins!

  1. Goods value: add the values inside shields on goods. Alcohol is both valuable and worth points; for example, one wine plus four coins can count as 2 points.
  2. Building and settlement value: add the values inside shields.
  3. Settlement value: each settlement scores the sum of the small-house values on itself and the four buildings or settlements directly above, below, left, and right of it.

Review

As I said at the beginning, Ora et Labora is titanxxh’s favorite game. In my view, its design—from mechanisms to details—represents the peak of Uwe Rosenberg’s work. Rather than repeat myself, I will quote a passage from an earlier article:

After two quiet years, Uwe returned to the fair with a new work: Ora et Labora, titanxxh’s personal favorite, which my friends and I usually shorten to “Ora.” If I had to summarize its design in one word, it would be elegance. When introducing the game to newcomers unfamiliar with Uwe’s earlier work, they may regard its small wheel with curiosity or even confusion. Veteran Uwe players, however, can only marvel at the brilliance of the design. The circle truly is a perfect form. Just as people become more tactful after being shaped by experience, this wheel seems to have been refined across many years of Uwe’s work until it became such an elegant solution: nudge the hand, and everything is done. Tzolk’in later borrowed something of this idea. The design eliminates the tedious work of replenishing resources in Agricola, combines it with the timing function of the rondel in Le Havre, and makes introducing new resources during play extremely easy. The wheel naturally has limitations—for example, resources of the same type can grow at different rates in Agricola, which is impossible here—but that does not keep us from praising its elegance. Beyond substantially improving resource growth, Uwe introduced the relative position of buildings into Ora et Labora, transforming scoring and deepening the layers of thought required. Players must decide not only when to purchase which building, but also how to arrange their buildings to increase settlement scores. That demands stronger global strategy. Perhaps because this increased complexity, Uwe eliminated all randomness and controlled the number of every building to reduce the burden on players. The familiar feeding phase from Uwe’s earlier games also disappeared, replaced by a subtler and more flexible Settlement Phase. Players no longer suffer frustration from failing to feed their people. When building settlements, they have choices: even if they temporarily cannot construct a high-value settlement, they can build a slightly lower-scoring one, save resources, and prepare earlier for later stages. Because most settlement scoring comes from surrounding buildings, the settlement itself does not overly affect the final score, making the design friendlier. Another strength is player interaction. If another player constructs a building before you, that is not necessarily bad: you can still use it, perhaps even before its owner benefits, while saving the resources required to build it. On the other hand, doing so accelerates your opponent’s clergy cycle and slows your own. Finally, I believe the game’s greatest triumph is its kindness to trailing players. In many games, a poor early development—perhaps a key building is taken or a strategy disrupted—effectively removes someone from contention. Here, until the final stage, you still have opportunities to allocate resources sensibly, convert them into points, and catch up. For all these reasons, Ora et Labora became titanxxh’s favorite game, the one I have played most often by far, and one of the very few I rated a perfect 10 on BGG. A game can earn a high score for novelty, polished mechanisms, an enjoyable experience, and many other reasons. But if a player awards a perfect score, I think there is only one reason: profound love. If loving the right person at the right time is happiness, then meeting the right people and playing the right game at the right time must be another kind of happiness.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 6. Mombasa: Introduction and Review
entry.content:
Game Introduction

Mombasa is Kenya’s second-largest city, a beautiful place and the largest port on Africa’s east coast. Zheng He’s voyages to the Western Oceans even reached it. The Pegasus Spiele game, however, is set during such a dark chapter of human history that its rulebook avoids discussing the subject. Europeans may prefer silence, but we can still name it: the age of colonialism, when capitalist powers used military, political, and economic means to occupy, enslave, and exploit weaker countries, peoples, and less-developed regions, turning them into colonies and semi-colonies.

The designer does not simulate those details. Players simply act as investors in four companies operating across Africa, buying shares and directing investment. This distances the game from its historical setting and turns it into a medium-weight economic game.

As with Nippon, a player translated the rules into Chinese in the Yih Guan group’s chat, so I will not repeat them here.

Review

Compared with Nippon, Mombasa does not feel like an especially unified whole. Its main theme is investing in companies and increasing one’s shareholdings, but the end-game score includes far more than the share value of each of the four companies multiplied by one’s holdings. Points from the diamond track and bookkeeping track also account for a substantial portion of the total. During play, however, advancing those two tracks feels only loosely connected to the game’s central company competition.

If you focus exclusively on companies fighting over the map and neglect the diamond and bookkeeping tracks on your player board, you certainly cannot win. Advancing both tracks is difficult. The diamond track is comparatively straightforward, while the bookkeeping track demands exceptionally strong planning.

The four companies have different powers, and each company board is double-sided. Because one side of each is selected for every game, there are sixteen combinations. Developing substantial holdings in all four companies is nearly impossible and, more importantly, unwise: their trading posts compete and displace one another across the center of the map, so holding more shares in the dominant companies is the only sound principle.

The hand-management system resembles deck-building, but requires painful planning. Cards played each round are divided among three separate piles, and at the end of the round you return only one pile to your hand. A card may therefore take several rounds to come back. If you unlock an additional card slot, you must also buy another card to keep your hand large enough.

The bookkeeping track tests planning even more severely. Each book you acquire may be placed in any position, and if you can satisfy all the displayed resource requirements of the chosen book at once, you can advance many spaces in a single action.

My impression is that the game asks you to do too many things in too few rounds—perhaps one more round would help—and its planning is indirect and mentally exhausting. It is best played when everyone is alert. If your hand contains many exploration cards, you will naturally exert greater control over competition in the center of the map. Even then, you must read the situation and raise the share price of the company that benefits you most. Players with fewer exploration cards should buy more commodity cards and use them to increase their holdings.

Money is hard to obtain, while advancing continuously on a share track often requires paying cash first. The bonus action that trashes a card from your hand for money therefore deserves serious attention.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 5. Nippon Introduction and Review
entry.content:
Introduction

At the beginning of the Meiji period, Japan was a closed, isolated feudal society, but its people desired change and hoped to transform it into a modern country. Japan sent emissaries abroad to study, brought engineers and scholars back from the West, and constructed a railway network, completing a rapid industrial revolution at astonishing speed.
