In Nippon, each player leads a great zaibatsu during the Meiji Restoration. By developing technology, constructing new factories, shipping goods across the country, and exporting them overseas, players expand their influence. The player with the most influence at the end wins.

Another player has already translated Nippon’s rules into Chinese, so this article will not provide a detailed rules explanation and will focus instead on my impressions.

Review

On each turn, a player may perform one of the nine actions on the board or carry out a consolidation phase to produce coal, receive income, and pay wages. Wages depend on the colors of the workers the player has taken: every different color costs 3,000. Workers must be an abstract concept here, since otherwise it is difficult to understand what this design represents. When choosing actions, you must therefore consider both the colors of your current workers and those that will enter the supply later. This is a difficult strategic point to master because predicting which stack will empty first is hard.

Available actions include increasing coal production, raising the technology level, building factories, producing goods, fulfilling contracts, buying machinery, building ships and trains, and—most importantly—placing goods in regions of the board to increase influence. The game has a very clear central thread: area control. Its three scoring phases each resolve the four regions on the board. The three players who supplied the most goods and therefore hold the greatest influence receive points, with each later scoring worth more than the one before. Almost every action a player takes leads toward these moments. During play, players can also acquire scoring-multiplier tiles that increase points from particular categories at the end, a feature similar to What’s Your Game?’s earlier Zhanguo.

I have played Nippon three times, twice with four players and once with three. Every session felt different, suggesting that replayability is at least respectable. Its core objective is unmistakable: competing for ranks of influence across the map. This reflects the opening of the rulebook. As newer Eurogames increasingly decentralize their scoring systems, Nippon’s approach may seem somewhat old-fashioned. Yet that clarity greatly helps players grasp the heart of the game and learn it quickly.

In the introduction, the designers describe Nippon as a fast-paced, medium-weight game. In reality, the length of a round can differ greatly from one session to another. A round ends only when all replacement workers have been used and the supply must be filled again. At one extreme, all five action spaces might have only one worker remaining. At the other, all three workers might be taken from a single space. These situations differ by eight actions—two full circuits in a four-player game. When the round-end condition triggers, every action space is refilled, so the longest possible game contains sixteen more actions than the shortest.

Finally, Nippon has several weaknesses. First is the art. What’s Your Game? titles are repeatedly criticized for their visuals, and the spectacular cover cannot rescue a plain board. Second, the factories are unbalanced: two have obviously excessive power, yet for some reason every factory costs the same. Third, the technology track is poorly designed. Because blueprint bonuses exist, technology is far weaker than the coal track, yet advancing either costs the same. That is difficult to understand.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 7. Signorie Overview and Review
entry.content:
Introduction

Fifteenth-century Italy was a great land, but also one filled with intrigue. Its chaotic political environment gave rise to a new form of government—the signoria—while many ambitious noble families grew steadily stronger.
After years of maneuvering in the shadows, their moment finally arrived. It was their turn to control the cities and shape Italy’s future; their stories would enter the history books.

In Signorie, each player represents a noble power. You are lord of a celebrated Renaissance family, increasing your influence and building a mighty dynasty by arranging marriages with six of the most prestigious houses.

You must choose your children’s destinies wisely. Give the men of your family one of three forms of training—military, religious, or political—then send them on diplomatic missions to the right cities at the right time, or strategically arrange political marriages for them.

At the beginning of each round, roll twenty dice in five colors. Players take turns choosing a die from the common area. Its color determines the action available, while its number indicates the discount on that action. Hiring assistants improves the efficiency of a player’s actions.
The dice mechanism is simple yet somewhat innovative. Each player can take at most four actions per round. Money is always tight, so high-numbered dice are tempting, but their values require careful trade-offs: a player whose total exceeds 13 loses the round’s reward.

The player with the most Influence at the end wins.

Review

Signorie‘s design has a very strong Zhanguo flavor, yet neither of its designers worked on Zhanguo, which makes me curious about WYG’s development process.
In Zhanguo, playing a card into a region increases the efficiency of actions there. Here, hiring assistants adds effects to a particular action. As in Zhanguo, the player must decide when to stop hiring assistants.
In Zhanguo, players complete two groups of tasks that score at the end of the game. In Signorie, players work through marriage objectives on their own boards, also scored at the end. Completing all three subtasks in Zhanguo yields a very high score, while missing one reduces the multiplier dramatically. In Signorie, all four objectives require at least three marriages before they score, creating an equally hard threshold.
By comparison, building the Great Wall and palaces in Zhanguo is more thematic than advancing three career tracks in Signorie.

Based on one four-player and one two-player game, however, Signorie does have advantages over Zhanguo. Player interaction is stronger: die values can block other players, as can marriage objectives on the map. The starting-player track is also well designed. Its scoring efficiency is slightly lower than the career tracks, but earlier turn order compensates, so it feels reasonably balanced. One interesting detail is that the action for hiring an assistant sits in the column immediately to the right of every action track. To create combinations early, players must therefore build their engines carefully. Since each round permits only four actions, abandoning one action column is entirely viable.

Overall, Signorie is a medium-weight engine-building game. WYG’s lighter tastes in recent years are fairly friendly to me. Downtime is average, the game hangs together reasonably well, and the artwork remains characteristically undistinguished. Die-hard WYG fans should definitely buy it; newer Eurogame players can try it to learn the common design patterns of recent years.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 8. ...and then, we held hands: Overview, Unboxing, and Review
entry.content:
Game Overview

…and then, we held hands, which we simply call “Holding Hands,” is a nonverbal cooperative game for two players. Their goal is to save a relationship on the verge of collapse. Each player’s perspective changes continuously with their position, and the pair must cooperate to balance both their inner emotions and their shared relationship, repairing the rift between them.

Players complete a sequence of objectives by ending their turns on the corresponding nodes. Once every objective is complete, both must enter the central ring together to achieve final victory.

Players may not discuss the game itself. Each must independently consider both their own cards and their partner’s, anticipate possible movement, and avoid trapping either player and losing the game. Conversation unrelated to the game is allowed. For an additional challenge, the entire game can be played in complete silence.

Components

  • Four glass player tokens, two blue and two red, although the glass is a little too opaque…
  • 48 emotion cards: three copies of each of sixteen types
  • 2 cover cards
  • 24 objective cards: six each for anger, sadness, serenity, and happiness
  • One game board

Setup

  1. Place the board between the players. Each player puts one glass token at the center of their balance track and the other on the middle node of the outer ring nearest them.
  2. Shuffle the emotion deck. Each player draws six cards and arranges them in a row, each card covering half of the next.
  3. Each player may inspect the six cards and choose whether the left or right halves will be used at the beginning—their initial perspective.
  4. Put a cover card over the topmost card.
  5. Shuffle the objective deck, divide it into three piles of eight cards, and reveal one card from the first pile.
  6. The younger player becomes the starting player, and the game begins.

Gameplay

Players alternate turns until the game ends. On each player’s turn:

  1. If there is no active objective card, reveal one.
  2. Play any number of emotion cards to move. For every card, move to an adjacent node matching the emotion on the card’s exposed half. Each anger or sadness card moves your balance marker to the left, while serenity or happiness moves it right. Regardless of whose tableau supplied the card, it enters the current player’s discard pile.
    • Objectives: move onto an emotion node shown on the objective card to complete it. Immediately discard that objective and end the turn. Once all eight objectives in the first pile are complete, players may enter nodes in the middle ring; shuffle whichever player’s discard pile is larger back into the emotion deck. Once all eight objectives in the second pile are complete, players may enter the inner ring and repeat that reshuffle. Only after all eight objectives in the third pile are complete may the players attempt to enter the center and win.
    • Restrictions on playing cards:
      • You may not pass through the same node twice in one turn.
      • You may not pass through the other player’s token.
      • If your marker has already reached the far left of the balance track, you may not make another movement that would push it left, and likewise for the far right.
  3. Draw emotion cards. If your balance marker is in the center, refill your tableau to six cards.
  4. Adjust perspective. According to the position of their token on the board, the player adjusts which half of each emotion card is visible. If the token is in the middle, the player chooses either the left or right half.

Game End

Victory:
Both players must enter the center on consecutive turns—one immediately after the other—and both balance markers must be centered. In other words, each person must regain inner balance while the couple once again holds hands. When moving from the inner ring to the center, follow a connecting line, but any emotion card may be played.

Defeat:

  • The players fail to enter the center on consecutive turns, or a balance marker is not centered when someone enters.
  • A player has no legal movement during their turn.
  • The emotion deck is empty and the cards in front of the players cannot be used.

Argument Variant

The gray bar on an objective card represents an argument. In this variant, both players must stop on the same node matching the objective’s emotion to complete it. One player therefore reaches the node first, and the other moves onto it during the following turn. After completing the objective, either player may leave in any direction. This is the only circumstance in which one token may pass through the other.

Players can choose the difficulty: treat only cards with a one-third-height bar as arguments; treat cards with one-third- and two-thirds-height bars as arguments; or use every card bearing a gray bar.

Unboxing


The cover is understated and elegant. The artist is Marie Cardouat, who also illustrated Dixit.


The back briefly introduces the game’s story.


All the contents


The two sides of the board support players with and without color-vision deficiency. What thoughtful design—this color-blind player could cry.


The sixteen emotion cards. Only ten are shown because the other six merely swap the left and right halves while retaining the same artwork and card names. Look carefully and each emotion’s two sides make good sense.

Review


A game in progress. We successfully held hands in both plays, although we played the variant incorrectly in the second, so it does not really count.

As a small two-player game, …and then, we held hands is not especially strategic. Its brilliance lies instead in the designers’ ingenuity. Merely reading the rules makes you suspect that the designers must have experienced some complicated relationships. Theme and mechanics fit one another extraordinarily closely, and the rules already explain most examples. I will add two more.

First, whenever cards are recycled, only the larger discard pile is shuffled back into the deck. This encourages one person to complete an objective rather than having both split up and pursue separate tasks—a particularly important consideration in the variant. It reinforces the idea that the pair must consider the larger picture and act as a single whole.

Second, the argument variant requires both players to reach the same node. That greatly increases the difficulty, yet perfectly expresses the extra effort required to resolve a quarrel. Only a couple capable of truly standing in the same place and considering each other’s feelings can resolve an argument perfectly.

entry.title: Touring a City Alone
entry.content:
With full-time work about to begin, I slipped away to Beijing alone last week. I had wanted to explore the capital properly ever since attending a conference there the previous year. My only earlier visit had been when I was too young to remember anything, while last year’s schedule was so limited that I visited only the Forbidden City and the National Museum of China. As my final chance to relax before starting work, traveling alone felt free and pleasant.


Shamelessly borrowing a photograph of the Corner Tower to open the post—I really want an ultra-wide-angle lens.


A group portrait of my ticket stubs

Day 1: Peking University and Tsinghua University





The buildings on the Peking University campus are relatively old and in places even dilapidated, so I prefer Tsinghua’s environment and architectural design.

This was my first time booking accommodation through Airbnb. The host was a charming young woman. There was only one room, but it was clean and tidy and perfectly sufficient for sleeping.

Day 2: Temple of Heaven, Eight Great Hutongs, Prince Gong’s Mansion, Nanluoguxiang, and the National Library


The legendary douzhi, fermented mung-bean drink. It tasted like swill, but I forced myself to finish it. Beijing was the imperial capital and therefore contains every kind of regional cuisine. Its truly distinctive food is instead ordinary people’s street fare. Poor households made dishes that were either watery soups or used assorted scraps, such as quick-fried tripe, so the flavors can be strange.



A foreign head of state visited the Temple of Heaven while I was there, and the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests was placed under security restrictions.

This is said to have been one of Mei Lanfang’s stage costumes. Its color looks wrong because once an opera performer became famous, costumes were generally never washed. This is what resulted.

This setting has also appeared in many films, including Farewell My Concubine.

At noon I tried zhajiangmian and still did not find it tasty.

This was where Heshen stored his treasures in Prince Gong’s Mansion. Every room has a different lattice pattern on its window, and nobody but Heshen knew which pattern corresponded to which treasure inside.


Nanluoguxiang is much like Kuanzhai Alley in Chengdu. There is not much for someone alone—especially a man—to browse.

I was meeting friends for dinner that evening, so I did not go inside the library.

Day 3: Old Summer Palace, Summer Palace, and National Centre for the Performing Arts




The Old Summer Palace is a place of sorrow. Some of the twelve zodiac fountain heads remain overseas, while the whereabouts of others are unknown.


Victor Hugo’s furious condemnation of the burning of the Old Summer Palace!


The broken walls of the Great Fountain seem to possess a different kind of beauty.

The imperial seal is missing from the dragon’s claw at the Summer Palace, symbolizing the Guangxu Emperor’s lack of control over power.

Boating on Kunming Lake, with the Seventeen-Arch Bridge in view

The Summer Palace contains the world’s longest covered corridor. Its paintings are said to have been added voluntarily by students from the Central Academy of Fine Arts.

A panoramic view over Kunming Lake


The National Centre for the Performing Arts!

The boat from the Italian opera Aida

A prop from Aida—so magnificent.

At half price, a symphony concert cost only 25 yuan. I mainly went because my feet were dead after a day of walking. People in the capital are fortunate.

Day 4: Badaling Great Wall, Jingshan Park, Corner Tower, and National Centre for the Performing Arts




If you visit Beijing, do not go to the Great Wall. The value for money is far too low.

This is said to be the crooked tree from which the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself.


A panoramic view of the Forbidden City from the summit of Jingshan Park. Once again, I was defeated by the lack of a wide-angle lens.

Oh, my beloved Corner Tower—why could I not create the same effect even after choosing sunset? Those photographers must have added a mountain of special effects. Duang!

I entered the National Centre for the Performing Arts again, once more after walking my legs off. Having a snack there and listening to other people perform was pleasant.

The play Rules of Survival felt a little like Twelve Angry Men. The entire story took place inside this small room.

Day 5: Capital Museum


One of the Capital Museum’s two major spring exhibitions featured the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun. Liu He was emperor for only twenty-seven days and later held the ranks of king and marquis—quite a legendary life.


The B1 level also contained an exhibition on the historical development of Beijing.


The other major spring exhibition marked the fortieth anniversary of the discovery of Fu Hao’s tomb. This is Fu Hao’s hairpin—or is it a knife?

A painting of the Two Immortals of Harmony and Union, telling the story of Hanshan and Shide. According to legend, they were as close as brothers and loved the same woman. When Hanshan learned on the eve of the wedding that Shide loved her too, he left home to become a monk. Shide also gave her up and went looking for Hanshan. After reuniting, both became monks and founded Hanshan Temple. From then on, the folk deity of harmony divided from one figure into two. They still look like monks: disheveled, smiling gods, one holding a lotus and the other a round box. In Chinese, “lotus” sounds like harmony and “box” like union, expressing a harmonious relationship.

At the porcelain exhibition, a volunteer explained the story behind this disc-shaped piece depicting the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen.

Afterword

I walked a complete circuit along the Tongzi River around the Forbidden City. I heard many Beijing residents explaining the city’s history to visitors and listened to conversations between older local men. Much of what they said was unofficial history, but their deep affection for the city was unmistakable. Beijing life is not the kind I am accustomed to, yet I would still gladly visit again if the opportunity arose—at the very least, there are exhibitions to see. Perhaps I will have no chance in the next few years, though. Any visit would be a business trip, without much free time.

entry.title: titanxxh's 2016 Board Game Review
entry.content:
BG Stats

The BG Stats app records board-game sessions and provides statistics, making it the perfect assistant for an annual review.

Across 2016, I played 105 different games, a number that surprised even me. BG Stats currently does not recognize relationships between base games and expansions very well, however, counting non-standalone expansions as separate games. That is annoying, though I rarely play with expansions, so this figure should remain fairly accurate. My H-index was only 6, meaning just six games reached six plays, so the 2016 10 × 10 Challenge definitively failed again. There are simply too many new games these days. BGG’s database grows by almost 10,000+ titles every year, the number of halls at Essen increases annually, and chasing new releases is a consensus within my gaming circle—yes, President Wen, I mean you. Combined with the drastic loss of free time after beginning full-time work, these factors have made repeated plays increasingly rare. I miss my university years, when we could play Ora et Labora dozens of times.

Breaking the numbers down, I played 158 sessions during the first four months, before starting the job, though online Agricola accounted for a large share. After I joined the company, only 35 percent of the year’s plays remained; May and September both recorded zero sessions… This will probably deteriorate further in 2017, so instead of another 10 × 10 Challenge, I plan to attempt 100 × 1. After Club A stopped hosting open events, I never had a fixed venue. Chengshan Road now looks likely to become the place I visit most often, mainly because it is close to both E and me. As a standard Eurogamer, more than half my plays were at four players, demonstrating just how deeply the common overseas family structure of two parents and two children has influenced German-style games.

E, Bowl King, and the Editor-in-Chief became my best gaming buddies this year—last year it was Xiaoda, E, and Bowl King. I thank them for their company, especially the Editor-in-Chief, who read the rules alone and taught us T.I.M.E Stories and Pandemic Legacy. Sadly, after I stopped going to Club A, I never saw the Editor-in-Chief again T_T… Bowl King left to study in Hong Kong, so I barely saw him during the second half of the year. E was probably still the person I met most often. In a year without a regular venue, we even held one session inside Ctrip’s headquarters and visited the legendary senior executive’s office—the one whose routine is running at work and playing with his child after work. I also thank all our other friends and everyone on the editorial team. I even saw C this year, although she is really E’s fan…

The Fallen King — Agricola

Online Agricola on iOS was unquestionably my most-played game of 2016, accounting for a quarter of all sessions. I just checked the BGG rankings and found that Agricola has fallen out of the top ten, which is deeply saddening. On this day last year, Twilight Struggle, which had held BGG’s number-one spot for five years, was displaced by Pandemic Legacy. Another year has passed, and the second-generation ruler of the board-game world, Agricola, has now left the top ten too. Look at the games that overtook it: the American-favorite Star Wars setting of Star Wars: Rebellion, Kickstarter darling Scythe, lightweight two-player strategy game 7 Wonders Duel, and even its old companion Stefan Feld’s The Castles of Burgundy. Have these games truly surpassed Agricola in gameplay? I doubt it. The main reason is that the people submitting BGG ratings are no longer the “geeks” implied by Geek Rating. More and more mainstream players are joining BGG and giving newer games high scores, while older games suffer simply from being born first. Their rating-distribution histograms show this clearly. Yet the expansion of the board-game audience is also what produced the rapid growth mentioned at the beginning, so perhaps this is historically inevitable. No reign lasts forever.

Every online Agricola session occurred in the first four months. During that period, I met the experts in a Chinese iOS Agricola group and realized how low-level my previous play had been. It felt like ten years earlier, after I had played Heroes of Might and Magic for years and first opened the Gamer’s Home website. Games against experts repeatedly transformed my understanding, especially those against Koko. His fluid, effortless play crushed us even after we forced two Begging cards on him—actually, the three of us combined to deny him food for a round. Ordinary-looking cards became miraculous in Koko’s hands, and even cards we considered garbage turned from ugly ducklings into swans. I later learned that the best platform for online Agricola is PlayAgricola, whose many new cards almost transform the game itself. Strategies without Family Growth are everywhere. One has to admire both the players’ limitless imagination and the vitality of this old game. To this day, President Wen, Xiaoda, and I remain devoted to Agricola. Despite the flood of new releases, we are willing at any moment to pull out the complete game and all expansions for a face-to-face session. They even brought new Agricola cards back from Essen. This year marks the game’s tenth anniversary, and Uwe surely will not miss such a perfect opportunity to make money. A tenth-anniversary edition containing a thousand cards is reportedly ready. What are Agricola devotees waiting for?

Best Party Game — The Codenames Series


The black—adult—edition of Codenames

Codenames is the best party game for both laughter and strategy. Its number-one position among BGG party games is thoroughly deserved, and our 33 sessions prove it. We played Xiaoda’s English copy at Club A until it was worn out. Even after the initial novelty faded, whenever a gathering is about to end and half an hour remains, we pull out Codenames without hesitation and complete one tense yet brisk game.

This year brought Codenames: Pictures. It moves faster, removes language dependence, and is better for teaching new players and family gatherings. Yet after our limited number of plays, everyone agreed that the picture edition was less interesting than the word edition. That is fascinating: images appear to contain more information, yet offer less than words. Perhaps pictures are more concrete while words have wider associations. Books and films create a similar contrast.

A Worthy New Number One — Pandemic Legacy


A gathering in Montreal: the four leaders meet to exchange information, research the final cure, and prepare for victory.

Like many veteran players, the Editor-in-Chief, E, President Wen, and I doubted PL—Pandemic Legacy—as it shot up the rankings. After fighting through “ten months,” however, we had to admit that the new number one deserved its position. The difficulty grows gradually, and the unfolding plot generates real tension. During my first few months with the team, we swept through every monthly scenario in a single victory. By September and October, however, E and President Wen collectively slacked off and caused us to lose; I even sacrificed my own character to force a win. In our final month, a seemingly minor mistake by the Editor-in-Chief and me directly triggered outbreaks across the entire map, leaving little hope of a later victory. Although I did not complete the full twelve-month campaign—I do not know whether they finished it afterward—I strongly recommend finding four people and experiencing a true “pandemic.”

How an Expansion Skeptic Changed His Mind — Power Grid: The Stock Companies

People who know me may know that I dislike expansions. When a game receives one, my opinion of it generally declines. In recent years, the formerly simple and self-contained world of board games has caught the video-game industry’s DLC habit. Content that could have appeared together is deliberately withheld for a supplement or expansion, which is deeply irritating. But Power Grid: The Stock Companies made me reconsider the relationship between an expansion and its base game.

The Stock Companies expansion changes the classic structure of this old game—not in the inconsequential way of earlier map expansions, but by changing its objective. It retains the core play while shifting the focus toward stocks. It adds three variants, all involving stocks. They cannot compare with the many heavier railway-and-stock games, of course, but they play briskly and satisfyingly. Most importantly, they reduce the headache-inducing exact calculation, preserve interaction on the map, and introduce competition over companies. You can even win without operating a company yourself. (What I will not tell you is that the real reason this game addicted me is my perfect four-for-four record, hahaha.)

Best of the Year — Great Western Trail!

Great Western Trail looks like a railway game, but players are cowboys driving cattle, so we affectionately call it “Driving the Big Cattle.” If I could recommend only one new game from 2016, this would be it. The flow is simple, but the variations and scoring paths are numerous. That alone would not make it stand out amid the recent Eurogame trend toward multiple point-scoring routes—think of WYG’s games, Mombasa, and so on.

What made me immediately declare it the year’s best on my very first play? Simple: in Great Western Trail, the players completely control the game’s rhythm. Most board games use a fixed number of rounds. Some have no fixed round count and instead use an end-game trigger, but the number of player turns is effectively fixed. In Great Western Trail, players control the speed at which they enter Kansas City and thus determine their own number of turns, while the frequency with which everyone reaches Kansas City collectively determines the game’s pace. Its elements are also tightly integrated—the previous game that gave me this feeling was Nippon, though that has severe balance problems. Players feel great freedom of action, yet interaction remains strong. It provided my best play experience of the year, making it my 2016 game of the year.

Other Recommendations

  1. Among Nobles
  2. Railroad Revolution
  3. Mombasa
  4. Stronghold, Second Edition
  5. A Feast for Odin
  6. Alchemists + expansion

entry.title: [A Life in Board Games] Episode 7: The Art and Way of Agricola
entry.content:
The Trough of Fatigue

Time is always the greatest enemy. No matter how deeply we once loved something, we have to admit that fatigue eventually arrives. What reaches an extreme must reverse; what flourishes must decline. In one sense, my love for something feels a little like this technology maturity curve.

As time passes, a board gamer’s enthusiasm for the hobby follows roughly the same curve. At first, everything looks fresh and the newcomer frantically chases new releases. Then passion gradually cools. Current designs begin to reveal familiar patterns, and every new game recalls some old classic. A trough follows, when fewer and fewer games seem genuinely fun. Yet only after passing through that process and washing away the glitter is a player willing to look back at older games: classics that were never explored deeply during the frantic pursuit of novelty—such as Agricola. So today, let us properly discuss this former titan of the board-game world.

Agricola is a standard Eurogame that demands both short-term decisions and long-term strategy, and it excels at both. As in every traditional abstract strategy game, the outcome is theoretically determined from the beginning; there are simply too many game states for even a computer to calculate every decision. That does not prevent generation after generation of masters from continuing to explore their craft—although AlphaGo recently dealt humanity a heavy blow. Agricola is not a traditional abstract game. It contains randomness and hidden information, but limits both so that replayability increases without allowing the system to escape control. One might say it preserves the soul of the Eurogame as fully as possible.

Three Levels of Understanding

Since the end of the year before last, I have been playing Agricola on iOS with Xiaoda, Boss Wen, experts from the Agricola group, and random opponents. By now, I have played nearly two hundred games, most of them extremely slow asynchronous sessions with a one-week limit. Combined with earlier face-to-face play at university, my understanding of the game has passed through three levels.

  1. Seeing water as water, and water as water
    This stage covers roughly the first twenty to thirty games. It is easy to fall into fixed patterns and believe you have grasped the rhythm, only to discover quickly that the strategy is flawed. You are not yet familiar with the cards, so your judgment of their strength usually rests on limited personal experience or guides written on some website. Even when you win at this stage, your score is rarely high—perhaps just over forty. If your routine is blocked, you may score only in the twenties.
    Incidentally, Agricola’s essence lies in the standard four-player game. Two- and three-player Agricola are different games, and many cards perform poorly with fewer players, producing a weaker experience. Overall, however, Agricola still balances player counts better than many modern designs.
  2. Seeing mountains not as mountains, and water not as water
    Depending on a person’s insight, this stage may last about fifty games. If you regularly face experts such as Teacher koko, perhaps ten games are enough to make a breakthrough. Based on my own limited experience, I would not dare claim that I have completely passed this second level.
    Here, players gradually recognize the limits of their own understanding, usually through defeat after defeat. Strategies that once seemed powerful lose their shine, while cards you considered useless appear formidable in somebody else’s hands. After dozens of repetitions, you begin trying new approaches and boldly use cards you had never considered. Most of the time you still lose, of course, but once or twice you win and discover that your final score has reached a new height: more than fifty.
  3. Seeing mountains once more as mountains, and water as water
    After repeatedly trying new ideas, failing, and being proven wrong, you gradually recognize the game’s central idea: action efficiency. What determines your efficiency across an entire game is neither some supposed measure of card strength nor a fixed formula. It is the simplest, plainest quality, one that almost represents the soul of Eurogames: depth of thought.
    The Art of War says: those who win in the temple calculations before battle make many calculations; those who lose make few. Many calculations lead to victory, few to defeat—how much more certain is defeat with none at all. A player who reaches this level finds that even with the iOS edition’s limited card decks, EIKG, scoring fifty in a standard four-player game becomes relatively easy, though not every time; sixty may occasionally be broken. Most importantly, you know why you won and why you lost. That feeling is exceedingly rare. How many people go through life truly understanding how they live? As another saying has it: I searched for her a thousand times among the crowd; suddenly I turned, and there she stood where the lantern light was dim. Wang Guowei’s third realm resembles this in some respects.

Action Efficiency: The Way of the Farm

Let us examine the idea. What is action efficiency? Readers probably already have that question. Looking at Agricola globally, there are only two ways to earn a higher score: increase the number of your actions or improve their efficiency.

Beginners feel the importance of the first immediately when encountering a worker-placement game like Agricola. The mechanism explicitly tells players to grow their family and thereby gain more actions. This is why so much of Agricola’s banned-card list concerns family growth or room construction. Ignoring banned cards, growing your family one round earlier means gaining one additional action. In a standard four-player game, the last person to grow usually does so three rounds after the first. Statistics show that the first player to grow has a win rate as high as 40%, while each later player wins roughly 20% of the time. The first-family-growth player therefore seems to possess an enormous advantage, twice the win rate. Should everyone chase that position in every game? Clearly not. Even the leading player’s win rate remains below 50%, while all later positions are similar. There is also an intuitive demonstration: download the game and play against three Master-level AIs. They seem programmed always to build a room and grow first, going so far as to take a single reed. I trust that everyone can still defeat them easily.

In this extreme example, I defeated the computer with only two family members. Action efficiency is often the true key to victory.

Against human opponents, differences in action efficiency are not so enormous and usually appear in small details. The iOS game has an excellent log. At the end of a session, count how many inefficient actions you performed. An average game of Agricola provides about forty-two actions. A small shortfall in each accumulates across more than forty turns into a large divergence. How, then, do we increase efficiency? In one sentence: think more.

Returning to the extreme example above, I took only twenty-eight actions in the entire game, but synergies among occupations combined with the resources accumulated while the computers fought over family growth in the middle game made those actions effective.

Miscellaneous Notes

Note: this section exists only to keep the article from feeling too abstract. It will probably offer little value to the experts in our group. This resembles programming: simply reading without practicing accomplishes little. The Way described in the Tao Te Ching cannot be found inside the Tao Te Ching.

What Is Inefficient?

My list of inefficient actions includes:

  1. Using only half of any “and/or” or “and then/or” action—for example, taking Starting Player alone, sowing without baking bread, or renovating without playing an improvement
  2. Taking Day Laborer without a bonus
  3. Taking 4 or fewer clay
  4. Taking 2 or fewer reed, or reed you cannot use late in the game
  5. Taking RSF in the middle or late game
  6. Taking 3 or fewer wood
  7. Sowing fewer than two fields
  8. Taking grain or vegetables without a bonus
  9. Playing one improvement card
  10. Building only one room
  11. Taking 2 or fewer sheep, or 2 or fewer wild boars
  12. Fishing or Traveling Players for 5 or less food without a supporting ability
    Actions near the top are generally less efficient, but none of these rules is absolute. Occupations and improvements often transform an inefficient action into an efficient one. The one unshakably foolish move may be taking Starting Player with no other benefit.

How to Think

As noted earlier, the soul of a Eurogame lies in depth of thought. In Agricola, that can be divided into several key points:

  1. During the draft, fully consider turn order and the arrangement of your eight actions in the first period. Ensure that your cards cover the early, middle, and late game, ideally with strong individual cards at each stage rather than blindly chasing combinations.
  2. Before every action, consider whether your plan must change. When the plan requires many actions to complete, do not be tempted by an unrelated opportunity, such as taking six wood. Agricola is not a game in which you can decide one move at a time. Even in the first period, much must be planned.
  3. Build a food engine. The most direct way to improve action efficiency is usually to establish an effective food engine. Many kinds are effective and differ only slightly. You must still understand which are somewhat more efficient and which fit your plan.
  4. Act outside peak demand. When everyone fights over the first family growth, do something else, such as plowing or fencing. A good food engine can release its potential in the middle and late game.
  5. Calculate scores precisely after turn 12. Once the turn-12 action card is revealed, the game’s final random element disappears. Ignoring each player’s first picks during the card draft—usually strong occupations and minor improvements are played early rather than held this long—the final three rounds can theoretically be calculated completely.

Common Agricola Misconceptions

  1. You must secure the first family growth. Already discussed.
  2. Banned cards are overwhelmingly strong. Their power is not as great as imagined. Cards are often banned merely because they are annoying, such as Taster, or broadly useful, such as those related to family growth. Without improved action efficiency, one banned card offers little advantage. I have even seen a game where someone played Reed Hut in turn 3 and still finished last.
  3. A begging card means the game is over. Begging cards are certainly frustrating and are one reason many newcomers find Agricola unfriendly. But one or two are discouraging, not hopeless. I once believed otherwise until a game with Teacher koko. In turn 7, the other three of us blocked him and forced him to take two begging cards. He still finished second and lost by only a few points. Even now, I occasionally take one or two begging cards and can continue competing if I play well afterward. In a Eurogame, first place is not the only winner. The same is true in life.

    Please ignore the Bowl King who timed out.

    I lost this game but still decisively defeated banned-card king icanfarm.
  4. Plowing and fencing early lose tempo. Plowing has the same effect early or late. In most games, the first period contains enough spare actions for one plow, and even in the worst case it is no less useful than the inefficient actions above. Fencing requires an animal-breeding food engine and strong minor improvements to amplify its return, but can reverse the disadvantage of expanding your home late.
  5. Passive abilities trigger unreliably. Completely wrong! In most cases, cards saying “when another player does X, you may do Y” are good because they provide extra actions.
  6. Bonus-point cards are weak. Completely wrong! Agricola has a ceiling on ordinary scoring, and bonus cards raise that ceiling, though some also raise other players’ ceilings. In general, a bonus card that provides four wood and is completed produces three points. An average Agricola action comes nowhere near that return, even before counting the extra wood. All you need is one food to play the occupation and advance planning.
  7. Avoid improvements that require played occupations or improvements. Completely wrong! Such cards usually offer very high returns. The designer uses their restrictions merely to delay when they enter play, but designers never defeat the players. With proper planning, a fully utilized stable, mine, or similar occupation can generate value equal to several actions.

Afterword

I originally intended to write only some Agricola tips—the miscellaneous section. As I wrote, however, they kept connecting with my recent work and life, so I decided to add the article to the A Life in Board Games series. In truth, I merely wanted to show off without making it obvious.

My GopherChina 2020 Review
entry.content:
If you are a new gopher, I strongly recommend watching Go Programming Patterns. This conference featured many talks about frameworks. Of those, go-zero felt the most complete and the easiest for a small company or individual to adopt, and its author was passionate. I also recommend the talks on the Go compiler, the issues TiDB encountered, and Tantan. The weakest was a foreign speaker’s Go in the Cloud — Why People Choose Go for Cloud Computing…

The second day split into two tracks, so one person could hear only some of the talks. I bounced repeatedly between rooms 1 and 2 and selected a few. Unfortunately, I missed Alibaba’s EDAS talk, which was reportedly quite good.

The conference slides are available in this Git repository.

I unexpectedly ran into a former colleague at the venue—amazing. I was not certain at first because of the mask; only after sitting down and messaging on WeChat did we confirm it.

  1. Tantan ttdb
    Tantan, a co-organizer of the conference, is a social app for young people—though its promotional video at the venue seemed to include users in their sixties. Suppose you had to design a system that scanned the geographic paths of two people and matched those who had passed one another. How would you do it?
    They shared practical lessons from their own database:

    • SQL parsing optimizations such as predicate pushdown
    • Columnar storage, using cache coherence during the selection stage to improve performance
    • For failure detection, they chose centralized timeout detection instead of decentralized gossip. During recovery, rather than directing all traffic to a new replica and creating a spike, they occasionally send requests to replicas to keep data hot.
    • They use this library to detect goroutine leaks.

  2. Go Programming Patterns
    The talk covers small techniques we commonly use in ordinary code as well as ideas such as inversion of control. I especially recommend it to anyone new to Golang. Pay close attention to the idea of studying open-source code to learn good programming patterns. The author apparently knows the characteristics of many languages and therefore has plenty of complaints about Golang too.

    • Functional options: probably the most widely used pattern; virtually every major open-source project uses it. It elegantly distinguishes optional and required parameters, preserves internal encapsulation, makes calls self-documenting, and solves several related problems.
    • Go generation: because the language did not support generics—at least before 2021—using go generation well was often essential.
    • Error handling: the speaker mentioned an ancient Rob Pike article worth reading, though I am not sure which one. Go 1.13 added errors.Is and As to support error handling, while fmt.Errorf gained %w for wrapping errors.
    • For the Kubernetes visitor, decorators, pipelines, and so on, see the slides; the explanations there are clear.

  3. Grab Food
    Grab is another long-time GopherChina sponsor. It is a Southeast Asian behemoth that can be understood as Meituan + Alipay + Didi + Amap.
    The speakers first introduced Grab-Kit, their service framework. Like other frameworks, it supports middleware, validation, tracing, throttling, and so on, plus chaos for simulating failures—a chaos monkey?
    They then introduced Grab Food’s internal ML pipeline:

    1. Candidate set
    2. Filtering
    3. Reranking
    4. Post-ranking
      Citing a Google article, they listed current pain points in machine learning and explained how their Chimera system automates continuous integration, continuous training, and continuous delivery to achieve MLOps. They also mentioned using a multi-armed bandit A/B test to solve model-adaptation problems.

  4. go-chassis
    This was presented by someone from my company, so I will skip it.

  5. Functional Options and Config for APIs
    This talk overlapped with the second one above. Just watch that instead.

  6. Baidu BFE
    This speaker’s talk was not primarily technical, so I left after listening briefly. It discussed some aspects of technical management.

  7. go-zero
    Another framework talk, but this speaker was interesting. He said that although he was born in the 1970s, he still wrote code tirelessly. go-zero evolved through use inside his company, unlike some frameworks that may have been produced without a concrete business context. From the talk, go-zero’s functionality seemed very complete. It genuinely provides a one-stop solution to boilerplate development code. The speaker began by saying that he wanted his team’s style to be as consistent as possible, which was why the framework exists. Beyond go-zero itself, several solutions drawn from his product left a strong impression:

    • Program for failure.
    • Do not join!
    • Design caches correctly to prevent penetration, breakdown, and avalanche.
    • For load balancing, he mentioned the Power of Two Choices algorithm. It maximizes locality while dynamically avoiding excessive processing times on nearby services. These two articles—1 and 2—deserve careful study.
    • Adaptive circuit breaking: they abandoned Netflix’s Hystrix and introduced the Google SRE algorithm they use, including support for custom trigger conditions.
    • Adaptive load shedding.

  8. Go+
    Since its evangelist, Xu Shiwei, did not attend, a substitute presented at short notice and the result was poor. Despite piling up slides, the talk failed to explain why Go+ needed to replace Python for data science. Go+ can run by translating into Go and compiling, or by translating into bytecode and executing directly with somewhat lower performance. The latter feels pointless—why not use Python directly? It also did not support interfaces at the time and lacked runtime optimizations.

  9. PingCAP — Go Runtime-Related Problems in the TiDB Production Environment
    We had encountered the issues mentioned in this talk at work as well. The speaker is the author of Golang Internals.
    The first issue was higher latency caused by Golang’s goroutine scheduling. I do not really consider that a problem, or rather, that is simply how Golang’s goroutine scheduler is implemented. Unlike other languages, Golang supports coroutines natively and thereby commits to its implementation. Many other languages implement coroutines through libraries, allowing the scheduler implementation to be replaced according to need. Therefore, solving scheduling problems in Go may require pinning high-priority work to CPU cores.
    The third issue was a GC bug.
    The fourth concerned NUMA usage. The GC was not NUMA-aware and performed poorly on many-core systems after assist scanning was triggered during allocation. This has been optimized in current versions.

  10. Introduction to the Go Compiler — Shi Bin
    This speaker was truly hardcore: one of the fifty most prolific contributors to Golang, with commit access to Go’s Git repository and an annual invitation from the Go team to attend meetings in the United States.
    He explained that Go uses a self-hosted compiler rather than a general infrastructure such as LLVM. Many optimizations implemented in LLVM are therefore absent from the Golang compiler and must be added separately—perhaps that is where all your commits came from, master. There are 48 stages from Golang source to assembly; even three days would not have been enough for everything he could say. He ultimately selected several frontend, middle-end, and backend optimizations and explained his own patches, which was quite interesting.

  11. GORM Analysis and Best Practices
    This is probably the best Golang open-source project developed in China. Its author introduced the GORM 2.0 refactoring and design, along with some best practices. Interested readers can study it closely. I am not using it currently; once I do, I will return and review the talk.

entry.title: Dynamically Injecting Instances of Types from Go Plugins Through Reflection
entry.content:
Imagine a scenario in which we need to develop something together with another team but do not want to build from source. In other words, the final deployment should integrate a binary published by the other team.

There are two ways to solve this:

  • Define an inter-process API, build separate processes, and communicate across the process boundary.
  • Define an interface, have implementers compile a dynamic library, load it at runtime through some mechanism, and find a way to obtain an instance of the corresponding implementation.

Compiling a dynamic library is natural in C. In Go, however, it requires the plugin mechanism.

First, use go build -buildmode=plugin to compile code containing a main package into a dynamically linked library.

Note that plugin.Open does not execute the main package. It calls only the init functions of all packages.

p.Lookup("routerFactory") finds a global variable named routerFactory. We can require implementers to expose our interface through a fixed global variable, after which we only need to type-assert it to our own interface before making calls. Remember that only exported variable or function symbols can be found.

Suppose we want something more flexible: finding an unexported symbol, or reflecting an instance from a package name plus a type name—for example, because we need methods rather than a global function. What then?

It is time to deploy the time-honored technique of copying source code. Go’s reflect package contains this function, typesByString.

We can use go:linkname to link to the reflect package’s internal implementation, declaring only its signature. This requires importing unsafe.

For a complete implementation, we also need to copy several structures and methods from the source, such as the definition of type and the pkgpath() method. There is no need to copy everything; extract only the fragments that will actually be called.

Finally, wrap this questionable code in our internal package:

Only a single API needs to be exposed:

Let us test it:

It still fails to reflect the type correctly, reporting github.com/titanxxh/di/example/en, en.english not found in executable image. That is strange: I clearly imported the package anonymously.

After further investigation, I discovered that Go optimizes away unused types. We need a global variable that references our type so it remains in the binary:

At last, the program prints hello correctly.

Combine this with the plugin mechanism above and you have our example.

The project is available here. A star would be appreciated.

entry.title: Notes on Compression Algorithms
entry.content:
Know how to solve every problem that has been solved.

What I cannot create I do not understand.

–Richard P. Feynman

An internal competition at work forced me to learn several compression algorithms within a short time last month. I also implemented some of them, including lz77, deflate, bwt, and bcm. You never know until you practice: the moment you begin writing code, you discover that some things you thought you understood were never truly understood. I also recently watched a series of videos about the late physicist Richard Feynman. One detail left a deep impression. After his death, people found that he had preserved the two sentences above in the upper-left corner of his office blackboard, where they would not be erased accidentally.

From a young age, Feynman’s father taught him that knowing and understanding were two different things. He therefore retained the curiosity to think through every problem.
The two sentences express essentially the same idea: only when you can create something yourself do you truly understand it. Reaching that point requires knowing how every problem was actually solved, not merely remembering a conclusion. The highest level of understanding a concept is being able to teach it to somebody else.

Inspired by that idea, I wrote this article to record my recent exploration of compression algorithms.

First, an excellent survey website about compression is Data Compression Explained. It begins with the simplest algorithms and proceeds all the way to state-of-the-art compression. Its section Compression is an Artificial Intelligence Problem is particularly worth reading.

Second, kanzi-go is an open-source library implementing a remarkable number of compression algorithms. The original version was apparently written in Java; I do not know why the author rewrote the entire thing in Go.
The library’s greatest advantage is that it lets you combine arbitrary front-end transforms with back-end entropy coders and test how different combinations compress your files.

deflate = lz77 + Huffman coding

This is probably the simplest compression algorithm. Many languages include an implementation because it is fast and effective for text. On the data files used in our competition, deflate achieved a compression ratio of roughly 0.37.

The lz77 algorithm is very easy to explain: use the already encoded portion as a “dictionary” for encoding the content that follows.

Take mississippi as an example. Suppose we have already encoded miss. As we continue, we can use a pair (jumpBack, matchLen) to reduce repetition and compress the data. jumpBack tells us how many characters to move backward, while matchLen gives the number of characters to match.

At this point, for example, we could output (3, 3), because moving back three characters lets us match the three-character string iss. We could also output (3, 4), matching the four-character string issi. Notice that the final i of the earlier issi and the first i of the newly matched issi are actually the same character. This overlap is allowed.
The goal of lz77 is to make matchLen as large as possible, so the correct output here is (3, 4).

Very long continuous matches are generally unlikely. We can therefore limit maxMatchLen to 256, requiring one byte, and choose maxJumpBack according to our needs. If maxJumpBack occupies two bytes, the search for the longest match covers at most a range of 2^16 positions.

We then use three bytes to represent one pair. Clearly, replacing a match whose matchLen <= 3 is useless; retaining the original characters takes no more space. Implementations therefore usually search only for matches of length four or greater.

On the other hand, ordinary string matching across a 2^16-position range is very inefficient. We can cache the most recent positions of each four-character hash in a linked list. When searching for the longest match, calculate the current four-character hash and inspect the maintained list directly. This greatly improves search efficiency.

I will not introduce Huffman coding in detail. The basic idea is to count symbol frequencies and assign code lengths in descending order of frequency, ensuring that common symbols receive shorter codes.

All right! At that point, I began writing code because I believed I understood both algorithms. When the first implementation was complete, however, I could not achieve the same compression ratio as Go’s standard-library implementation no matter what I tried. My result was far higher than 0.37.

The principal problem was that when jumpBack, matchLen, and literal values—ordinary characters—were mixed together as input to Huffman coding, matchLen and jumpBack distorted the frequency statistics for literals. Their own frequency distributions also differed from those of literals.

Short matchLen values occur especially often, while longer ones become increasingly rare. Lengths 4, 5, 6, and 7, for example, occur much more often than 8 and 9.

jumpBack, by contrast, appears highly random because the range of 2^16 positions is enormous. Huffman coding offers little advantage for data with nearly uniform symbol frequencies.

I had not read the deflate RFC directly. I found the solutions only by comparing my work against the standard library, debugging and examining how it encoded matchLen and jumpBack, which wasted a great deal of time.

The deflate RFC clearly specifies variable-length encoding for matchLen and jumpBack. The matchLen range 4–258, for example, can be mapped to 0–31. Since lengths 4, 5, 6, and 7 occur most often, they may each occupy one value, such as 0, 1, 2, and 3. Values 8 and 9 can both map to 4, with one extraBit distinguishing between them.

After this kind of predetermined frequency-based encoding, a full eight bits are unnecessary for matchLen in most cases. The much larger jumpBack range is handled similarly: compress it to 0–255 and combine the code with extra bits.

To prevent matchLen and jumpBack from distorting literal frequencies during Huffman coding, we encode them separately. In practice, values 0–255 represent ASCII literals, 256 represents EOF and marks the end of the file, and 257–288 represent matchLen. We then calculate frequencies over the range 0–288.

During decoding, if a symbol falls between 257 and 288, subtract 256, use the resulting value to determine how many extra bits to read and recover the actual matchLen, then read the encoded jumpBack. This reconstructs the pair (jumpBack, matchLen), which allows decoding to continue.

With all of that in place, I finally achieved the same compression ratio as Go’s standard-library implementation.

Deflate has additional tricks for reducing output size. Compression generally proceeds block by block, and every block must begin with its own Huffman-code dictionary, which creates cumulative overhead. Canonical Huffman coding can reduce the size of that dictionary data further.

Arithmetic Coding

Clearly, an ancient compression algorithm such as deflate cannot compete with others on compression ratio, so we need to study more advanced algorithms.

In general, compression algorithms can be divided by principle into transforms and entropy coding. Most compression systems on the market combine several transform stages followed by one entropy stage. The kanzi-go library mentioned above lets you experiment with these combinations.

Lz77 is a transform; dictionaries, BWT, and other methods are also transforms.

Huffman coding, meanwhile, is an entropy-based compression algorithm. Its problem is that it cannot achieve the theoretical optimum of information theory.

Suppose we have a bit stream, streamA, in which the probability of 0 at every position is 0.99, and another, streamB, in which that probability is 0.51. Huffman coding constructs the same dictionary for both.

From the perspective of information theory, streamA clearly contains less information and should be easier to compress. Imagine the extreme case where the probability of 0 is 1. We could achieve an infinite compression ratio because we would need to output only the length.

Arithmetic coding solves this problem elegantly. It maps the input to a subinterval between 0 and 1. For each encoded bit, it narrows the current interval according to the bit’s value and probability. Once every bit has been encoded, a very small interval remains. In fact, any number within that interval can serve as the final encoded result.

Decoding reverses the process and restores the input one bit at a time.

Because arithmetic coding can achieve the theoretically optimal compression ratio, almost every state-of-the-art compressor uses it in the final entropy stage.

State-of-the-Art Compression Algorithms

Arithmetic coding itself is not complicated, but estimating probabilities well is extremely complex. In theory, the more accurately you can use existing content to estimate the probability of what follows, the higher the compression ratio. Dynamically adjusting probabilities also improves online compression.

This is the purpose of modeling. Different input sources require different models; an image, for example, needs a two-dimensional model.

The newest compression algorithms often use more complex modeling methods, including machine-learning models from PAQ8 onward and even mixtures of several modeling approaches. That is another complicated subject, and I did not have enough time to understand every model in PAQ. We ultimately chose the Burrows–Wheeler Transform—another classic example of an idea that is easy to understand but difficult to implement—followed by arithmetic coding with a mixed model considering only order 0, order 1, and whether the previous two characters match. If you are interested, the website above provides some simple introductions.

One final complaint: information about compression is genuinely scarce. Search after search eventually led me to a Russian forum, where experts of every kind publish their code. One cannot help admiring the strength of the Russians’ mathematical foundations.

entry.title: Injecting Time-Shift Faults into Go Programs
entry.content:
When testing, we often need to manipulate a program’s clock or timers. Different languages implement time retrieval and timers differently. After searching online, I found that Chaos Mesh provides a way to inject faults into Golang and Rust programs.

To inject a time shift into a particular process, we first need to understand how that process obtains the time. In a Golang program, calling time.Now() actually uses the vDSO (virtual dynamic shared object) mechanism. The vDSO accelerates system calls such as gettimeofday and clock_gettime. Both Golang’s time.Now() and the heap maintained by its timer implementation use clock_gettime.

Once we know which function is called, the next problem is modifying it. Chaos Mesh uses ptrace to modify the target process’s memory and redirect clock_gettime to its own implementation.

Chaos Mesh also provides a wrapper for testing called watchmaker. It can be run directly; simply provide a PID and an offset to complete the injection.

The main function is func ModifyTime(pid int, deltaSec int64, deltaNsec int64, clockIdsMask uint64) error.

The overall process is:

  1. Call runtime.LockOSThread() to bind the current goroutine to a Linux thread. My guess is that this prevents the goroutine from being switched away and invalidating ptrace.
  2. Use ptrace.Trace(pid) to attach to the PID. Obtain every thread in the process through /proc/pid/task, use the PtraceAttach syscall to attach to each TID, and read the process’s virtual-memory mapping from /proc/pid/maps.
  3. Search for the [vdso] keyword to find the starting address of the vDSO entry.
  4. Prepare a fakeImage containing the redirect implementation, with the final 24 bytes holding the three parameters. This part involves assembly; I did not study the fakeImage implementation closely.
  5. Check whether this process has previously received our fakeImage. If not, use mmap to map a new fakeImage; otherwise, locate the previous entry. Rewrite its final 24 bytes with the parameters for the current configuration.
  6. Find the original address of clock_gettime in the vDSO entry. This requires Golang’s debug/elf package to locate the corresponding symbol address.
  7. Rewrite the jump for clock_gettime in the vDSO entry.

We can write a program to test the effect:

For easier observation, start two test processes simultaneously, one with an argument and one without:

./test & ./test x &

During normal operation, the output looks like this:

After waiting for process 99334’s timer to expire once, immediately use watchmaker to inject a 30-second shift:

sudo ./bin/watchmaker -pid 99334 -sec_delta 30 -nsec_delta 0 -clk_ids "CLOCK_REALTIME,CLOCK_MONOTONIC"

If we only want to affect time.Now() in the process, changing CLOCK_REALTIME is enough. Here, however, we also need to affect timer expiration. According to Golang’s timer implementation, the timer data structure reads time with runtime·nanotime1, whose assembly implementation uses CLOCK_MONOTONIC. The clock IDs we modify must therefore include both CLOCK_REALTIME and CLOCK_MONOTONIC.

The program outputs:

This also shows that even an ordinary Go program starts many threads…

Returning to our test process, its output has changed to this:

When Golang’s default time data structure is printed, the number after m=+ is the monotonic time since the process started. Here, process 99334’s monotonic time suddenly jumps from 38 to 68, immediately triggering the second timeout.

We have now completed the injection of a time shift into a Golang process. Go test your production code for problems. According to the Chaos Mesh team’s presentation, many open-source projects have issues of varying severity.

entry.title: Little World, Big World
entry.content:
Epigraph: a child’s big world may be only a little world to an adult, but I hope every adult can find joy inside it and be happy together with the child.

Before You Were Born

He and she had just returned from their long honeymoon and were happily planning future journeys to see the wonders of the world, as though the whole globe lay beneath their feet. Not long afterward, she became pregnant. At that moment, he did not understand what awaited him, because he had almost no memories of his own childhood. Perhaps welcoming a little life would not change his own very much, he thought hopefully.

She had no particularly severe reactions during pregnancy, and every prenatal examination was normal. Perhaps you were one of those angel babies displayed on Xiaohongshu. They continued eating, drinking, and going out much as before, even traveling with her large belly and visiting Faxi Temple to make a wish.

Yet the world does not always move as he wishes. He did not know that over the next few days his world would change completely, its boundaries contracting to a tiny hospital room where day and night became indistinguishable.

Everyone had expected the due date to be delayed, but ruptured membranes meant she had to enter the delivery room early. He paced anxiously outside. The number of husbands waiting there fell from more than a dozen to several and finally to him alone. Night had deepened when someone suddenly told him that an emergency cesarean was necessary. Still dazed, he remembered only a few keywords from everything the doctor said, then signed his name with a trembling hand and watched the little window close. He hurried to the operating room and stared at the sole name on the display. He tried opening a wiki to search for information and calm himself, but failed. Tears finally escaped beyond restraint. The operation was actually quick, but to him it felt exceptionally long. Only when a nurse appeared at the window and told him that mother and child were both fine did he exhale. Yes: he had become a father.

The First Five Days

Dad stayed awake to monitor whether Mom’s IV had finished and kept waiting until after six in the morning, when your observation finally ended and you were brought to her. He stared at your tiny face for a long time and genuinely could not find a single feature resembling his own. Only many days later, after returning home and comparing your face with photographs of himself as a newborn, did he understand what an uncanny resemblance meant.

To be honest, you looked a little ugly immediately after birth. But all the nurses said you were impressive. You could cry real tears from the moment you arrived and were exceptionally good at drinking milk. Lying against Mom, you quickly learned the trick without hurting her. Everyone says that newborns lose weight during their first few days, but yours had already stopped falling on the second day. Amazing!

Because of the pandemic, only one family member could accompany Mom and that person could not be replaced. Dad remembers squeezing sleep into every available gap during those days and at one point feeling almost neurasthenic. Yet on the day of discharge, he became excited instead. Watching you wrapped little by little in a tiny blanket, then carrying you through the hospital doors, Dad felt that he might someday become the person you relied upon most after Mom.

The First Three Months

Science still had to be trusted: such a tiny baby did not recognize people at all. During your first two months, your world was confined to the crib and the thirty centimeters within your vision. Mom, Grandma, and the maternity nanny were the people nearest to you. Dad quickly fell out of the rankings.

At three months, your active nature gradually revealed itself. You lifted your head and rolled over ahead of other babies. A crib could no longer satisfy your world, and wherever you were, you seemed eager to try moving. You were still tiny enough for Dad to place you on his thighs and guide your limbs through passive exercises. You responded with a barbell-like laugh and the simplest interaction. Since your hair had been shaved, from certain angles you looked exactly as Dad had in childhood—so much so that he posted the comparison on Instagram.

Looking back over those first hundred days, Dad found everything about you wonderful. Only one problem kept you from becoming one of the angel babies on Xiaohongshu: you were a terrible sleeper. Dad seems to have successfully put you to sleep only once, but you slept so well that time that he excitedly announced the achievement to everyone. Babies at this age cannot avoid feeding at night and generally sleep poorly, so Mom and Dad did not yet consider it a serious problem.

Before You Could Walk

Your advanced gross-motor development soon let you crawl forward, so Mom built you a little realm of your own. Dad, however, only wanted to sing: “Youzi, Youzi, you are extraordinary. A little playpen cannot hold you; crawl out and become an athlete.” From the beginning, you wanted to escape. We still remember your first attempt. Your short arms and legs hung in the air before you landed face-first, completing a thoroughly undignified jailbreak. Grandma simply watched from beside you—and even filmed it.

To make your little world inside the playpen more entertaining, Dad began teaching you how to use toys. You never grasped what adults considered the important part, so Dad started finding his own entertainment. With a ring-stacking toy, for example, he taught sorting algorithms to a baby who did not even understand relative size. You nevertheless appeared to listen very seriously. Who knows whether you will retrieve any of this knowledge from the depths of memory when you grow up?

By then, you could say “Dad” and “Mom” without conscious intention, but what you loved most was imitating random sounds. Whenever Mom and Dad taught you something, you learned their onomatopoeia fastest. At first, Mom did not know where that trait came from. Later, your great-aunts visited, demonstrated their own vocal sound effects, and revealed it as a traditional talent of the Xu family.

As during your first three months, you remained a terrible sleeper. Mom and Dad were both experts at sleep and could not understand why, so Dad entered a period of anxiety—mostly expressed aloud. He spent every day saying, “You still cannot sleep through the night. What are we going to do?” Then during the National Day holiday, you suddenly slept through several nights. Dad thought you had finally awakened to the idea and prepared to celebrate, only to discover that it had been an accident. From then on, he completely accepted the truth. If you were a bad sleeper, so be it. Do whatever you want.

Learning to Walk

Because the crawling mat had a fence, at a little over eight months you could pull yourself upright against it. The adults then gave you objects requiring both hands, causing you to release the fence unconsciously. Gradually, you learned to stand independently. You already moved very quickly while holding the fence and could circle the playpen within seconds. Dad’s long observation showed that your legs were strong enough, while Grandpa exclaimed at the force of your little feet, far surpassing the limp children we encountered outside. Everything suggested that you possessed all the prerequisites for independent walking. Inside the playpen, Dad would move quickly from one corner to the opposite one, using your desire to reach him as walking practice. At first, you took only one or two steps before recognizing the danger and grabbing the nearest fence. Dad moved to another corner, and you tried again. Within two days, you could cross almost the full diagonal. Greed spoiled only the final few steps: instead of walking them, you threw yourself directly into Dad’s arms.

Even before you learned to walk, the tiny fenced world could no longer satisfy your desire to explore. Afterward, you raced throughout the home. Grandpa followed constantly, afraid that you would fall, but you were actually very steady. The little anti-fall backpack we bought was used only a few times because you could walk perfectly well. Looking back, Mom and Dad seem never to have told you to walk slowly while you were learning. Perhaps that is why you became bolder than children your age. “Trying to run before learning to walk” describes you exactly.

Playing “Together”

Children truly see the world differently from adults. Mom filled your little realm with all kinds of classic toys, but at first you never used them as adults expected and instead formed your own interpretations. So although we called it playing together, Dad often played by himself in your little world while you played by yourself beside him. Then, at some particular moment, you might notice that his activity looked interesting and come to interact.

Take the building blocks at home. At first, Dad tried to teach you how to build shapes. The moment he stacked one or two pieces, you knocked them down. He eventually gave up and invented other games for himself. One time, he arranged blocks of different shapes in a single layer on the round lid of their container, trying to fit as many as possible by using space efficiently. You watched him rearrange existing blocks to make room for one more. When Dad began a second layer, you seemed to understand and joined in, performing the same process yourself.

Mom also bought you a “busy block.” Each of its six faces held a familiar object involving rotation, including a key in a lock, a fidget spinner, and a screw and nut. It was intended to keep you busy on planes and high-speed trains. But perhaps you could not understand the correct way to use the objects or why the consequences of those actions mattered. You applied only brute force, found no enjoyment, and defeated the keep-you-busy plan. Later, Dad played with the block himself. He tilted it so that the spinning fidget spinner struck the hanging key. You may have watched the key spring upward, fall, and be launched again and found it interesting. You began striking the spinner with your hand to keep it rotating. Once you understood rotation, you also learned that repeatedly hitting the nut with one hand made it climb the screw, while hitting it with the other made it descend.

Of course, there were even more toys that we could never teach you to use, such as the shape sorter we demonstrated for six months. Looking back now, perhaps Dad had never found the fun in it either.

Afterword

In the blink of an eye, this article was delayed until you were nearly eighteen months old, entirely because Dad was too lazy. Looking back over that journey, Dad has thought more deeply about what raising a new life means to a person. As he accompanied you, watched your world grow from small to large, and played “together” with you, Dad felt as though he too was growing beside you, rediscovering the joy of childhood—genuine joy.

Written as Dad’s Thirtieth Birthday Approaches

While Dad recently organized photographs of his and Mom’s childhoods, an amusing imagined conversation between father and daughter kept appearing in his mind.

After seeing a childhood picture of Dad, his daughter curiously asks for the little boy’s story. Dad might tell it like this:

“There was once a little boy. In primary school, his world was a tiny football field, and even heatstroke could not stop him from sweating beneath the sun. The year 2002 gave him his perfect football memory: China reached the World Cup for the first time, Brazil completed seven victorious matches, and Ronaldo returned as king with eight goals and the Golden Boot.
