“In middle school, he moved to a large city. Algorithm problems on a small screen became another interest. Even when failure to solve one meant punishment laps, he happily remained in the computer room solving problems on the online judge. He now made his own decisions and actively explored the larger world beyond his textbooks.

“Later, he entered university, where every kind of board game became his new passion. He left behind the lonely little world of video games played alone. In Reiner Knizia’s auction games, he could experience schemes and intrigue; on Uwe Rosenberg’s farm, he could score points while going hungry. He could deceive rivals and rule from the Iron Throne in A Game of Thrones, or manage railway routes while manipulating company share prices and experiencing the rises and falls of commerce in a train game.

“Then he met the love of his life. His favorite thing became doing everything with her: plays, musicals, art exhibitions, making pottery, and traveling—riding the Star Ferry in Hong Kong, getting soaked together on campus during the World Cup final, and taking an extraordinarily long honeymoon across Iberia.”

“And then what happened?”

What happened next returns us to the beginning of this article.

entry.title: From Boy to Father, in Just a Few World Cups
entry.content:
Childhood

I was a late-blooming boy, and my memories from before middle school are hazy. Moving to Shanghai for middle school in 2002 made the divide from my childhood feel even sharper. Yet one thread has remained crystal clear from beginning to end: football.

I was in primary school when enthusiasm for football in China was at its height. After class, my friends and I headed straight to the pitch. My mother enrolled me in football lessons, and even after getting heatstroke I still insisted on going. I repeatedly scraped my knees until the wounds became infected, but I kept playing. I was hopeless at Chinese class, yet I once played football alone at home and wrote a little story about a match between my left foot and my right. It was even published in a newspaper.

The 2002 World Cup in Korea and Japan was the first World Cup I remember. China had reached the finals for the first time, and schools suspended classes so everyone could watch. We all know what happened afterward: what I thought was the beginning of a glorious era for China turned out to be its peak.

That was also when I found my national team—Brazil. The three Rs were unstoppable, and Brazil won all seven matches to claim its fifth title. It is no exaggeration to say that the city was awash with yellow No. 9 shirts—quite literally. Ronaldo won everyone over. Even today, he remains the only football star I have ever truly followed.

After moving to Shanghai, I suddenly lost the environment in which I had played: none of my new classmates played football. I was still at school and rarely had a chance to watch television, so I followed the game through Soccer Weekly and programs such as Football Night and Total Soccer. In today’s language, I gradually became an armchair fan.

Back in 2002, I had been a child in a small city with very few sources of information and knew little about the players. The magazines and television programs opened up a much wider football world. I learned about Ronaldo’s extraordinary story—how repeated, devastating injuries had kept him out of almost every match in the preceding years; how few people fancied Brazil before the tournament; and how almost nobody expected him to score eight goals at a single World Cup.

The 2006 World Cup in Germany arrived just after my high-school entrance exams, so I could watch without restraint. Brazil’s squad looked invincible: the magical quartet of Ronaldo, Ronaldinho, Kaká and Adriano, backed by recent Copa América and Confederations Cup triumphs. Everyone expected Brazil to reach a fourth consecutive World Cup final, lift the trophy for a sixth time, and put Ronaldo alongside Pelé.

Instead, Brazil fell to France once again. I still remember sitting alone in my small room, miserable for a long time. It was the first—and only—time football made me cry. What I could not have imagined was that the match would also be Ronaldo’s last for Brazil.

As Ronaldo put on weight, his career entered an irreversible decline. People lamented the collective early decline of Brazil’s gifted generation and condemned the players for their lack of discipline. I was a hot-blooded teenager and, like plenty of kids today, loved arguing with strangers on Tieba. I would not admit it aloud, but the truth was unavoidable: Brazil was producing fewer and fewer exceptional players. The center of world football had shifted decisively to Europe, the Champions League mattered more than ever, and every player was expected to adopt a European way of playing.

University

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, Brazil’s centerpiece was Kaká, whose style was thoroughly European, while the manager was the stubborn Dunga. Dunga had led Brazil to the Confederations Cup the year before. I still remember how thrilled I was when Brazil came back from two goals down to score three in the final. Overall, though, Dunga’s relentlessly pragmatic football was difficult to love. He also left Neymar—already famous in Brazil—out of the squad, for which I cursed him in my head ten thousand times.

This team, caught awkwardly between Brazilian and European football, also went out in the quarterfinals. As four years earlier, the match made no sense. Brazil dominated the Netherlands in the first half, and Felipe Melo produced a sublime through ball for the opening goal. In the second half he became the villain: an own goal and a goal from a corner sent Brazil home, and Dunga was dismissed soon afterward.

Dunga’s stubborn team selection denied young players enough opportunities to develop, helping create a long talent drought in Brazilian football. Brazil lost to Paraguay at the first knockout hurdle of the 2011 Copa América and sank to its lowest point, but after years of watching football I could accept it calmly.

By the 2013 Confederations Cup, Brazil qualified only as the host, and even I had little confidence that this young Seleção could win. Once again, the team proved me spectacularly wrong. In hindsight, however, the 3–0 demolition of a declining Spain in the final may only have reinforced returning manager Luiz Felipe Scolari’s faith in an outdated tactical system.

University gave me more freedom, so this was the period when I watched the most football. The head-to-head brilliance of Messi and Ronaldo was compelling, of course. Yet perhaps because I supported Brazil, the more matches I watched, the harder it became to recover my old excitement.

Then Neymar arrived in Europe. His unmistakably Brazilian style was exhilarating: he dared to try things on the pitch, even if that naturally earned him plenty of “special attention” from defenders. Europeans did not necessarily appreciate that style, but so what? Is that not precisely what Brazil supporters come to see?

The university network made PT downloads extremely fast. I joined one tracker after another and gradually began collecting recordings of Brazil matches from years gone by. By the eve of the 2014 World Cup, I had found recordings of almost every Brazil match at every major tournament since the 1994 World Cup. Most people on the Brazil supporters’ forum probably downloaded something I shared.

At the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, every Brazil supporter was eager to see how Neymar would perform in his first World Cup. To be honest, my expectations were modest. Then he scored four goals in the group stage, and Brazil even made it past the quarterfinals.

Neymar and captain Thiago Silva were both unavailable for the semifinal against Germany, but I still thought Brazil had a chance if they played conservatively. By the time it was 5–0 in the first half, I was so angry that I slammed the table and injured my little finger. It took me a long time to recover from that match. I stopped collecting match recordings too.

Once I began working, my free time shrank dramatically and I had to pare down my hobbies. Staying up at night for football was an extravagant one, especially with the ungodly kickoff times in La Liga and the Champions League. I could manage a few Premier League matches or find a replay the following day.

I watched quite a few of the dozen or so matches in which Neymar led Barcelona while Messi was injured. He looked destined for greatness, equally capable with or without the ball. Sadly, Neymar’s most dazzling peak never coincided with the best version of Brazil. After six matches in South American qualifying for the 2018 World Cup, Brazil had played dreadful football and, if I remember correctly, won only once. Fortunately, Tite took charge, produced a long winning streak, and secured qualification early.

Working Life

The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the closest I have ever come to the tournament: I was there in person, together with the person I love most. (See my 2018 World Cup in Russia vlog.)

The moment FIFA opened ticket sales—before the group draw had even taken place—I blindly bought a semifinal ticket. Rationally, I chose the wrong half of the bracket: the host was fixed as A1, so the probability of another seeded team landing in the same half was only 3/8. I later secured a ticket to the third-place match as well and arranged a long holiday far in advance. When the draw was finally made, my semifinal turned out to be in Brazil’s half of the bracket. I was ecstatic.

I had already put on my Brazil shirt before boarding the flight to Russia. Then Brazil were eliminated almost as soon as I landed. My phone did not even have a signal when the young man behind me announced that Belgium had knocked Brazil out. I was devastated; Russia would simply have to become a holiday.

To be fair, Russia’s combination of ruggedness and delicacy was captivating, and prices were low. It was well worth visiting. For the World Cup final, we walked an extraordinarily long way to reach the Fan Fest at Moscow State University. Packed shoulder to shoulder in the square with a crowd of strongly scented European gentlemen, we watched the entire match. All I remember is that the instant the final ended, the heavens opened. The resulting aroma was truly unforgettable.

Becoming a Father

The year 2020 carried a special significance. The beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic transformed everyone’s life, while the birth of Molly—our little Youzi—made me a father. Nobody could have foreseen the timeline the world would enter after 2020. Looking back, I feel fortunate that my wife and I visited Russia in 2018, followed by Spain and Portugal in 2019.

After Molly arrived, Dad’s free time dropped all the way to zero. In that case, I decided to hand my unfinished football career over to her. We gave her a ball to play with when she was tiny. Her gross motor development was well ahead of schedule, and she learned to walk, run and kick a ball very early. A broad lawn downstairs gave us the perfect place to run around. Whenever her mother saw other little girls playing on the grass in dresses, she would tease us for raising ours like a boy.

Shanghai spent several months under lockdown in 2022. If we could not travel to Qatar, we would watch from home—but we still had to create a proper World Cup atmosphere. I ordered Brazil’s new 2022–23 shirt and the children’s version from Nike well in advance. I have to say, a whole family walking down the street in matching Brazil shirts looks exceptionally cool.

In twenty years, Brazil fell from its pedestal, dropped out of the world’s top ten at its lowest point, rose again, and returned to No. 1.

In twenty years, one generation’s footballing idol retired, while the Brazilian children who grew up watching him became idols to a new generation of Brazil players.

In twenty years, the little boy who played football on muddy ground every day became a father running across the grass with a little girl.

Looking back, twenty years amount to only five World Cups. As long as the passion for the game remains, so does the little boy within.

entry.title: 7 Wonders Duel with All Expansions: Embracing Uncertainty
entry.content:
Introduction

The Lord of the Rings: Duel for Middle-earth was released recently. After trying it a few times, I felt that it lacked a little of its predecessor’s flavor. It may be more suitable for playing with children: every missing resource costs only one coin, reducing the arithmetic.

So instead of chasing the trend and recommending Duel for Middle-earth, I still prefer its predecessor and what I consider the best light strategy game for two players: 7 Wonders Duel, with both expansions.

That is not merely my personal enthusiasm. If BGG’s rankings are filtered to two-player games, the only title ahead of it is a former overall number one, Twilight Struggle.

Someone may ask whether discussing a game almost ten years after release is rather late. There is another important reason: I have recently played it constantly on Board Game Arena, and my Elo reached a new high of 652, number eleven in the world. I feel that my understanding has risen another level. I previously made several game-analysis videos on Bilibili, but looking back now, much of my thinking at the time was mistaken.

Only 7 Wonders Duel with Both Expansions Is the Real 7 Wonders Duel

Simply look at the empty slots left around the game board and you can tell that everything was designed together. The publisher shamelessly split it up for separate sale, the same drip-feed strategy as video-game DLC—though this particular drip tastes excellent.

In my view, adding both expansions transforms the original game completely. In the base game, any opponent with a little experience will usually drag the contest into final scoring, making the overall experience rather dry. To play well, you can do little beyond improving the precision of your calculations for a tiny advantage.

The first expansion, Pantheon, introduces gods in Age II. Gods bring many powerful effects, while players can partly control which gods will appear during Age I. This further increases the importance of planning in the first age and gives the game greater cohesion.

The second expansion, Agora, introduces the Senate and conspiracy systems. The Senate greatly increases the early value of blue cards and enriches the choices in Age I. Conspiracies add hidden information. Because some conspiracy cards are extremely powerful, using them well can accelerate a player’s path to victory dramatically. With a new win condition—political supremacy—many games no longer reach final scoring, and tension throughout play rises enormously.

For those reasons, many highly ranked Elo players use both expansions, and plenty, like me, play nothing else. I must complain briefly about BGA’s Arena design. Each season’s format is decided by the group that played the most during the previous season, so players who grind only Arena always vote for vanilla. I am not alone in criticizing this: the world’s top-ranked player, frankenstain, complains about it constantly too.

The expansions appear to increase randomness. Does that mean they reduce strategic depth? I do not believe so. Conspiracies decrease predictability and the value of exact calculation, but require players to understand the broader position more deeply. When behind, conspiracies provide chances to reverse the game. Put differently, a player who is ahead must know how to prevent an opponent’s conspiracy from stealing victory. Frankenstain’s record provides evidence: his win rate against nearly every other elite player is at least seventy percent.

What Are We Playing When We Play 7 Wonders Duel?

Everything below concerns games with both expansions.

The first task is understanding how the game is won. The rules provide four victory conditions: military, scientific, political, and civilian, meaning victory on points. Those conditions are not equally balanced. As BGA premium members, we can view everyone’s statistics:

frankenstain: political 28%, military 16%, scientific 11%, civilian 18%. The remaining percentage consists of losses.

Me: political 24%, military 12%, scientific 6%, civilian 20%.

Ninety percent of my 292 games used both expansions. Most of frankenstain’s probably did as well, though I am not certain.

Political victories occur most often, while final scoring is relatively uncommon. Our first conclusion is therefore that most games end early, and political supremacy is the easiest route.

This makes intuitive sense because the game’s victory paths are not orthogonal. Advancing the military track also supports the struggle for the Senate: military progress always contributes toward political victory, while political progress does not necessarily contribute toward military victory. Political victories are therefore most common. Political supremacy can even be achieved in Age I. Scientific supremacy, by contrast, is possible only in Age III, and military supremacy generally also requires the third age.

The routes to victory differ enormously. Because the starting wonders are drafted and each game’s setup changes, the two players may be trying to accomplish entirely different things. In that sense, this is fundamentally one of today’s popular asymmetric competitive games. Compared with rules that distinguish the two sides from the outset, 7 Wonders Duel’s approach feels more elegant.

Once this is understood, another common beginner’s error becomes clear: trying to take everything and ultimately failing on every front.

How Will I Win?

After understanding how the game can be won, the next task is identifying how you personally will win this particular game. Once you know that, you largely understand how you could lose too. The two are not perfectly symmetrical because conspiracy cards exist.

We need to understand the typical route for each victory condition:

  1. Political supremacy

Political supremacy requires you to outnumber your opponent in all six Senate chambers. In other words, you need at least six more influence cubes in total. Cubes come from many sources:

  • When you own two or four blue cards, every white Senate card you acquire places two or three cubes. If your opponent has only one blue card or none, they place only one, creating the difference: +1/+2/+3.
  • Controlling the blue +2 Senate chamber means your blue-card count is treated as two higher. In practice, each white card will usually place one additional cube: +1.
  • A black conspiracy card places one cube directly: +1.
  • One conspiracy places one of your cubes, removes one opposing cube, and moves one of yours: +2.
  • Advancing the military track lets you place a cube. Advancing again can remove an opposing cube and move one of yours: +1.
  • The god Neptune can remove one military penalty token and resolve its effect: +1.
  • Selecting the wonder Knossos lets you place one cube immediately; building it lets you place one and move another: +1 and +1.

Clearly, reaching six more cubes than the opponent is easy. Because many conspiracies also move a cube, rearranging your influence is not difficult.

A typical political route is therefore to build two blue cards early in Age I, then acquire two white cards and control four Senate chambers. With further help from the military track or Neptune, fill the remaining chambers.

Money is the most important resource for political supremacy. The worst possible situation is for an opponent to reveal a white card when you cannot afford it. Avoid that as much as possible. Some resource shortages can instead be covered through chamber effects.

Political supremacy can generally be achieved in Age II. Even when it is not, controlling more Senate chambers provides many bonuses and often yields a substantial advantage, especially after entering Age III with chambers that pay money for red, yellow, or blue cards.

  1. Military supremacy

Military supremacy requires pushing the conflict pawn all the way to the opponent’s capital—in other words, gaining nine more military strength than the opponent.

  • Red cards in the three ages provide different amounts of military strength: +1/+2/+3.
  • Mars provides two: +2.
  • One conspiracy provides two: +2.
  • One conspiracy lets you construct any one card from the three, six, or nine cards excluded from the game: +?.
  • The Strategy progress token adds one military strength whenever you acquire a red card.
  • One Senate chamber adds one military strength while you control it: +1.
  • Several wonders provide one; the Colossus provides two: +1/+2.

Because three-strength red cards appear only in Age III, military supremacy usually cannot happen before then without Strategy. Once Age III begins, controlling which player reveals cards becomes the most important factor. Effects that change the reveal order, such as extra turns or gods that let a player pass without taking an age card, are therefore among the most valuable resources.

A typical military route is to build two or three two-strength red cards in Age II, keep a military wonder or a two-strength conspiracy in reserve, and wait for a chained finishing blow in Age III.

Military buildings themselves provide no effects, so a purely military strategy is inferior to Senate development. Military progress does provide one or two advantages in the Senate, however, so it often begins as a by-product of pursuing political supremacy and converts into military victory later.

  1. Scientific supremacy

Scientific supremacy requires six different scientific symbols.

  • Remember that Law counts as a symbol and is available both on a god card and as a progress token. In practice, seven symbols exist and you need six. Because two kinds appear only in Age III, scientific victory cannot occur before the third age. You generally need four symbols by the end of Age II, and must be careful that the opponent does not bury crucial cards beneath a wonder or conspiracy.
  • Age I contains two science cards costing two coins that chain into Age II cards with the same symbols.
  • Nisaba can copy one of the opponent’s symbols, but naturally requires the opponent to possess one.
  • One conspiracy swaps one of your green or blue cards with one belonging to your opponent and can assemble the sixth symbol.
  • The Mausoleum wonder can recover a discarded card.
  • Hades can recover a discarded card.
  • One conspiracy lets you build any card from the three, six, or nine excluded from the game.

The scientific route has major problems. First, it is incompatible with the other victory conditions. High-level players rarely begin with scientific supremacy as their first priority. Second, the available progress tokens may not be powerful enough to justify science as a side benefit. Third, the route places heavy demands on Age I: you may need to construct one or two science cards immediately, creating considerable economic pressure. Finally, the reveal order in Age III may not favor you.

A typical scientific victory therefore begins by building one or two science cards in Age I while maintaining an acceptable economy, surviving the opponent’s pressure in Age II and using Law to reach five symbols, then waiting for a chained finish in Age III—often while already on the edge of defeat.

Scientific supremacy is usually a comeback mechanism in a disadvantaged game, not the primary strategy. It may also be worth considering when the five face-up progress tokens include something especially powerful, making two science cards attractive in Age I.

  1. Civilian victory

Because civilian victory is determined by points, Age III—with the highest-scoring cards—is crucial. Major sources include:

  • Athena: 9 points.
  • The Great Pyramid: 9 points.
  • Temple cards: one is worth 5, two 12, and three 21. BGA does not display these points in real time.
  • Blue cards in Age III.
  • Yellow cards in Age III: a base of 3 points plus some money.
  • A progress token worth 7 points.
  • The military track, worth 2–10 points.

Other points are easy to forget:

  • If Astarte’s coins remain unspent, the god is effectively worth 7 points.
  • Senate chambers. The two central chambers are worth 3 points each, so compete for them whenever you have movement abilities.
  • One conspiracy swaps a green or blue card between players. Exchanging a three-point blue card for a seven-point one creates an eight-point swing.

There is no single typical route to civilian victory. It normally becomes relevant when, at the end of Age II, a player predicts that neither side can win early. It appears more often in dry games or when both players follow balanced, conservative plans. Frequently one player pursues an alternate victory while the other must defend and score simultaneously.

From a scoring perspective, most Age III cards do not differ dramatically in strength. If each side can take one normally, the gap stays small. The real danger comes when Age III reveals an unhelpful black card, or a blue card that your broken resource chain makes unaffordable. If you can control the reveal order to avoid those situations and keep your resources intact, you gain a large third-age advantage.

After analyzing how you will win a particular game, one repeated keyword is impossible to miss: revealing cards.

Control over reveals is the most important element in the game. Skilled players treat every reveal with extreme caution. If the card turned face up is exactly the decisive card their opponent needs, the work of the entire game may be wasted.

Anything That Can Go Wrong Will Go Wrong

Imagine these situations:

  • You reveal a three-strength military card for the opponent, who follows it with a two-strength conspiracy plus another three strength and destroys you instantly.
  • You have controlled the opponent’s access to stone perfectly, then reveal an Age II yellow wild resource card that solves their emergency.
  • Your opponent has no wonder capable of granting an extra turn. You reveal a science card whose symbol they already own; they take the Theology progress token, and suddenly all their wonders grant extra turns.

After experiencing these scenes repeatedly, you overturn the table in fury and shout, “Trash game. Nothing but luck.”

If you have read this far, however, you know that poor luck alone cannot explain everything. Otherwise frankenstain could never have reached an Elo of 888.

Those reveal results are frustrating because the worst outcome among all possibilities occurred, moving the game completely toward the opponent and destroying your advantage. It is Murphy’s law: “Anything that can go wrong will go wrong.”

We will not debate the philosophy here. Within this game, when such situations keep occurring, ask:

  • Why is it your turn to reveal a card right now?
  • If a reveal is unavoidable, why choose this card rather than another?
  • If this particular card must be revealed, how many possible results can you accept and how many are intolerable?

The first question is the most important. People remember bad results but overlook basic facts:

  • Is it possible that you simply reveal more cards than your opponent during a game and therefore encounter more bad events?
  • When you reveal a card, it usually means no good face-up card remains. Where did the good cards go?
  • When you do not want to reveal a card, your opponent often does not want to either. Can you use some method to force them to reveal?

Once that logic is understood, it becomes clear why reveals are the game’s central concern. If we assume that a reveal is unavoidable, we must answer the second and third questions:

  • Will revealing this card reverse the order of later reveals?
  • Is the card beneath it face down or face up? Is it black or white, or an ordinary age card?
  • Could you reveal a card that kills you immediately?
  • Might the opponent be unable to afford the revealed card?

Success often hides in details. This reminds me of tennis great Roger Federer’s commencement address at Dartmouth College. Federer played 1,526 singles matches and won 82 percent of them. Yet measured point by point, he won only 54 percent. His original lesson was that once you understand that you lose nearly one point for every two you win, you learn not to torture yourself over every shot but to play the next point well.

Let us view the issue from another angle. If every point has only a 54 percent chance of being won, what is the probability of winning a match under tennis rules? It can be calculated recursively. I also found a website, Probability and Tennis, whose data show:

With a 54 percent chance of winning each point, the probability of winning the entire match is an astonishing 91 percent! So, Mr. Federer, what happened in those other nine percent of matches? The explanation is straightforward: tennis uses elimination tournaments, opponents become stronger in later rounds, and Federer’s point-winning probability there was surely below 54 percent, causing his match-winning probability to fall sharply.

Question Uncertainty → Understand Uncertainty → Embrace Uncertainty

Finally, I want to explain why I particularly love 7 Wonders Duel. As they grow older, every board gamer must face the inevitable decline in time and energy available for games. Board games require people around you, and the friends who once played beside you often confront the same problem, reducing your number of sessions even further. I call this the board-gaming world’s Davis double kill. Games with the lowest possible player count—two—naturally become the last refuge for middle-aged players like us.

Limited energy and time also mean that a complex, lengthy game is difficult to study deeply. I am not very satisfied with the growing trend toward “mechanism stew” in modern board-game design. I prefer games with simple mechanisms, easy entry, and enough randomness that a beginner’s wild punches can sometimes defeat an old master.

My view of board-game design did not begin this way. It traveled through a complete cycle. Borrowing today’s popular phrasing—question X, understand X, become X—we might say: question uncertainty, understand uncertainty, embrace uncertainty.

When I first discovered board games, my taste favored highly deterministic designs: Uwe Rosenberg’s Ora et Labora, with zero randomness; the worker-placement ancestor Caylus, also with zero randomness; or the three-versus-three mode of Legends of the Three Kingdoms. Such deterministic games gave me an illusion: when I won, it was because I anticipated the enemy and calculated everything; when I lost, it was because I failed to think far enough. In competitive sport, weakness is the original sin.

That attitude may be connected to meritocracy throughout childhood, or what could be called a student’s mindset. For a small-town test taker, the world one experiences for a long time is often a deterministic environment constructed by adults after external interference has been screened away.

As I played more games, I gradually realized that, just as in school, someone is always stronger. In classic abstract games, no amount of time may let you defeat a Go master. What is the point of a game you always lose? Slowly, I understood the need for randomness. Many games introduce uncertainty precisely so that newcomers can experience the joy of victory within their first few plays. It resembles encountering a good opportunity, the right person, or a rising era in life: the road becomes much smoother.

Randomness creates hope, but sometimes it also inflicts brutal misfortune. Lose several games in succession and you may still erupt: “Trash game. All luck.”

Later, my understanding of uncertainty changed again. Like 7 Wonders Duel, Agricola has always been one of my favorite games. Whether Family Growth appears in round five or seven has a decisive and completely random effect on the position. After enough games, however, you notice that experts manage randomness extraordinarily well. Every game somehow seems to follow their rhythm.

7 Wonders Duel gave me a similar experience. Its overall weight is slightly lower than Agricola’s and lands exactly in my sweet spot. Meanwhile, BGA dramatically increased the number of games I could play, accelerating improvement. I defeated players rated above 700 even when my own rating was still low. The experience of a weaker player overcoming a stronger one greatly increased my affection, and gradually it became my favorite two-player game.

At the end of this article, reading the guide probably will not grant you mastery of 7 Wonders Duel. I hope, at least, that when you face uncertainty in life—good or bad—you can meet it with a calm heart.

entry.title: [Open Agricola Development Diary] EP 1: Why Rebuild Agricola?
entry.content:
Agricola is more than a decade old. By today’s standards, it is not especially heavy. How hard could a complete digital version really be?

Its rulebook is not frighteningly thick. The trouble is that a lot of traps can fit inside one sentence. Take Hammer Crusher:

Immediately before you renovate to stone, you get 2 clay and 1 reed and you can take a “Build Rooms” action.

I glanced at that text and thought: what is so hard about this? Hand out the resources, let the player build, done. Once a program has to run it, the questions arrive immediately. Exactly when does it trigger? Can someone who cannot yet afford a stone renovation choose Renovation in the first place? How many more traps can you spot? I spotted none the first time. I will come back to them later.

This afternoon, I made the first commit to Open Agricola. Before I started, my thoughts kept returning to the card that had already caused me so much pain.

A Farm I Can Never Finish

I found Agricola soon after getting into board games. Back then it felt genuinely heavy: feed a family, grow crops and animals, and somehow turn a broken wooden hut into a respectable farm before fourteen rounds were over. It was unlike the games I had played before. The game might end at the table, but the replay in my head often ran for several more days.

From face-to-face games at university to nearly 200 slow matches on iOS, my score did rise, just never in a straight line. At first, even a win might score only a little over 40, while a disrupted plan could leave me in the twenties. Later I occasionally reached 50-plus or even broke 60, then got stuck somewhere new. In my 2017 essay, The Art and Way of Agricola, I described the process as three levels of understanding. By the end, I thought action efficiency mattered most. Even now, I do not feel that I have finished this game, much less understood it completely.

BGA Brought an Old Game Back to Life

In the iOS era, reliably gathering four players was difficult, and many matches crawled forward over an entire week. BGA made it much easier. Starting a farm no longer required calling for players in a chat group and waiting. There were more opponents, games started faster, and unfamiliar decks and strange positions appeared all the time.

As the game count grew, the players grew stronger together. Ideas once shared within a small group were quickly tested again by a much larger player pool. A strategy I thought was mature could meet a stronger opponent and be sent straight back to training. My average score still rose, stalled, then rose again. I used to advance mostly by making my own mistakes. Now the constantly evolving understanding of Agricola players around the world pushed me along as well.

Incidentally, the idea that every old game must slowly lose its players does not fit Agricola at all. On the day I begin Open Agricola, it remains one of BGA’s most popular heavy strategy games. More games mean more strange combinations and rules disputes, and even expert players still run into unfamiliar situations. I have kept playing all these years, and there is still more to learn.

From User to Developer

Several years ago, when the E deck was being brought to BGA, a group of Chinese players volunteered to join Agricola’s development team, and I was one of them. From September 2023 to June 2024, I made 105 commits during an intense stretch of development. At first, the work mainly involved bringing a batch of E-deck cards into the game. It quickly turned into fixing combinations, covering edge cases found in real matches, and maintaining messy logic coupled together in several places. Implementing one card feels satisfying. Maintaining dozens of cards that can all affect one another brings a very different kind of pain. This was also my first encounter with the legendary “best language”: PHP. There were no AI agents to help at the time, so I had to grit my teeth, read the code piece by piece, and work through each implementation step by step. Pain level: x2.

Because I was already a programmer, I skipped the low-hanging fruit of simple cards from the beginning and searched the spreadsheet for complex cards that had not yet been implemented. As luck would have it, the second card I chose was Hammer Crusher, the card from the opening. Pain level: x3.

Hammer Crusher Took More Than One Pass

Now back to the card from the opening. Hammer Crusher is the card I remember best. At the time, I also thought it did nothing more than insert one small action before renovation, something I could surely finish in half a day. Then the game slapped me down again.

The real trouble lies in these seven questions:

  1. Does “before renovation” mean before checking whether renovation is possible, or after the player has chosen to renovate but before paying the cost?
  2. If the player cannot initially renovate to stone, but the 2 clay and 1 reed granted by the card make it possible, should the system first allow an action that currently appears impossible?
  3. What if the granted resources are not enough by themselves, but become enough when combined with effects from other cards? How can the system know that in advance?
  4. Once the effect begins, how does the system ensure that the player must renovate to stone rather than switch to clay?
  5. What happens if the player spends the required resources during the extra room build and invalidates the prerequisite for renovating to stone?
  6. If the extra room build triggers another player’s card, what happens when the flow fails to switch to the correct acting player?
  7. After control switches back, what happens if the renovation prerequisite is no longer satisfied?

It was first implemented in March 2023, temporarily disabled over boundary problems that September, and restored after its combination logic was fixed. It was disabled again in January 2024, then returned after another fix in February. The card had one sentence on it, yet I spent almost a year returning to it. The text did not change. It simply encountered more combinations, and the holes I had missed kept showing up.

Some of the blame is mine, and I have no right to dump all of it on the old code. When I built the card, I just wanted players to use it as soon as possible. Adding one special case really was the easiest choice in the moment. The trouble began when the next card did the same thing. Every later change to renovation or room building meant digging through those branches again and hoping I had not missed one.

BGA’s Answers and Its Baggage

BGA has run an enormous number of real games, and that is valuable. Whenever players encounter something the rulebook never fully explained, the program still has to answer: when does a card trigger, how do payment options combine, what happens after a cancellation, and which card resolves first? Its interface answered another practical question for me too: what does the player need to see and choose at each step?

The code is another matter. A football club that has played for years will inevitably have temporary arrangements left by several managers on its tactics board. They may have won matches at the time, but a new club cannot simply copy them. BGA’s code felt much the same to me: many choices have a history and solved real problems, but I would not carry them unchanged into Open Agricola.

Five Code Smells in BGA

While deciding the direction of Open Agricola, I went through BGA’s implementation again. These five things bothered me most:

  1. Changing one card often means editing several files. Its trigger, choice, resolution, and cleanup may all live in different places. After changing one piece of the rule, the developer has to find the rest and make sure they still agree.
  2. Shared code contains too many checks for specific cards. Renovation knows about one card, room building knows about another, and each gets its own branch. Once enough exceptions accumulate, who dares touch the shared flow?
  3. There is plenty of global state, but no consistent way to represent a card’s own state. Complex cards need to preserve choices and progress across several steps. Where that data belongs, what it should be called, and when it should be cleared are not clearly defined.
  4. Card resolution order has to be specified by hand. When discounts, alternative payments, and modifiers collide, the developer writes the partial order between cards manually. Adding a card often means adding its relationships with old cards too. Miss one, reverse one, or create a conflict, and resolution happens in the wrong order.
  5. Triggers after cooking are particularly awkward. The cooking and exchange flow has no stable place for them. With D056, the implementation cannot grant the extra food when cooking is detected. It first records the reward in card state, then waits for a general response window to grant it later. One event becomes “record, wait, grant,” and there was even a bug where the card listened before it had been played.

I eventually started calling this bill the expansion tax. A new card pays for its own implementation and for old exceptions left in shared flows. The larger the card pool becomes, the harder the bill is to calculate. Eventually, adding one card is no longer a one-file job.

Afterword

After that detour, I am back at the opening question: why start Open Agricola? The most immediate reason is that I want to try building a cleaner architecture from scratch, so future cards do not keep paying this expansion tax. The other reason is simple. I want to use a project I know well, and one difficult enough to be interesting, to find out how far Vibe Coding can actually carry development.

There is another practical reason: contributing is not the same as owning. BGA’s Agricola implementation is constrained by the platform and its licenses. The code cannot be public, and we do not decide which expansions may be added or when work begins. That is not BGA’s fault; licensing and scheduling are normal concerns for a commercial platform. From my side, though, I still want a public implementation that anyone can read and verify, with an expansion roadmap I can choose for myself.

BTW, Open Agricola itself still has not received formal authorization. I have sent Uwe Rosenberg a private message, but he has not replied.

Writing this brought me back to the action efficiency I wrote about years ago. In Agricola, a strong hand can still produce a low score. Code works the same way: finishing one card in half a day does not mean the project is moving quickly. Special cases pushed into shared flows to save time will show up again during the next change.

I do not know how far Open Agricola will go. But if I really want to fit more cards and expansions into it, the code cannot keep moving forward on “just get this card working first.” Otherwise, the year I spent wrestling with Hammer Crusher will simply happen again.
